v. AI/ML will be applied to large -scale data analysis for better understanding of 
polar and ocean processes. The National Polar Data C entre will be upgraded 
with advanced curation, real-time processing, and AI-driven analytics. 
vi. An operational sea ice advisory system will be developed to support expeditions 
and research activities in polar regions. 
vii. PACER will augment scientific infrastruc ture with automation and real -time 
processing, replace the Maitri station, acquire a Polar Research Vessel, and 
establish a Polar & Ocean Museum. Global collaborations and participation in 
international forums shall also be strengthened. 
 
PRITHVI-SAGE 
 
i. Earthquake Studies 
 
Under SAGE it is planned to modernize and densify the National 
Seismological Network with real -time accelerographs. It is aimed to improve 
earthquake source understanding for disaster preparedness, strengthen hazard 
maps for resilient i nfrastructure and urban planning, and enhance public 
awareness through education initiatives. 
 
ii. Borehole Drilling 
 
The program will expand beyond Koyna to study geohazards, geo -resources, 
and climate change. It will map stress and strain across regions usin g borehole

OBS instruments, improve geodynamic modelling, integrate multidisciplinary 

25

i. Specific Calls in Earth Sciences

Maitri-II 
 
3.11 The Committee enquired whether NCPOR proposed to establish Maitri-II, a 
new research station in Antarctica, and sought details regarding the present status of 
the proposal, the reasons necessitating its establishment, and the expected timeline for 
the station to become operational.The Ministry submitted that NCPOR proposed the 
establishment of Maitri -II in Antarctica as a replacement for the existing Maitri 
Research Station. The present Maitri station, commissioned in 1989, has exceeded its 
designed operational life and is experiencing structural deterioration as w ell as 
limitations in waste -management and environmental compliance systems. The 
Ministry stated that, in view of safety considerations, operational sustainability, and 
evolving environmental norms under the Antarctic Treaty System, the establishment 
of a modern replacement station has become necessary to ensure the continuity of 
India‘s year-round scientific presence in Antarctica. 
 
3.12 The Ministry further submitted that Maitri -II is envisaged as a state -of-the-art, 
year-round, multidisciplinary research  facility equipped with modern laboratories, 
enhanced atmospheric, geological and geophysical observation systems, and 
advanced waste -management and treatment facilities in accordance with 
environmental regulations under the Antarctic Treaty. The proposed station will also 
have e1xpanded accommodation capacity to support a larger number of scientists and 
technical personnel, thereby strengthening India‘s research capabilities and sustained 
presence in Antarctica. 
 
3.13   The Ministry stated that the Department of Expenditure (DoE) has accorded in-
principle approval for Project Maitri-II at an estimated cost of ₹2,150 crore. Owing to 
the limited construction window during Antarctic summer seasons and the 

28 
 
requirement of obtaining a Comprehensive Environmental Evaluation (CEE) under 
the Antarctic Treaty framework, the project is planned to be implemented over six 
years (2026 –27 to 2031 –32). At present, a Detailed Project Proposal is being 
prepared for submission to the Public Investment Board for consideration i n 
accordance with existing guidelines. The architectural and design consultant for the 
project has already been identified through a global design competition.

Desalination plants in Lakshadweep  
 
3.16 The Committee enquired about the number of desalination plants currently 
operational in Lakshadweep and asked whether it is a fact that these plants are 
operated using diesel generator sets.The Ministry submitted that NIOT established a 
Low Temperature Thermal  Desalination (LTTD) plant at Kavaratti in 2005 with a 
freshwater generation capacity of one lakh litres per day. Subsequently, two LTTD 
plants, each with a capacity of one lakh litres per day, were established at Agatti and 
Minicoy in 2011. The Ministry f urther submitted that five additional LTTD plants, 
each with a capacity of 1.5 lakh litres per day, were established at Kalpeni and Amini 
(2022), Kadamat (2023), and Kiltan and Chetlat (2024). These LTTD desalination  
plants utilise electricity supplied thr ough diesel generator sets, which provide power 
for the entire island system. 
 
3.17 The Committee recommends developing advanced indigenous technologies 
for desalination plants that run on non -renewable energy. Deployed in coastal 
areas and cities, these plants would augment fresh water supplies to help address 
existing shortages. 
3.18 The Committee acknowledges the significant role played by the PRITHVI 
(Prithvi Vigyan) Scheme  in strengthening India‟s capabilities in Earth System 
Sciences through its integrated focus on atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, 
geosciences and societal applications. The Committee notes that several Low-
Temperature Thermal Desalination (LTTD) plants  have been established in the 
Lakshadweep islands under the PRITHVI-OSMART initiative to address the 
critical issue of potable water availability for island communities. While the 
Committee recognizes the importance of these plants in ensuring sustainable 
drinking water supply, it also notes that the desalination plants currently 
operate using electricity generated through diesel generator sets, which power 
the island systems. Considering the environmental sensitivity of island 
ecosystems and the broader national  commitment towards clean and renewable 
energy, the Committee is of the view that reliance on diesel -based power sources 

30 
 
should be progressively reduced. The Committee therefore recommends the 
Ministry to explore the feasibility of making t hese desalinatio n plants eco-
friendly by using sustainable power sources such as solar energy, Ocean 
Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), or other suitable renewable energy 
technologies.  
3.19 The Committee also examined the proposal for establishing Maitri-II, a 
new research station in Antarctica to replace the existing Maitri station, which 
was commissioned in 1989 and has now exceeded its designed operational life. 
The Committee notes the Ministry‟s submission that the present station is facing 
structural deterioration and  limitations in waste -management and 
environmental compliance systems, making the establishment of a modern 
replacement station necessary to ensure safety, operational sustainability, and 
India‟s continued year -round scientific presence in Antarctica in ac cordance 
with evolving environmental norms under the Antarctic Treaty System.  
However, the Committee notes that the architectural and design consultant for 
the Maitri-II project has been selected through a global design competition and 
that the winning con sortium comprises Ramboll Deutschland GmbH and 
bofArchitekten, Germany. In this regard, the Committee recalls that India‟s 
first Antarctic research station, Dakshin Gangotri, was constructed with the 
involvement of the Indian Army, demonstrating indigenous  capability in 
undertaking complex operations in extreme polar conditions. The Committee is 
therefore of the view that greater consideration could have been given to Indian 
firms with relevant engineering and infrastructure expertise in cold -weather 
construction technologies. Such an approach could have contributed to cost 
savings while also providing impetus to the objectives of Make in India  and 
promoting greater self-reliance in specialized polar infrastructure development. 
The Committee recommends that, in future projects of this nature, the Ministry 
explore ways to ensure greater participation of Indian companies, either 

31 
 
independently or through collaborations, so that domestic capabilities in polar 
infrastructure and extreme-environment engineering are further strengthened. 
DEEP OCEAN MISSION 
 
3.20 As a Maritime nation with a coastline of about 11,098 km and around 30% of 
the country's population living in coastal areas, oceans play an important role in the 
Indian economy. The Government of India‘s Vision of New India by 2030, 
enunciated in February 2019, highlighted the Blue Economy as one of the ten core 
dimensions of growth. With a view to exploring the deep ocean for resources, 
developing deep -sea technologies for sustai nable use of ocean resources, and 
improving our understanding of the deep sea, the Government of India launched the 
―Deep Ocean Mission‖ at an estimated cost of Rs. 4077.0 crores for a period of 5 
years. This mission mode project will support various prior ity areas illustrated in the 
Blue Economy policy document of the Government of India. Ministry of Earth 
Sciences (MoES) is the nodal implementing Ministry for this multi-ministerial, multi-
institutional mission.   
3.21 The Deep Ocean Mission encompasses six verticals, which are: 
 
a. Development of Technologies for Deep-sea mining, Human Submersible, and 
underwater robotics. 
b. Development of Ocean Climate Change Advisory Services. 
c. Technological Innovations for exploration and conservation of deep -sea 
biodiversity. 
d. Deep-ocean survey and exploration. 
e. Energy and fresh water from the ocean. 
f. Establishment of Advanced Marine Station for Ocean Biology.  
 
3.22 The significant tangible scientific outcomes achieved under the Deep Ocean 
Mission (DOM) to date are as follows:  
 The design and system engineering of India‘s flagship human submersible 
MATSYA-6000, capable of reaching a depth of 6000 meters with three 
aquanauts, has been completed.  Its subsystems have been realized, and the wet 
tests were successfully conducted at L&T Harbour in Katupalli, near Chennai, in 
January-February 2025. Scientists at the National Institute of Ocean Technology 
(NIOT), Chennai, entrusted with the development of MATSYA -6000, have 
gained pilot experience with the French submersible NAUTILE in August 2025.  

32 
 
 The prediction of 100 -year return extreme sea level along the coas ts of the 
Indian subcontinent has been completed and associated coastal vulnerability 
maps have been prepared. To strengthen ocean observation, the Indian National 
Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad, has successfully 
completed 11 gli der missions along predetermined transects in the Arabian Sea 
(67°E) and the Bay of Bengal (89°E), and deployed 60 directional Wave Spectra 
Barometric Drifters and 92 physical and biogeochemical Argo floats in the 
Indian Ocean. 
 Nearly 1,845 deep -sea microb es have been isolated from water and sediment 
samples of the Indian EEZ, and rare deep -sea microbes previously not reported 
from the Indian Ocean have been discovered. A total of 25 seamounts 
(biodiversity hotspots) are surveyed by the Centre for Marine Li ving Resources 
and Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi, in the Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar 
regions, documenting 195 deep-sea species (including 39 potential new taxa). 
 Two active and two inactive hydrothermal vents have been identified on the 
Indian Ocean seafloor through AUV (Autonomous Underwater Vehicle) surveys 
by the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (NCPOR), Goa, indicating 
potential locations of sulphide minerals. The contract for the construction of an 
all-weather multi-purpose research vessel was awarded to GRSE, Kolkata, under 
the Ministry of Defence in 2024.  
 A total of 142 collaborative research projects have been sanctioned under the 
Mission, resulting in capacity building across nearly 70 national government and 
private institutions in the fields of ocean sciences and engineering.  
 
3.23 The major milestone initiatives proposed for the scheme in the future are as 
follows:  
 Conducting 500 -meter shallow water demonstration trials and 6000 -meter 
exploratory trials of India‘s flagship MATSYA-6000.   
 Development of future climate projections for sea -level rise, cyclones, and 
waves, a Web-GIS map of multi-hazard coastal vulnerability.  
 Survey and mapping of ten additional seamounts for biodiversity assessment, 
followed by isolation, characterisat ion, identification, and inventorisation of 
deep-sea biodiversity samples. Development of the Deep Sea Sampler and its 
deployment for studies on deep -sea microbes. Establishment of a referral facility 
for deep-ocean biodiversity specimens‘ studies.  
 Continuation of the survey of an additional five hydrothermal sites for locating 
potential multi-metal deposits and completion and acquisition of the Ministry‘s 
all-weather multi-purpose research vessel. 

33 
 
 Studies on the generation of hybrid renewable energy (floa ting solar+wind) and 
freshwater from deep -water, towards the demonstration of a suitable pilot -scale 
plant in the Lakshadweep Islands.  
 Construction of Advanced Marine Station for Ocean Biology in Nemelli, 
Chennai, and continuation of expansion of capacity  building programs, 
translational and industry -oriented research programs, and international 
cooperation in marine sciences.

3.30  The Committee notes that the Deep Ocean Mission , launched in 2021 ,

ocean technologies. While the Committ ee acknowledges the efforts made by the 
Ministry and its institutions in progressing with certain components of the

not appear commensurate with the objectives and timelines originally envisaged. 
The Committee further notes that key components of the Mission, including the

the Committee recommends that the Ministry establish clearly defined and

MISSION MAUSAM 
3.31    Mission Mausam (MM) was approved by the Union Cabinet in September 
2024. The scheme adopts a multi -faceted, transformative approach to make Bharat a 
―Weather-ready and Climate -smart‖ nation by developing cutting -edge weather 
surveillance technologies; implementing high -resolution atmospheric observations; 
deploying next -generation radars, wind profilers, satellites, and advanced HPC 
systems; enhancing understanding of weather and climate processes; developing 
advanced Earth system models and AI/ML -based methods; creating weather 
management technologies and protocols; establishing state-of-the-art decision support 
and last -mile dissemination systems; and strengthening capacity building and 
research collaborations. 
3.32  To achieve this, nine inter -related verticals have been established under the 
program, each with specific objectives and deliverables. 
 
(i) OBSERVEAll: Comprehensive weather monitoring and data collection for 
nowcasting, data assimilation, model development and decision support. All MoES 
institutions.  
(ii) DEVELOP: Development of next -generation Earth System Models (ESM) f or 
improved forecasts. 
(iii) IMPACT: Focus on high-impact weather forecasting and early warning systems and 
research to operations. 
(iv) FRONTIER: Establishment of advanced technologies for weather observation and 
measurement. 
(v) ATCOMP: Air quality monitoring and decis ion support systems for pollution 
management. 
(vi) DECIDE: Development of decision support systems for various service sectors. 
(vii) WeatherMOD: Protocols for weather modification strategies, including rain 
enhancement, hail/fog suppression 
(viii) LEAD (Leading Effort for Advanced Decisions): Capacity building and innovation 
in weather information dissemination. 
(ix) NEAT (National Enterprise for Atmospheric Technology): Establishment of a unified 
observational approach through public-private partnerships. 
 
3.33 Tangible scientific outcomes achieved under the scheme so far are as follows: 
 
 Nationwide strengthening of observational infrastructure with commissioning of C -
Band DWRs at Raipur and Mangaluru and X -Band dual -polarised DWR at 
Mahabaleshwar, improving real-time monitoring and nowcasting. 
 Indigenous 3D -printed AWS units developed by IITM to cost -effectively densify 
observation networks and enable hyper-local forecasting. 
 Bharat Forecast System (6 km) operationalised to deliver precise localized forecasts 
of extreme weather, supporting agriculture, disaster management, and public safety. 
 Mithuna Forecast System (12 km) operationalised as a coupled land –ocean–
atmosphere–sea-ice model, reducing biases and improving medium-range forecasts. 
 AI-based forecast tools integrat ed with numerical models for automated weather 
interpretation, bias correction, downscaling, and nowcasting. 

38 
 
 IITM-ESMv3 global Earth System Model developed, contributing to CMIP and IPCC 
AR7, with high-resolution climate projections for impact assessment. 
 Severe weather forecast accuracy improved by ~40%, with and better cyclone track 
and intensity guidance. 
 Block-Wise Rainfall Monitoring Scheme (BRMS) operationalised to provide high -
resolution real-time rainfall data at block level. 
 ―Mausamgram‖ platform launched for village and PIN-code level hyperlocal forecasts 
with hourly updates. 
 Indigenous Multi -Hazard Early Warning DSS developed by IMD and awarded the 
National Award for e-Governance 2025. 
 Heat Action Plans developed with NDMA and states to mitigate i mpacts of extreme 
heat events. 
 Aviation weather safety enhanced through expanded RVR and DCWIS deployment at 
airports. 
 Urban weather monitoring networks established, including the Delhi Urban Mesonet, 
with similar testbeds in Chennai and Visakhapatnam. 
 Cloud seeding protocols formulated and scientific understanding of aerosol -cloud-
precipitation processes strengthened through CAIPEEX. 
 Strengthened national severe weather monitoring through deployment of advanced 
Doppler Weather Radar systems under Mission Mausam. 
 Establishment of a nationwide Lightning Location Network under Mission Mausam, 
significantly strengthening lightning detection, early warning, and public alert 
services across India through real -time monitoring, research integration, and 
dissemination support to IMD and State Governments.

INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TROPICAL METEOROLOGY (IITM), PUNE 
4.15 IITM is a premier research Institute and functions as a national centre for basic 
and applied research in Atmosphere, Ocean, Climate System and climate change 
science required for improvement of weather and climate f orecasts of the tropics in 
general with special reference to monsoon meteorology over India and 
neighbourhood. The objectiv es of IITM are to generate  scientific knowledge and to 
promote and guide research in the field of meteorology and atmospheric sciences that 
has potential application in various fields such as agriculture, economics, health,

(CCCR). An allocation of ₹103 crore has been made for IITM in the Budget

4.16 The Committee enquired whether IITM has undertaken any research under 
Mission Mausam to study the meteorological factors contributing to severe air 
pollution in Delhi during the winter months, and the details and key findings of such 
studies. In response, the Ministry stated that IITM has undertaken several initiatives 
under Mission Mausam to investigate Delhi‘s air pollution. The findings have been 
published in several peer -reviewed research papers. The studies indicate that very 
stable meteorological conditions during winter weaken atmo spheric ventilation, 
leading to the trapping of pollutants near the surface and a rapid escalation of air 
pollution to severe levels. Aerosol –radiation feedback further aggravates these 
conditions and intensifies pollution. Severe to very severe air pollut ion episodes are 
generally associated with such stable meteorological regimes. 
4.17 The Ministry further informed that another study examined the shift in the 
timing of stubble burning, which has shortened the interval between crop harvesting 
and sowing. T his shift increasingly overlaps with periods of stable synoptic -scale 

51 
 
atmospheric conditi ons. When combined with aerosol -radiative feedback, these 
factors suppress atmospheric ventilation and reduce boundary layer height, resulting 
in greater accumulation of PM2.5. Consequently, the frequency of severe air pollution 
episodes has nearly tripled, with around 40 per cent of the  increase attributed to 
aerosol-radiative feedback mechanisms. 
4.18 The Committee recognizes the significant role played by the Indian 
Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, as a premier national research 
institution engaged in advanced studies on the atmosphere, ocean and climate 
systems, particularly in improvin g weather and climate forecasts for the tropics 
and understanding the dynamics of the monsoon over India.  The Committee 
notes the research undertaken by IITM under Mission Mausam to examine the 
meteorological factors contributing to severe air pollution in  Delhi during the 
winter months. In view of the continuing severity of air pollution in Delhi and 
the National Capital Region, the Committee is of the opinion that scientific 
research findings such as those generated by IITM are extremely valuable for 
informed policy -making and mitigation planning . The Committee therefore 
recommends that the research findings and analytical insights generated by 
IITM should be shared regularly with relevant regulatory and policy -making 
bodies, including the Central Pollutio n Control Board (CPCB), Delhi Pollution 
Control Committee (DPCC), and the Commission for Air Quality Management 
(CAQM), as well as other concerned agencies.

4.21 The Committee inquired whether NCMRWF is undertaking any research or 
model development to improve the prediction of cloudburst events, particularly in 
vulnerable regions such as the Himalayas. The Committee also sought details 
regarding the dynamic models being used, the improvements achieved in forecast 
skill, and their application in early warning and disaster management.The Ministry 
submitted that NCMRWF is actively engaged in research related to cloudburst 
prediction, especially thro ugh the use of high -resolution numerical modelling for 
Himalayan weather events. In this context, NCMRWF has developed a High-
Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR)  forecasting system designed for short -range 
prediction of short-lived and rapidly evolving high-impact weather systems. 
4.22 The Ministry informed that the system is based on the Advanced Research 
Weather Research and Forecasting (ARW) dynamic core , coupled with the Grid-
point Statistical Interpolation (GSI)  data assimilation framework. It operates at 
convection-permitting resolutions of 5 km and 1km , with hourly data assimilation of 
conventional observations, satellite radiances, and Doppler Weather Radar data using 
a three-dimensional variational (3DVAR)  assimilation approach and hourly update 
cycles to improve model initial conditions. The 5 km domain covers the entire Indian 
region, while the 1 km domain  focuses on the north -western Himalayan region to 
better capture complex terrain and localized convec tive processes. The Ministry 
further stated that these models are currently under testing, and the generated data is 
regularly shared with the IMD for operational use by forecasters. 
4.23 It was further informed that recent upgrades include the introductio n of a 2 km 
HRRR domain covering the whole of India and neighbouring countries. Case studies 

53 
 
of intense rainfall events over the Himalayas indicate that the high -resolution HRRR 
system provides significant improvements in the spatial positioning and intens ity of 
heavy rainfall compared to the existing 5 km domain, thereby demonstrating better 
forecasting skill than coarser -resolution models. Objective verification using 
statistical scores and spatial verification techniques has also shown improved 
representation of rainfall patterns, highlighting the importance of higher resolution 
and frequent data assimilation. 
4.24 The Ministry added that the HRRR modelling system generates 18-hour 
forecasts every hour using updated initial conditions, making it highly suitable for 
nowcasting applications. Ongoing research efforts are focused on assimilating radar 
observations over the Himalayan region into the HRRR system, which is expected to 
further enhance the prediction capability for cloudburst events in the region. 
4.25   The Committee notes the important role played by the National Centre for 
Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida , in developing and 
operating advanced numerical weather prediction models for s hort-range, 
medium-range, extended-range and seasonal forecasts, which are widely used by 
various user agencies including the India Meteorological Department. The 
Committee appreciates the development of the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh 
(HRRR) forecasting  system, which is designed for short -range prediction of 
rapidly evolving weather systems, particularly in complex terrains such as the 
Himalayan region. Considering the increasing occurrence of extreme rainfall 
and cloudburst events in the Himalayan regio n and the serious damage caused 
by such incidents in recent years, the Committee is of the view that 
strengthening scientific capabilities for their prediction and early warning is of 
critical importance. The Committee , therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
provide sustained support to NCMRWF for furth er development and 
operationalization of high -resolution modelling systems such as HRRR, 
including enhanced assimilation of radar and satellite observations over 
mountainous regions. The Committee further reco mmends that efforts be made 
to integrate the outputs of these advanced models with early warning 

54 
 
dissemination systems so that actionable and timely alerts can be provided to 
disaster management authorities and vulnerable communities.

4.29 The Committee notes that the National Centre for Seismology (NCS), 
Delhi, established in 2015, plays a critical role in monitoring seismic activity 
across the country, maintaining the National Seismological Network, conducting 
earthquake hazard assessments, and supporting research in seismology, 
earthquake precursor studies, and deep boreh ole investigations. However , the 
Committee is constrained to note that even after nearly a decade of its  
establishment, the NCS does not have any sanctioned posts of its own and 
continues to function with personnel drawn on a loan basis from the Ministry o f 
Earth Sciences (MoES) and the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The 
Committee finds it difficult to understand why a specialised national institution 
entrusted with such crucial responsibilities is still operating without a dedicated 
cadre of scient ific, technical, and administrative staff.While noting the 
Ministry‟s submission that proposals for the creation of dedicated posts for NCS 
have been submitted under the PRITHVI scheme, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the matter be pursued on priori ty and that the approval 
process be expedited.  
INDIAN NATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN INFORMATION SYSTEM 
(INCOIS), HYDERABAD 
4.30 The mission of INCOIS is to provide ocean information and advisory services 
to the society, industry, government and scientific com munity through sustained 
ocean observations and constant improvements through systematic and focused 
research. The objective is to provide coastal and ocean advisory services, potential 
fishing zone advisory service (PFZ), ocean state forecast, national ts unami early 
warning etc. The Tsunami and Storm Surge Early Warning System started in October, 
2007 at INCOIS provides information on ocean waves swell etc. which are quite 
valuable for Navy, Coast Guards, Merchant Ships. Similarly Fishing Zone Advisories 
are utilized by a large number offishermen.An allocation of  ₹30 crore has been made 
for INCOIS in the Budget Estimates (BE) for 2026–27. 

56 
 
Ocean observation network 
 
4.31 The Committee enquired whether INCOIS is considering any steps to 
strengthen the ocean observational network in the medium and long term.The 
Ministry submitted that under the PRITHVI Scheme, it is planned to install GNSS 
systems co -located with tide gauges  at 50 locations, of which installations at 15 
locations have already been completed. The remaining installations will be carried 
out subject to the availability of funds.  The Ministry further submitted that under the 
Deep Ocean Mission, INCOIS is operatin g deep -sea gliders along two sustained 
transects—one in the Arabian Sea (along 67°E) and the other in the Bay of Bengal 
(along 89°E). These observations, which measure physical and biogeochemical 
parameters, will be continued on a long-term basis. In addition, the Ministry informed 
that a sub -sea cabled observatory is being established off the Andaman and Nicobar 
Islands to enable long -term measurements of bottom pressure and seismic activity, 
thereby strengthening the tsunami early warning system. The Ministry also stated that 
under Mission Mausam, INCOIS plans to establish shipboard automated aerological 
observatories to better understand air –sea interaction processes for weather studies.  
Further, it added that an observational test -bed with automated met -ocean 
observations is being planned for the development, improvement, and validation of 
ocean models, as well as for calibration and validation of satellite data. 
 
Wave Monitoring Along Nearshore (WAMAN) project 
 
4.32 The Committee sought information on the objectives and scope of the Wave 
Monitoring Along Nearshore (W AMAN) project being implemented by INCOIS, the 
progress achieved so far, the outcomes of the project, its contribution to ocean 
observation, forecasting and disaster management, and whether the project covers the 
entire coastline and if there are plans for expansion.  The Ministry responded stating 
that theW AMAN projectis a dedicated initiative aimed at establishing a sustained, 
real-time coastal wave observation network in nearshore regions around India. It 
stated that the principal objectives of the project are to fill long -standing 
observational gaps in nearshore wave measurements, support and improve 
operational wave forecasting and early warning services, and generate long -term 
wave datasets for scientific research, coastal zone management and maritime safety. 
The Ministry further submitted that the project also adopts a community-participatory 
model, wherein local stakeholders assist in the deployment, maintenance and 
protection of instruments, thereby ensuring the sustainability of the network.  The 
Ministry informed that the W AMAN network consi sts of wave buoys deployed at 

57 
 
strategic locations along the Indian coastline and island regions, which provide real -
time measurements of wave height, period and direction. Over the past 17 years, 
INCOIS has established and operated a network of about 16 –17 nearshore buoys, 
generating one of the most continuous and reliable coastal wave observation datasets 
in the region. 
 
4.33 With regard to progress and outcomes, the Ministry stated that continuous real-
time observations from the W AMAN network now support operational ocean state 
forecasts, including warnings for high waves, swell events and hazardous sea 
conditions. The assimilation and validation of these observations have improved the 
accuracy of wave models, thereby enhancing advisory services for fisher men, ports, 
coastal planners, offshore operators and disaster management authorities. It further 
submitted that the long-term data generated under the project has supported scientific 
research on ocean waves, improved understanding of swell propagation and  coastal 
wave climate, and contributed to scientific publications. The community -based 
maintenance model has also reduced vandalism and instrument downtime, and has 
been recognised as a good practice in the global ocean observing community. 
 
4.34 The Minis try added that W AMAN strengthens the national ocean observing 
system by providing essential nearshore wave measurements, which directly feed into 
operational forecasting systems and improve early warnings related to high waves, 
cyclones and swell surges, t hereby contributing to coastal disaster preparedness, 
maritime safety and risk reduction.  Regarding coastline coverage, the Ministry 
clarified that the WAMAN network currently covers key segments of the Indian 
coastline but does not yet provide uniform cov erage along the entire coast. The 
existing deployment strategy prioritises high-impact and data-sparse regions. 
 
4.35 On expansion, the Ministry stated that INCOIS is actively considering 
expansion of the nearshore wave buoy network, including increasing t he number of 
buoys along the Indian coast and integrating them with other emerging coastal 
observation technologies. It further submitted that there are plans to extend the 
W AMAN network across the entire Indian coastline through multilateral and bilateral 
collaborations, subject to the availability of resources, to further improve ocean 
forecasting capabilities. 
 
Shore Stations  
 

58 
 
4.36 The Committee enquired whether INCOIS is planning to set up shore stations 
along India‘s coastline, how these stations would strengthen the ocean observation 
system, and the proposed timeline for their establishment.The Ministry submitted that 
coastal regions in the country remain relatively under-observed, and there is a need to 
increase the number of observation platforms to collect physico -chemical, biological 
and fisheries-related data. It stated that the limited availability of coastal observations 
and the absence of data on several parameters currently constrain the accuracy of 
ocean information and advisory services.  The Ministry submitted that strengthening 
coastal observation is essential for upgrading present ocean advisory and forecast 
services, p articularly by incorporating user requirements and improving forecast 
accuracy through downscaled models capable of predicting conditions very close to 
the coast. It further noted that enhanced observations would also support the 
customization of ocean ser vices for offshore and coastal industries, in line with the 
emerging requirements of the Blue Economy. 
 
4.37 The Ministry further stated that regional coastal stations will play a critical role 
by enabling long -term observations at multiple spatial and tem poral scales. These 
stations will also serve as centres for model development and validation, particularly 
for implementing localized ocean models with improved accuracy. With regard to the 
proposed plan, the Ministry informed that INCOIS has proposed to e stablish five 
regional centres during the next five -year plan period, equipped with necessary 
laboratory facilities and infrastructure. The initiative aims at strengthening coastal 
data repositories, enabling timely analysis of field samples, supporting ca pacity 
building, and enhancing collaboration with academic institutions. The Ministry added 
that the establishment of these regional centres will support continuous improvement 
of ocean information and advisory services, sustain existing observation platfo rms, 
enhance coastal observation capabilities, and promote capacity building for future 
generations. 
4.38 The Committee recognizes the critical role played by the Indian National 
Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)  in providing ocean 
information and advisory services that support fisheries, maritime operations, 
coastal management and disaster preparedness. The Committee is of the view 
that a robust and comprehensive ocean observation network is essential for 
improving the accuracy and reliability of ocean forecasts, early warning systems 
and long -term marine research.The Committee notes that there remain long -

59 
 
standing observational gaps in nearshore wave measurements along several 
parts of the Indian coastline. In th is regard, the Wave Monitoring Along Near  
shore (WAMAN) project has played an important role in generating real -time 
coastal wave observations that support operational wave forecasting, early 
warning services, maritime safety and scientific research. Howev er, the 
Committee observes that the present WAMAN network covers only selected 
segments of the coastline. The Committee therefore recommends that the 
network of wave buoys under WAMAN be progressively expanded to cover the 
entire Indian coastline so that a  more comprehensive and reliable nearshore 
observation system can be established. 
4.39 The Committee also notes that coastal regions in the country remain 
relatively under -observed, with limited availability of physico -chemical, 
biological and fisheries -related data. The absence of observations for several 
parameters constrains the accuracy of ocean information and advisory services 
and limits the effectiveness of forecasting systems. In this context, the Committee 
emphasizes the importance of establishing regional shore stations equipped with 
appropriate laboratory and monitoring facilities to support long -term coastal 
observations, data analysis, model validation and capacity building.The 
Committee is of the view that strengthening coastal observation infr astructure 
through an expanded WAMAN network and the establishment of shore stations 
will significantly improve ocean forecasting capabilities and generate valuable 
long-term datasets. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry 
provide adequate f inancial support to INCOIS for strengthening the WAMAN 
network and for establishing the proposed regional shore stations in a time -
bound manner. 
CENTRE FOR MARINE LIVING RESOURCES AND ECOLOGY (CMLRE), 
KOCHI 

60 
 
4.40    CMLRE, an attached office of MoES at Kochi is entrusted with the mandate of 
implementing the Marine Living Resources Program of the Ministry and 
management of the Fishery Oceanographic Research Vessel, FORV SagarSampada. 
The major activities under th is program are charting of exploitable resources of the 
deep sea, promoting operational fishery oceanographic services, ecosystem 
monitoring &modelling, promoting, basic R&D on MLR and transfer of technology 
for societal development. The research vessel, F ORV SagarSampada, forms the 
backbone of MLR research surveys. 
 
Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel (FORV) Sagar Sampada 
4.41   The Committee enquired about the year of commissioning of FORV Sagar 
Sampada, the operational and maintenance challenges arising due to the ageing of the 
vessel, whether CMLRE requires a modern Fishery and Oceanographic Research 
Vessel with advanced facilities, and whether any proposal has been submitted for the 
acquisition of a new vessel and the present status of such prop osal. In response, t he 
Ministry submitted that the FORV Sagar Sampada was built and acquired from 
Denmark with financial assistance through a Danish soft loan and was delivered in 
Mumbai on 23 December 1984.Regarding the requirement for a new vessel, the 
Ministry stated that CMLRE requires a modern and advanced Fishery and 
Oceanographic Research Vessel to support its expanding field -based scientific 
observations in deep and distant waters. It submitted that the proposed vessel would 
support ecosystem monito ring, marine biodiversity and habitat assessment in deep 
waters (greater than 1000 metres up to the full ocean depth) and in areas beyond the 
Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), in line with the objectives of the Deep Ocean 
Mission, the PRITHVI Scheme and Mission Mausam.  
4.42   The Ministry further informed that the new vessel would be equipped with 
state-of-the-art facilities for fisheries and oceanographic research, including deep -sea 
profiling of water and sediment, deep -sea trawling operations beyond 1000 metres, 
acoustic and optical observation systems, and drop and towable camera systems for 
non-invasive monitoring and sampling. It also noted that the vessel would require 
advanced dynamic positioning systems, modern winches, and launch and recovery 
systems. With regard to operational challenges, the Ministry stated that FORV Sagar 
Sampada has completed about 41 years of service and has been the primary platform 
for fishery oceanographic studies in the country. It submitted that the ageing of the 
vessel has resulted in several operational limitations, including a reduction in cruising 
speed from 13 knots to about 7 –8 knots and a decline in endurance from 45 days to 
around 25 days, which restricts the ability to undertake long -duration deep -sea 

61 
 
research cruis es. The Ministry further informed that ageing hydraulic winches and 
reduced bollard pull have made deep -sea fishing operations difficult, while frequent 
engine and generator failures, drainage and evacuation system blockages, and hull 
thinning have signifi cantly affected operational efficiency. It also stated that the 
vessel‘s trawling speed has declined from the ideal 4 knots to around 2 –3 knots, 
affecting the reliability of fishery data due to variations in the escapement factor. 
Consequently, the number of days the vessel can be deployed for scientific work has 
been declining, while time spent in port, lay -up or dry -dock repairs has increased, 
leading to significantly higher operational costs. The Ministry added that with its 
current condition, the vessel  may remain operational for deep -sea surveys for only 
about seven more years. 
4.43  Regarding the proposal for replacement, the Ministry informed that a proposal 
for acquisition of one multidisciplinary oceanography research vessel and one fishery 
oceanography research vessel as replacements for the ageing FORV Sagar Sampada 
and ORV Sagar Kanya has been initiated by the National Centre for Polar and Ocean 
Research (NCPOR), Goa, under the Ministry. The Ministry submitted that a concept 
note was forwarded to the Department of Expenditure on 22 January 2025, and the 
proposal was subsequently examined. It stated that in -principle approval has been 
conveyed by the Department of Expenditure for the acquisition of the two vessels at 
an estimated cost of ₹1,990 cror e. The Ministry further informed that the Director of 
NCPOR has constituted a committee to review and update the scientific facilities to 
be installed onboard the proposed new vessels, and this process is currently 
underway. 
4.44  The Committee notes that the Fishery and Oceanographic Research 
Vessel(FORV) Sagar Sampada , which serves as the backbone of the Marine 
Living Resources programme  implemented by the Centre for Marine Living 
Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), was commissioned in 1984 and has been in 
service for more than four decades. The Committee is concerned that the ageing 
of the vessel has resulted in several operational limitation s and that, in its 
current condition, the vessel may remain operational for deep -sea surveys for 
only about seven more years.  In view of these limitations and considering the 
growing requirements of deep-sea research under programmes such as the Deep 
Ocean Mission and the PRITHVI Scheme, the Committee strongly feels that the 
country requires a modern and advanced Fishery and Oceanographic Research 

62 
 
Vessel capable of supporting expanded scientific observations in deep and 
distant waters. Given that FORV Sagar  Sampada is already nearing the end of 
its operational life, the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
necessary procedural formalities and take time -bound steps for the acquisition 
and construction of the new vessel. The Committee is of the view that the new 
Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel should be built and commissioned 
at the earliest, preferably within the next two to three years, so that India‟s 
marine research programmes are not adversely affected due to the declining 
operational capability of the existing vessel. 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR POLAR AND OCEAN RESEARCH (NCPOR) , 
GOA 
4.45 The mission of NCPOR is to plan, promote, co -ordinate and execute the entire 
gamut of polar science and logistic activities of the country in order to ensure a 
perceptible presence of India in Antarctica and Arctic and to uphold our strategic 
interests in the global framework of nations in the southern continent and the 
surrounding oceans. The Indian Antarctic and Arctic Scientific Expeditions are 
launched through and under the guidance of this organization .NCPOR uses its 
research vessel, ORV SagarKanya  for various oceanographic researches in the 
country.Thecentre is also responsible to conduct and coordinate marine scientific 
surveys in the Indian Ocean for assessment of non-living resources. An allocation of ₹ 
37 crore has been made for NCPOR in the Budget Estimates (BE) for 2026–27. 
 
India‟s engagement in the Arctic  
 
4.46   The Committee enquired about the nature and extent of India‘s engagement in 
the Arctic region so far and sought information on the medium - and long -term 
initiatives proposed by the  Ministry and NCPOR to strengthen India‘s presence and 
research activities in the Arctic.  In response, t he Ministry s ubmitted that India‘s 
engagement in the Arctic region is multi -faceted, encompassing policy initiatives, 
multilateral and bilateral cooperation, and sustained scientific research activities. 
India is an Observer State in the Arctic Council and participates in its meetings and 
various Working Groups. India is also a Council Member of the International Arctic 
Science Committee (IASC). In addition, India regularly participates in the Arctic 
Circle Assembly meetings and hosted the Arctic Circle India Forum 2025 in New 

63 
 
Delhi. India also participates in the Arctic Frontiers Conference, organised under 
Norway‘s leadership. These engagements reflect India‘s commitment to multilateral 
dialogue and cooperative governance in the Arctic region. 
 
4.47 The Ministry further submit ted that in view of the growing scientific, 
environmental, and strategic importance of the Arctic, India released its India‘s Arctic 
Policy 2022, which provides a framework for strengthening scientific capabilities, 
expanding research networks, promoting a cademic programmes, and building 
institutional capacity for Arctic research.  On the scientific front, NCPOR  has 
established and operates the research station ‗Himadri‘ which facilitates sustained 
scientific observations and long -term research in the Arctic . Since 2023, winter 
expeditions to Svalbard have been initiated, enabling year -round presence of Indian 
researchers in the region. Under a Pan -Arctic approach, scientific expeditions have 
also been undertaken to the Canadian Arctic, and Indian scientists have participated 
in Central Arctic cruise expeditions in collaboration with Norway. Further, a 
dedicated East Greenland Shelf expedition in the Denmark Strait was conducted in 
2025 to study Arctic Ocean climate variability. The Ministry noted a significan t 
increase in research proposals from Indian academic and research institutions for 
Arctic studies. 
 
4.48 Regarding future initiatives, the Ministry responded that in the medium term, 
MoES and NCPOR propose to strengthen scientific research in Svalbard and the open 
Arctic Ocean through national and collaborative international expeditions. Efforts are 
also being made to enhance bilateral and multilateral cooperation with Arctic and 
non-Arctic countries by sharing research infrastructure and jointly developin g 
cooperative research programmes aligned with international Arctic science priorities.  
In the long term, the Ministry stated that MoES/NCPOR envisages strengthening 
India‘s Arctic research infrastructure through the establishment of additional 
oceanographic and atmospheric observatories and deployment of autonomous 
observational platforms across the Arctic region, including the open ocean. Space -
based observations from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) are also 
planned to support sea -ice monito ring, environmental change detection, climate 
observations, and improved navigation safety in the Arctic. Additionally, the 
expansion of India‘s Arctic research activities is proposed through scientific studies 
onboard an Indian Polar Research Vessel. 
 
Dedicated Polar Research Vessel 
 

64 
 
4.49 The Committee enquired whether India requires a dedicated Polar Research 
Vessel (PRV) for research, logistics, and year-round operations in the Antarctic region 
and sought information on whether any proposal for commissioning such a vessel has 
been submitted by NCPOR along with the present status of the proposal.The Ministry 
stated that India requires a dedicated Polar Research Vessel (PRV) to support 
scientific research, logistics, and year -round operations in the Anta rctic region. It 
stated that the absence of a dedicated ice -class PRV has been identified as a major 
constraint in the effective implementation of scientific and operational activities 
under the Indian Antarctic Programme. At present, India depends on the annual 
chartering of foreign vessels for expedition , logistics and research support. This 
dependence results in recurring expenditure and uncertainties in vessel availability 
and scheduling, which can affect the planning and execution of Antarctic expeditions. 
The Ministry also noted that the lack of a dedicated PRV limits India‘s ability to 
expand Arctic research beyond Svalbard and access the wider Arctic Ocean, which is 
strategically significant.  The Ministry further submitted that NCPOR submitted a 
proposal for the acquisition of a Polar Research Vessel. In July 2025, the Department 
of Expenditure (DoE) accorded in -principle approval for the acquisition of a 
research-cum-supply vessel with ice -breaking capabilities at an estimated cost of 
₹2,329.40 crore. The proposed vessel is intended to support annual Indian Antarctic 
expeditions and enable year -round polar and oceanographic research activities.The 
Ministry stated that pre -investment activities, including concept design and 
preparation of technical and  scientific equipment specifications, have already been 
completed by a consultancy firm. A detailed Public Investment Board memorandum 
has also been submitted to the Department of Expenditure for consideration and 
approval. Considering the technical comple xities involved in designing and building 
an ice -class research vessel, the proposed timeline for delivery of the PRV is five 
years, spanning 2026–27 to 2030–31. 
4.50 The Committee takes note of India‟s growing engagement in the Arctic 
through scientific expeditions, international collaborations, and the operation of 
the Himadri research station in Svalbard. The Committee observes that polar 
research has acquired incre asing significance in recent years due to its direct 
relevance to global climate systems, ocean circulation, sea -level rise and their 
impact on weather patterns, including the Indian monsoon. The absence of a 
dedicated ice -class Polar Research Vessel has b een a major constraint in 
expanding India‟s polar research activities, particularly in the wider Arctic 

65 
 
Ocean. The Committee notes with satisfaction that in -principle approval has 
already been accorded by the Department of Expenditure for the acquisition o f 
a Polar Research Vessel with ice -breaking capabilities at an estimated cost of 
₹2,329.40 crore. In view of the strategic and scientific importance of this project, 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the remaining 
procedural formalities a nd ensure that adequate financial resources are made 
available so that the project progresses in a time-bound manner. The Committee 
further recommends that, wherever feasible, Indian shipbuilding firms should 
be actively involved in the construction of the  Polar Research Vessel. Such an 
approach would not only strengthen domestic shipbuilding capabilities but also 
contribute to the objectives of promoting indigenous manufacturing and 
technological self-reliance in specialised marine infrastructure. 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY (NIOT), CHENNAI 
4.51  NIOT, Chennai is an autonomous institute under the Ministry, started in 1993 as 
the technical arm with a view to develop reliable in digenous technology to solve 
various engineering problems associated with harnessing of non -living and living 
resources in the Indian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), which are about two -thirds 
of the land area of India. The major functions are development of technology related 
to the country‘s needs in the field of deep sea mining, desalination, ocean energy, 
marine instrumentation, materials development, oceanic data collecting devices and 
observation systems etc. in consonance with ocean policy and national priorities, 
Research and development of ocean related technology pr ojects sponsored by the 
industry and development of required technologies for the management of coastal 
zone and islands of the country . An allocation of ₹79 crore has been made for NIOT 
in the Budget Estimates (BE) for 2026–27.

percentage of its revenue derived from non -budgetary sources, and whether such 
revenue is credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. The Committee also enquired 
how the amount is uti lized if it is not credited to the Consolidated Fund.  In response,

the Ministry of Earth Sciences, receives income primarily from (i) Grants-in-aid from

4.54  Subsequently, the Committee sought details of the technologies transferred by 
NIOT during the period 2020 –2025 including the firms to which these technologies 
were transferred and the fees received from them. The Ministry furnished the relevant 
details which are presented in the Annexure. 
4.55 The Committee enquired whether, apart from the license fee, NIOT  receives 
any other types of payments or fees for technology transfers,  what is the typical 
duration of the license validity, and  whether any fee is charged for renewal after the 
license expires.  The Ministry stated that NIOT receives only a license fee for 
technology transfers and does not charge any other types of payments or fees. It 
stated that the typical duration of a technolo gy license is five years. The Ministry 
further submitted that the fee or amount to be charged for renewal of the license after 
expiry has not yet been fixed. 
4.56 The Committee sought information on how the license fee for technologies 
transferred by NIOT is determined, the criteria used in this process, whether the 
license fee is linked to market size, how the market size for such technologies is 
estimated, and whether the technology transfer process has been fully digitized.  The 
Ministry stated that the license fee is determined by a Technical Committee 

67 
 
comprising representatives from the National Research Development Corporation 
(NRDC) and the concerned technology developer. It submitted that the Committee 
considers several factors, including the cost in curred in the development of the 
product, while determining the license fee.  The Ministry further informed that, given 
the limited market size of underwater technologies, the license fee is generally fixed 
at a level intended to encourage commercialization , particularly by MSMEs, 
entrepreneurs and start -ups. It added that although market considerations are taken 
into account, underwater technologies typically have a limited market size.  The 
Ministry also stated that the technology transfer process at presen t has not yet been 
digitized end-to-end. 
4.57 The Committee asked whether there is any provision for third -party audit of 
the Transfer of Technology (ToT) process, from the stage of determination of license 
fee to the transfer of technology to the firm. Th e Ministry submitted that, at present, 
NIOT does not have any provision for third -party audit of the technology transfer 
process. 
4.58 The Committee notes that the National Institute of Ocean Technology 
(NIOT) has transferred around 40 technologies between  2020–26, generating a 
total revenue of ₹1.64 crore. The Committee expresses concern that these 
technologies are being transferred at  relatively low prices compared to their 
commercial potential. It is observed that private partners often earn significant 
profits from these technologies, while the originating public institutes receive 
only a marginal share of the value created. The Committee understands that 
there is no robust mechanism to verify whether the benefits of these low -cost 
technology transfers reach the intended target users, and that the fees for 
renewal of licenses after expiry remain undefined. In view of this, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry of Earth Sciences should adopt a more 
competitive, market -aligned pricing framework for technology transfer. 
Licensing fees should reflect the true commercial value, uniqueness, and societal 
impact of publicly funded technologies. The Committee further recommends the 
establishment of clear procedures and norms for technology valuation and 
licensing, with the National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and 
the technology developer jointly determining fees.  To ensure transparency, 

68 
 
accountability, and pro per utilization of publicly funded technologies, all 
technology transfer agreements should be subjected to periodic third -party 
audits, and the outcomes of such audits should govern future licensing and 
renewal terms.
