NATURAL RESOURCES DATA MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (NRDMS)
47.Natural Resource Data Management System (NRDMS) is a Multi – Institutional and multi disciplinary Science & Technology
 programme of DST to develop methodologyand techniques for operationalising the concept of local level planning.It provides for
 creation of a database on natural resources and construct a socio-economic profile on district and sub-district levels to meet the
 information needs of the local administration forimplementing integrated micro level  planning.  The Geographic Information
 System (GIS) technique is adopted for storage, retrieval, analysis of the data collected from different sources on natural resources
 and socio-economic pattern of the area under investigation to produce useful information that helps in decision making.  Several
 national R&D and academic institutions are being involved for evolving the Decision Support Systems (DSS) in areas like
 watershed development, energy management, infrastructure development and land-use planning, by extending financial support
 to short duration research projects in spatial data management technology with focus  on following areas:
GIS Data Bases Centres
            The programme Strengthened the existing centres by updating them with state-of-the-art technologies like integrated
 database design, spatial decision support system for the identified sectors etc.  Supported creation of new databases centres in
 Lucknow in UP and Jallpaiguri in West Bengal.
Software Development
            An interface between indigenously developed GIS package, GRAM++ and hydrological model Soil Water Assessment
 Tool (SWAT) has been tested for land management in selected Upper Gandheswari Watershed in Bankura and Rampatna
 Watershed in Kolar.
Landslide Studies
            Landslide hazard zonation mapping have been completed in parts of Chamoli and Pithoragarh District of Uttaranchal State
 using remote sensing and GIS techniques.
            The Committee has been informed that during the year the Department proposes to Create  new NRDMS Database Centres
 to have a better coverage of variation states such as Tamilnadu, Nagaland, Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal. Development and
 dissemination of spatial data management tools for integrated rural development planning, evolve R&D projects in the area of 
 software development and upgradation of GRAM ++ and GIS software.
48.       The Committee observes that even though the country has  made  technological advances there are frequent cases of
 landslides.  In order to prevent this, it is necessary to have a complete hazard zonation map clearly demarcating landslide prone
 areas similar to the  one for earth quake prone areas.       Besides GIS data received from GRAM ++ should be utilized for the
 agricultural development

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF)
53.         The  objectives of the project include setting up of major infrastructure facilities like super computer, front-end
 processors and communication network and the on-line linkages with IMD and other Agro-meteorological research centres,
 development of global and regional numerical weather prediction models for medium range weather forecasting, and  
 development of appropriate data assimilation techniques for preparing initial conditions for the model. Preparation of NWP
 model  output and dissemination of the same to IMD for preparation and issue of medium range weather forecasts (3 to 10 days
 in advance) and development, preparation and dissemination of Agro-meteorological operation advisories including advisories
 for contingency crop practices to the end users through the Agro-meteorological research centres to be designated as
 experimental Agro-meteorological field units (AMFUs). Besides the project seeks to Promote and undertake studies on region
 crop-weather relationship and impact of  weather and climate on pest and diseases.
 
54.       The Committee feels that the thrust of weather forecasting should be on its accuracy.  The Committee observes that
 Department should consider enhancing the spatial resolution, range and accuracy of forecasts and advisories by constantly
 improving forecast models with use of available satellite data and techniques.
GUJARAT EARTHQUAKE – MISSION INITIATIVES IN REBUILDING & REHABILITATION
55.       In the wake of disastrous damages by the earthquake in Gujarat on 26
th January, 2001 the Advanced Composites Mission
 of TIFAC has come forward to contribute to the national efforts of re-building and rehabilitation.  A wide array of innovative
 composite products suitable for low-cost building & construction sector and bio-medical appliances has been developed by the
 Advanced Composites Mission.  Jute-coir composite boards, rice husk particle boards, FRP toilet blocks, multipurpose FRP
 handcarts and composite artificial limbs etc. address the crucial need of the hour – post-disaster relief at the quickest possible
 time.  The TIFAC Rehab Project at Bhuj was now fully operational in terms of complete occupancy of 400 shelters (20’12’). 
 Besides, 128 community toilet units constructed by the Mission were also in service.
56.       The Committee appreciates the work being done by the Department for rebuilding and Rehabilitation of Quake victims in
 Gujarat.  However it feels that in view of the massive destruction that took place there as a result of  the quake Department should
 involve certain financial agencies like Housing Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO)/ National Housing Bank (NHB) etc.
 for providing low interest loans for rebuilding so that these missions are a success. Besides, effective coordination and
 management of relief measures was very necessary.
Besides, these products must be popularized   for use in building and other similar activities in other quake prone areas in India to
 prevent loss of life and property.
SURVEY OF INDIA
57.       Survey of India, a national surveying and mapping organization acts as adviser to the Government of India on all Survey
 matters viz. geodesy, photogrammetry, mapping and map reproduction.  The main functions and responsibilities are
 establishment and maintenance of geodetic plan and height control network in the country, gravity and geomagnetic surveys, tidal
 surveys including tide predictions etc. topographical control surveys and mapping,   production of geographical map and other
 special maps, spelling of geographical names, demarcation of external boundaries of Republic of India, their depiction on maps
 and advice on the demarcation of interstate boundaries.
It transpires that an allocation of Rs.17.75 crores made in B.E. for the year 2001-2002 was increased to Rs.21.80 crores in R.E.
 last year for Publication of Map/Charts etc., and Rs.21.60 crores allocated for the year 2002-2003 did not seem justified. To this,
 the Department justified. The Committee has been informed that the activities of the Survey of India  relate to Publication of
 Maps, Charts and Reports etc., were carried out throughout the year.  The B.E. 2001-2002 was Rs.22.60 crores and the allocation
 in R.E. was raised to Rs.26.65 crores, in anticipation of increased work orders from client Departments.  It was also explained
 that the anticipated increases in work orders had not materalised. 
58.       The Committee feels it is time that Survey of India thought  of diversifying its activities.  Apart from preparing and
 bringing out political & physical maps of the country, it should endeavour to bring out maps of tourist interest of National
 Highways, towns and cities to meet the local needs.

INDIA METROLOGICAL DEPARTMENT (IMD)
59.       IMD is engaged in forecasting of Storms, Cyclones and severe weather conditions and provide climatological statistics for
 operation and Planning in the field of Agriculture, Aviation, Water Conservation, Oceanography etc.; maintaining of Network of
 large number of observations for acquisition of surface and upper air weather data; issue of forecast and timely disaster warning
 of severe weather conditions/phenomena including tropical cyclones, monitoring of Seismic activities and to locate intensity and
 center of earthquakes to understand their processes and mechanism;  to carry out and promote research and development in
 Atmospheric and Meteorological Sciences;  imparting of Meteorological training to persons of developing countries under World
 Meteorological Organisation (WMO) programmes and to Departmental persons;  monitoring and Forecasting of Occurrence of
 Snow & Avalanche over Himalayan Mountainous region at 10 km resolution, Monitoring & Analysing the air pollutants in
 sample survey observations; monitoring of Ozone depletion.
            During the Year, of the  two Doppler Radars received, one has been installed at Chennai and other is likely to be installed
 and commissioned at Kolkata in  2002,  procurement of three Doppler Radars, High Wind Speed Recorders (HWSR), Digital
 Cyclone Warning Dissemination Systems (DCWDS) were being finalized under World Bank Assisted Project for Andhra
 Pradesh.  High Wind Speed Recorder (HWSR) have already been installed.
Action was in progress for upgradation of existing Earth Station for METSAT and one complete Receiver Earth Station for
 INSAT-3.  Establishment of Seismo  Observation at Sihor & Bhavanagar and digitization of seismic charts were in progress,
 three  Seismographs has been installed under Seismological Telemetry System.
60.       The Committee expresses its concern over delay in commissioning of Doppler Radars which are needed for accurate
 weather forecasting.  Besides, In India occurrence of cyclones is a regular feature every year, the Commissioning of Digital
 Cyclone Warning Dissemination System (DCWDS), should be given a priority. The Committee would appreciate if these could
 be installed before the beginning of Monsoon Season.

 Germany and Washington, USA where wide range of programmes were conducted with a view to intensify cooperation between
 the countries.

Tokyo, Japan
            The S&T wing in Japan collected, collated and transmitted important scientific developments and policy decisions in
 Japan to various Department/institutions in India.  It identified institutions undertaking advanced scientific research and conveyed
 information to relevant institutions in India with a view establish link for collaboration in advanced area of research.
             The wing facilitated signing of a MOU between IIT-Madras and the Nagoya University. The MOU proposes to promote
 exchange of students, professors, researchers, scientific materials and information as well as undertaking joint research activities.
Berlin, Germany
            In order to intensify joint research programs in the field of Biotechnology, India  and Germany signed a special
 arrangement of cooperation at Forschungszentrum, Juelich as a part of the overall Indo-German S&T cooperation arrangements. 
 They agreed for cooperation in the fields of functional genomics; drug/vaccine development; tissue and cell culture;
 bioinformatics; NMR spectroscopy and cancer & Tuberculosis research.
            The University of Freiburg organized an Indo-German joint workshop on ‘Viral Hepatitis’ in June 2001.  An eight-
member delegation sponsored by ICMR attended the workshop, which resulted  in identifying a few major projects on the subject.
            The Indo-German workshop on ‘Nano materials Technology’ was held in June 2001 at Berlin.  An eleven member Indian
 delegation took part in the three-day event as an outcome of which joint projects were being worked out.
Washington, USA
            A High Level Indo-US Round Table on Science and Technology was held in Washington, DC, on the occasion of the visit
 of the Prime Minister to USA.  Distinguished scientists and administrators from both the countries participated in these meetings. 
 The Round Table was aimed at discussing new directions for the 21
st century in Indo-US collaborations in science and
 technology.

 in areas like agriculture, agricultural processing, agricultural biotechnology, education, capacity building and training and other
 areas of science and technology.

 &Technology through these Missions. The Committee has been regularly receiving journals on Science &Technology published
 by Indian Missions in Germany, Japan & Russia.  However, it reiterates that the journal brought out by Indian Mission in U.S.A
 be made available to the Committee.

 region for scientific cooperation and exchange of know-how.

TECHNOLOGY FOR BAMBOO PRODUCT
66.       The Committee has been given to understand that Technology for Bamboo Product is   a programme at the national level
 meant to impart a significant boost to the usage of bamboo, promote specialized products for commercialization and generate
 good employment opportunities. New tools and techniques would be introduced to enhance the manner in which the bamboo
 resources are used in the country leading to greater and sensitive use of new materials.
67.       When asked  whether a critical assessment has been made about bamboo, its growth & the employment potential it holds
 for rural areas/North East Region, the Committee has  been informed that the allocation for National Mission on Bamboo
 Applications (NMBA) reflects the growing realization that bamboo can be an important vehicle to support & catalyse economic
 activity along with employment & income generation, in particular in rural areas and in regions with substantial resources of
 bamboo such as North East India, the Andaman & Nicobar islands, the Western Ghats, Uttaranchal, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and
 Orissa.  Technology developments in recent years in many parts of the world have positioned  bamboo as an excellent wood
 substitute for building & construction and resource & support agencies.   The Committee has  been informed that all these
 assessments have highlighted the significant potential of the sector through the promotion of new value-added applications,
 technologies and markets.  Also, while developing and promoting environment friendly, value-added bamboo based product,
 practices, process technology & processing machinery under several sub-projects, the Mission would aim to empower people at
 the grass-root level encompassing farmers, artisans and other stakeholders for better employment generation with improved
 remunerative opportunities.
68.       The Committee is happy to note the Mission in Bamboo products.  However, it would like the states like Madhya Pradesh
 and  Maharastra, where sizable quantity of Bamboo is produced, have not been included in the Mission.   Besides,  the Quality of
 Bamboo needs to be improved by improving cultivation techniques.  The Committee has been given to understand that Chinese
 Bamboo is of superior quality, the Committee therefore recommends that areas like N.E. Region, which have weather conditions
 similar to those in the countries abroad must be chosen for cultivation of better variety of bamboo.
The Committee feels that the wood should be replaced by use of Bamboo for construction purposes particularly in quake prone
 areas or for making agricultural tools and for furniture.
69.       The Committee would like to add that more such mission modes could be considered for products like Jute & Coir, which
 have suffered due to cheaper substitutes available in the market and have a great potential to provide gainful employment to the
 masses.

 various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs.1014.25
 crores, as sought by the Department of Science & Technology for the year 2002-03, under Demand No.  70 , may be approved.

            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One
 Hundred-Third Report of the Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2002-2003) of the
 Department of Scientific & Industrial Research (Demand No.71).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 11
th  April, 2002 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department
 Scientific & Industrial Research gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought
 clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for
 Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by
 the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants
 of the Department Scientific & Industrial Research.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 9
th May, 2002.
 
 
NEW DELHI;
                                                                                                     C.RAMACHANDRAIAH,
May 9,2002                                                                                                                               Chairman,
                                                                         Committee on Science& Technology, Environment & Forests.
        R E P O R T
 
The Department of Scientific & Industrial Research (DSIR) is a Department of the Ministry of Science & Technology
 and is entrusted with the matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research; National Research
 Development Corporation; Central Electronics Limited; National Information System on Science and Technology
 (NISSAT); Registration and Recognition of R&D Units; United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
 (UNCTAD) and World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO); National register for foreign collaborations. 
 Creation of a pool for temporary placement of our Scientists and Technologists; and National register of Scientific
 Manpower. It acts as an administrative link between the Government of India and the CSIR Society.
2.         The Department is concerned with the following departmental programmes:
(a)        Plan Schemes relating to:
                       
(i)         Research and Development by Industry (RDI);
(ii)        Programme Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PATSER);
Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology
(SEETOT); and
(iv)       National Information System for Science and Technology. (NISSAT)
Besides, the Department is involved in various other activities/matters relating to;
International R&D collaboration involving industrial companies, and industrial
 R&D centres;International Cooperation/Collaboration agreements with other countries relating to industrial R&D with
 the concurrence of the Ministry of External Affairs;
Domestic technology, particularly the promotion of ventures involving the commercialization of such technologies 
 other than those under the Department of Science and Technology;Technology Exports including exports of Technical
 and Consultancy Services, in close cooperation with the Ministry of Commerce;
Technical, engineering and management consultancy organizations and services; andSupport in different forms, to
 industrial R&Dcarriedoutatdiverseunits/institutions/organization.  The Department also manages two Public Sector
 enterprises, namely National  Research Development Corporation (NRDC), and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) and
 an autonomous Organisation – Consultancy Development Centre (CDC)
3.         The Council of Scientific & Industrial Research constituted in 1942 by a resolution of the then Central
 Legislative assembly, is an autonomous body registered under the Registration of Societies Act XXI of 1860.  The 
 functions assigned to the Council are Promotion, guidance and coordination of Scientific and Industrial Research in

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/103rdreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:21:41]
 India including the institution and financing of specific researches; Establishment or development and assistance to
 special institutions or departments of existing institutions for scientific study of problems affecting particular industrial
 and trade; Establishment and award of research studentship and fellowship; Utilization of the results of the researches
 conducted under the auspices of the Council towards the development of industries in the country and the payment of a
 share of royalties arising out of  the development of the results of researches to those who are considered as having
 contributed towards the pursuits of such researches; Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories,
 workshops, institutes and organizations to further scientific and Industrial Research and  utilize and exploit for purposes
 of experiment or otherwise any discovery or invention likely to be of use to Indian industries; Collection and
 dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to industrial matters generally; Publication of
 scientific papers and journals; and any other activity or activities to promote generally the objects of the resolution.
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
4.         The Department of Scientific & Industrial Research (DSIR ) has been allocated Rs.1040.93 crores for the year
 2002-2003 as against Rs.963.47 crores in B.E. and Rs.927.68 crores in the R.E. of the year 2001-2002.

            The allocation on the plan side has been kept at Rs.440.00 crores, which represents an increases of about Rs.100

5.         The Committee was informed that CSIR derives its finances from three major sources namely, Budgetary
 support from the government under Plan and Non-Plan, undertaking of contract R&D, consultancy & technical services
 (External Cash Flow – ECF) and internal receipts.
6.         Secretary, DSIR informed the Committee that from the Tenth Five Year Plan it proposes to operate only six 
 plan schemes based on Zero Based Budgetary (ZBB) review  instead of nine schemes as in Ninth  Five year  plan.
 Besides, the ongoing five schemes the CSIR proposed to introduce a new scheme on infrastructure Renovation and
 Refurbishment from the Tenth Five Year Plan onwards. 
           
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
7.         The Committee has been given to an understand that CSIR has a network of 39 Laboratories and 50 field
 stations/extension centres/regional centres located all over the country which undertake R&D in various S&T areas and
 disciplines. These have been established to reach the diverse users and disseminate knowledge and information on
 R&D capabilities, techniques and technologies developed.
8.         The Ninth Five Year Plan (NFYP) was a watershed in the programme planning and implementation in the CSIR.
 During this phase the endeavour was to move the organization towards ‘Programme & Project’ based approach rather
 than discipline/area /sectoral approach.  As a result CSIR formulated and took up over 20 major mission mode projects
 with well defined deadlines, deliverables and cost ceilings. The organizational learning experience derived therefrom
 has given the requisite assurance and conviction to CSIR that  many of the ‘science’ programmes can be projectised
 and taken up in mission mode.
9.         The Committee was informed that during the Tenth Five Year Plan CSIR would  undertake programmes that
 promote: excellence in science; global competitiveness; local relevance innovation.  CSIR further seek to broaden and
 strengthen more of its activities in the project mode by networking and alliancing on a Team India basis. The
 programmes of National Laboratories have been categorized sectorally under Aerospace; Biology and Biotechnology;
 Chemical; Earth Resources and Natural Hazards Assessment; Ecology & Environment; Electronics and

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/103rdreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:21:41]
 Instrumentation; Energy; Food & Food processing; Health Care, Drugs & Pharmaceuticals; Housing & Construction;
 Information Dissemination and Products; Leather; Materials, Metals, Minerals and Manufacturing; Rural Development
 with a view to enable and facilitate an easy alignment with the overall ‘National Planning process’. The areas of thrust
 in these categories have been identified through interactions with various national agencies, government departments,
 industry associations and potential clients keeping in view the strengths and capabilities in the CSIR laboratories and
 the external opportunities. 
10.       When asked for the reasons for hike in allocation for National Laboratories by about 23% over RE last year, the
 Department informed that the budgetary allocation to National Laboratories during the year 2002-2003 is Rs.703 crore
 consisting of Rs.310 crore in the Plan and Rs. 393 crore under non-plan.  This represents an increase of about 23% over
 the  Revised Estimates of 2001-2002 and  the increase is essentially on the Plan component.  The year 2002-03 being
 the first year of the Tenth-Five Year Plan, the emphasis has been to evolve and formulate Core Programmes to be
 implemented in Project Mode as directed by the Planning Commission constituted Steering Committee on Science &
 Technology for the Tenth Five Year Plan.  CSIR laboratories would be focusing on these Core Programmes (fifty five
 projects) to be taken in the Mission-Project Mode.  Some of the significant ones are: (i) Spearheading small civilian
 aircraft design, development & manufacture; (ii) Exploration and Exploitation of Microbial Wealth of India for novel
 compounds and biotransformation process; (iii) Molecular biology of selected pathogens  for  developing  drugs 
 targets;  (iv) Pollution  monitoring  and mitigation systems and
devices; (vii) Positioning Indian nutraceuticals and neutrigenomics on a global platform; (viii) Asthmatic and allergic
 disorders mitigation mission; (ix) Newer scientific herbal preparations for global positioning; (x) Design analysis and
 health assessment of Special structures including bridges; (xi) Comprehensive Traditional Knowledge Digital
 Documentation and Library, and (xii) Developing technology packages for disaster prevention and management in
 underground coalfields.
Besides, the allocation is also for building up basic core competencies in new and emerging areas and providing housing
 facilities for scientific, technical and other staff or CSIR.
11.       The Committee notes with satisfaction the various activities in which CSIR laboratories are conducting
 research.  However, the pricing and the terms at which the technology is transferred to industry needs to be looked into
 afresh with a view not only to retain the competitive edge for the industry but it should also be profitable to the
 Government and if possible should also generate royalty for the Government.  From the experience gained in respect of
 ASMON being marketed by only one company, which was not able to cope with the demand, the Committee feels that
 the marketing  rights in respect of new drugs entering the market should be with more than one company to avoid
 inconvenience to customers.
 
PROGRAMMES FOR CORE COMPETENCIES IN BASIC RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT
12.       The Committee has been informed that CSIR needs to pursue free but focused  R&D that provides it the
 requisite knowledge base and core skills for generating newer techniques and technologies of the future. Absence of
 adequate investments in industrial research would deprive the CSIR & nation of any technology advantage on the
 global front that leading to denial of technological leadership.
And also, CSIR consciously invests about 15% to 20% of the resources on national laboratories for such focused but
 free basic research programmes.  The support for such programmes would vary from time to time and from laboratory
 to laboratory.  In the present-context this type of support would be more in the emerging areas of biology (genomics,
 proteomics etc.), new materials, (nano, ultra pure & fine materials etc.) and exploration of emerging crazy ideas in
 other domains.
 
NATIONAL S&T HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
13.       The Committee has been informed that CSIR was aware of the declining trend in the youth taking to science
 education and R&D as a career. One of the underlying causes of decline in science education is that the students were
 herded into dull classes, taught by faculty that was not abreast of the exciting & new development in science and given
 little academic guidance and motivation. In order to prevent this trend the Department aims to take up a training and
 motivation programme for selected Science Teachers to be the `fountain heads’ and `centres of excellence’ in science
 education in schools and under-graduate education. In order to promote interest, excitement and excellence in science
 education at school and undergraduate levels, each CSIR laboratory would adopt atleast one school and one college in
 its sphere of influence. Designated  escort  scientist will  be made responsible for the activity. The laboratory would
 offer
not only its facilities for project work and experimentation but also carry out student guidance and motivational

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/103rdreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:21:41]
 programmes.
CSIR would endeavour to inculcate a spirit of entrepreneurship in research scholars to help them establish their own
 R&D enterprises.  In order to attract bright school leaving children to pursue science it would enlarge on CSIR
 Programme on Youth for Leadership in Science (CPYLS). The Shyama Prasad Mukherjee awards were created to
 promote creativity and in nurturing at postgraduate level of science.
14.       The Committee observes that in order to encourage talented persons to take up research, they should be
 encouraged with remunerative schemes and wherever applicable attractive pay scales so that a suitable environment
 congenial to work culture is provided wherein they can sustain their interests in scientific research.  They should also be
 provided state of art laboratory facilities as this also would prevent them from going abroad and thus, reducing brain
 drain.
The Committee is also of the view that the efforts be made to utilize the services of scientists who have since retired by
 involving them in projects which were aimed at inculcating scientific temper among students and this would help utilise
 their talents.  This could be done through re-employment.  Infact the scientists should be allowed to work irrespective
 of the age of retirement, as long as they feel they can meaningfully contribute in the interest of the society and the
 country.
 
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY & TECHNOLOGY MANAGEMENT (IPTM)
15.       The Committee was informed that this  scheme was formulated to enhance the volume and  derive the optimal
 value  of Intellectual Property (IP) generated by CSIR and to share the best innovation and technology management
 practices organizationally and with the Indian S&T community at large. The volume of IP rights secured by CSIR has
 greatly increased, however the task of realizing adequate and appreciable  value from the IPR was yet to be achieved.
16.       The Committee has been informed that the IPR regime  in a state of flux and there were major unresolved issues
 with respect to `traditional knowledge’, `genomic sequences’, `copyright on the Net’ etc. This imposed a continuous
 need to refurbish the skills and knowledgebase of those in CSIR engaged in the IPR game and to advise the
 policymakers appropriately on the new developments and changes proposed in international IPR arena. Asked to
 explain the reasons for increased budgetary allocation for this programme and the number of patents filed last year and
 whether the Department had negotiated and tied up marketing of technologies with various Indian and Foreign
 companies, the Department replied that during the year 2000-01, CSIR had filed total of 862 patents of which 452
 Patents were filed abroad and 410 patents filed in India.  None of the Patents filed by CSIR were in dispute.  CSIR was
 at the second position in terms of Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) patents filed by entity in the year 2001.  However,
 CSIR has set a target of 1200 patents filing (700 foreign and 500 Indian) for the year 2002-03.  The enhanced allocation
 would help meet the cost of filing these patents, maintenance of the enlarged portfolio of existing patents, building
 capacity to defend and initiate patent infringement action and training of CSIR personnel on advanced  aspects of
 Intellectual property & Technology Management.

 before they get outdated.
 
NEW MILLENNIUM INDIAN TECHNOLOGY LEADERSHIP INITIATIVE (NMITLI)
18.       In order to capture  global leadership position the scheme was initiated in February 2000 for the country in few
 selected areas based on technology. The scheme necessitated intimate networking between diverse constituents of the
 innovation chain. The choice was to mount two or three large industry oriented projects or to seek windows of
 opportunity in farsighted science – technology intensive projects. Considering the  experience of Indian constituents to
 team up on large civilian commercial projects and the high risks in putting large investment in two / three projects  the
 scheme chose to focus on niche, high science- technology projects with high gain – risk potential. Even then the
 scheme has adopted a system of `options funding’ for the projects with flexibility to foreclose those projects that exceed
 the potential cost-benefit-risk thresholds. CSIR through large-scale national consultation and brainstorming is giving
 support to true Team India spirit, 9 projects encompassing 55 R&D institutions and 20 industrial firms.
19.       When asked about the reasons for reduction in allocation by Rs.5.00 crores and impact of the same on ongoing
 projects, the Department informed that the projects were of 2-3 years duration and thus it was envisaged that the
 majority of projects initiated in 2001 would be completed in the Financial Year 2002-03.  The reduced allocation was
 thus adequate for meeting the 2
nd year allocations of projects initiated in the present year 2001-02 and those to be
 initiated in the 2002-03 year.
20.       The Committee feels that department should take up such technology projects as were important to the country
 and  strive  to bring out the best quality technologies at flexible costs.  Efforts should be made to expeditiously

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/103rdreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:21:41]
 complete the project with regular monitoring by competent authorities/panels appointed for the purpose.
 
INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT
21.       In the course of his presentation the Secretary  informed the Committee that a new scheme for Infrastructure
 Renovation & Refurbishment was being initiated from the Tenth Five Year Plan. This was analogous to the scheme on
 Modernisation and had two components (i) rehabilitating, refurbishing and renovating the laboratories, aging buildings
 and infrastructure and (ii) putting in place a state of art most modern IT infrastructure in all the laboratories. CSIR
 infrastructure was built or acquired more than thirty to forty years ago.  Some of the laboratories like the Central Drug
 Research Institute (CDRI), Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI), Central Salt & Marine Chemicals

 approval obtained.

 efficient internet.

 context.  Infact  this  should have been done much earlier in pursuance of recommendations of the Committee in the
 context of modernization of laboratories.  The Committee has time and again reiterated that progressive modernisation
 or renovation was a continuous process and the Department should also ensure that the laboratories that were being

th plan

32.       As a result of rapid urbanization and industrialization most Indian cities have higher levels of gases, particulate
 matter and chemical pollutants beyond permissible limits.  Mortality and morbidity statistics also indicate that

 respiratory infections and chronic conditions were becoming wide spread within the urban population.  The quality of
 water in most water bodies has considerably degraded and in most cases cannot be used for any human purposes unless
 adequately treated. Solid wastes abound in cities and their hinterland. This imposes a high cost on the economy in terms
 of loss of man-days, productivity and production. This calls for an urgent need to undertake networked & coordinated
 mission programme to better understand pollution and its impact on human health so as to devise systems and devices
 for its mitigation.
In this direction, CSIR has been a major contributor of S&T inputs for evolving national policies for environmental
 management and to ameliorate environmental problems.  It has conducted special programmes/studies in the areas,
 namely,   
Oceanographic Studies
The Indian Ocean Experiment ((INDOEX) for measurement of the long-range transport of air pollution from South and
 South-East Asia towards the Indian Ocean were studied,
Through Coastal Ocean Monitoring & Prediction System (COMAPS) an extensive chemical and biological observations
 were made along the Ratnagiri – Mangalore coastal stretch which showed that the region was free from major
 contamination,
Air Quality Assessment
National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI) has taken up a programme National Air Quality
 Monitoring which  resulted in creation of valuable long-term database for 10 major Indian urban centers of pollution
 levels and trends of heterogeneous ionic specific and heavy trace metals. Benzene concentration were monitored in
 various localities of Mumbai spread over a number of seasons which had shown that substitution of lead by benzene in
 petrol as an antiknocking agent had its own deleterious effects.
Water quality assessment
 Under this programme nine urban centers in the country were selected for analysis of physicochemical and
 microbiological parameters including pathogenic organisms of different water sources used for drinking purposes.  This
 has yielded valuable information for planning of public health measures. Br
82 radio isotope and Rhodamine WT
 fluorescent dye were used as tracers to monitor  for monitoring sewage dispersion and bacterial die-off pattern in
 marine environment was also taken up.
33.       The Committee was informed that R&D activities in the area of waste management in India have so far largely
 been directed towards inventorization of sources of toxic wastes, selection of the disposal sites, assessment of
 environmental dangers due to indiscriminate disposal and adoption/adaptation of treatment of disposal technologies
 developed.  The growing concern for the quality of the environment requires the industries to actively seek ways to
 minimize the waste generation; in many cases to work towards an ideal goal of zero discharge.  Zero discharge was
 necessitated because of scarcity of fresh water, legislation banning priority pollutants, and waste minimization strategy
 that would enable the firms not only to save financial resources otherwise required in waste treatment and disposal
 costs but also reduce potential environmental liabilities.
34.       One of the techno-economically feasible example under this context was production of biodegradable plastics
 from waste derived renewable sources, which were expected to contribute to a paradigm shift envisaging consideration
 of waste as an economically exploitable resource and also substitution of non-renewable resource base with renewable
 resource.  Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are one such class of polymers and Polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) is one of the
 best-known PHAs.  The study aims to bring down the cost of PHB to be comparable to the currently available
 thermoplastics.  CSIR laboratories have contributed in providing appropriate solutions to mitigate pollution of diverse
 industrial wastes.
35.       The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in abating the pollution.  It feels that data
 generated regarding the various forms of pollution should be supplied to agencies like pollution Control Boards so that
 they can utilize the same in  ensuring pollution free environment.  Besides, Industries should also be supplied with
 newer technologies developed for pollution control, as their acceptance and application of these technologies was
 essential for control of pollution.

 four metropolis the incidence was placed as high as 30%. Genes and environment both played a very important role in
 this disease. Environment contributed in precipitating the disease due to the increased exposure to sensitizing allergens
 and reduced stimulation of the immune system.

 of the cellular and molecular mechanisms of this allergic disease was lacking, a group of scientists at the Indian

 remedy of Asthma (Bronchial), a plant based product known to be used by the people over the centuries.    Bronchial
 asthma patients of all ages could take this medicine safely.  Working on the inhibition of arachidonic acid oxidation by
 the preparation, it has been proposed as an anti-leukotriene asthma medicine.  Elaborating  Asmon, he  said, it inhibits
 oxidation of the arachidonic acid in an ex vivo
blood assay system wherein the blood cells were stimulated by calcium ionopher or known stimulator to enhance their
 oxidative activity.  Asmon helps to control asthma symptoms including the acute breathing problem arising out of
 bronchial asthma.  Asmon offers asthma patients a new treatment option to enhance the control of their asthma by
 inhibiting the oxidation of Arachidonic acid.

 rights to manufacture this drug had been exclusively given to one company, which could not cope with the demand. 
 The Committee feels that if adequate study of marketing had been done before giving the exclusive rights, the situation
 as obtaining, could have perhaps been avoided.  Nevertheless, the Committee notes with satisfaction that Asmon plus
 would be launched shortly and the manufacturing/marketing rights would be given to more than one company keeping 
 the interest of the users in view.
(Para 44)
12.       The Committee observes that the quality and cost of construction were two important requisites in the field of
 construction. It is necessary to develop low cost alternatives which the private sector alone can do.  But the technology
 therefore had to be developed & transferred to that sector by our laboratories/institutions after extensive research.  The
 laboratories etc. should therefore be geared up to develop cheaper & durable alternatives.
(Para 46)
13.       The Committee notes the development with satisfaction.
 (Para 48)
14.       The Committee feels that the technology, which is transferred to industry, should be in respect of quality
 products only.
(Para 51)
15.       The Department should endeavour to strengthen the library network with the help of latest IT tool & techniques.

R E P O R T
            The Ministry of Environment & Forests is concerned with the planning, promotion and co-ordination of environment and
 forestry programmes in India. The important activities of the Ministry incorporate conservation and control of pollution, afforestation
 and regeneration of forests in degraded areas, protection and conservation of forests and wildlife and protection of environment.
 These tasks are sought to be achieved by the Ministry through environmental impact assessment, eco-regeneration, assistance to
 organizations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, enactment of environmental legislation, formulation of
 environmental policies, promotion of environmental and forestry research, extension, education and training to augment the requisite
 manpower, dissemination of environmental information international cooperation and creation of environmental awareness among all
 sectors of the country’s population. The major activities of the Ministry are spread over four major sectors, i.e.
(a)
    Environment;
(b)   National River Conservation Directorate;
(c)    Forests and Wildlife and
(d)   National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board.

MAJOR SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
WILD LIFE PROTECTION
8.         The Ministry in reply to a Question, apprised the Committee that “Poaching and illegal trade in wild animals”, has become a
 lucrative trade because of increasing demand for various wildlife products across our borders. The pecuniary gain from the illegal
 trade was very high. The prices fetched by some of the wildlife products in the clandestine international markets were as follows:
(i)         Tiger bone        - US $2425/Kg.
(ii)        Rhino horn        - US $1150/ Kg.
(iii)       Musk               - US $50,000/Kg.
(iv)       Ivory                - US $ 400/Kg.
8.1       There were reasons to believe that routes and conduits of illegal wildlife trade were largely the same as those for smuggling of
 narcotics, arms, gold and other commodities. The masterminds running these operations operate either from Metro cities or areas
 quite far from the forest areas.
8.2       During its visit to Andaman & Nicobar Islands the Committee was apprised of poaching and smuggling of sea cucumber and

Bt. COTTON  & ISSUES RELATED THERETO
10.       In India, Cotton was grown on approximately 9 million hectare of land, highest in the world, accounts for about 20% of the
 world acreage.  India stands 3
rd in the lint production, producing only 319 kg/ha lint yield compared to the world average of 603
 kg/ha.  Cotton is highly susceptible to insects and consumes over 50% of the total insecticides used in the country.  India spends
 nearly Rs.1,200 crores worth of pesticides for controlling various pests of cotton.  Approximately, 60-70% of the pesticides are used
 only for control of the dreaded pest namely bollworm against the world average of 30%.  It is estimated that in India about 20-30% of
 the productivity of cotton is lost due to the damage of insect pests.
10.1     In genetically engineered foods, genes from bacteria, viruses, other plants or animals are inserted into crops such as corn,
 canola, soyabeans, potatoes, tomatoes, squash, and papayas to achieve favourable characteristics including higher yield, faster
 ripening, pest control and herbicide tolerance.   Similarly,  Transgenic Bt. Cotton is a  technology that has been proposed as
an alternative to overcome the problem of bollworm, reduction in pesticide use and improving the environment.
10.2     A gene from the soil borne bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis   has been introduced into the cotton plant.  This gene encodes a
 protein, Cry1A (c)  that has specific insecticidal properties to control bollworms.  This gene was transformed into cotton plants by
 M/s. Monsanto, USA and M/s. Maharashtra Hybrid Seeds Co. Ltd. (Mahyco), Mumbai (in which Monsanto has a 26 per cent
 stake)  has introduced it into Indian cotton germplasm by traditional breeding methods.  This transgenic cotton on which cotton pests
 namely bollworm feeds, interferes with the digestive tract of insect and kills it.  The new plant has no effect on other insects or pests.
10.3     Studies like gene flow, aggressiveness and cross-ability with wild near relatives of cotton, conducted with transgenic cotton
 revealed that the possibility of gene flow in nature becomes negligible and therefore there is a least chance of effecting the
 biodiversity and less chance of possibilities of cross pollination in nature.  The toxicity and allerginicity studies conducted on birds,
 fish, mammals including ruminants (goats, cows and buffaloes) on Bt. Cotton established that it is as safe as non-Bt. cotton has no
 impact on non-target insects and on bio-flora.  The Bt. cotton hybrids were further characterized for the absence of the Terminator
 gene and confirmed that these hybrids are not having any terminator gene sequences.  Composition analysis of Bt. Cotton showed
 that it is comparable with non-Bt. cotton. Contained limited field studies and large sale field studies in farmers’ fields and also in
 ICAR system indicated that Bt. cotton showed distinct agronomic advantage over non-Bt. cotton.
10.4     The economic benefit of Bt. cotton is estimated to be substantial when compared to current practices of cotton cultivation. 
 Significantly higher benefits are expected to be derived from the yield savings of the Bt. cotton in addition to savings in the cost of
 pesticides.  The farmers are expected to gain 50% to 70% of the economic benefits generated from the technology. Small farmers are
 more likely to adopt this technology as they do not have to spray every 3 to 4 days and 20 to 25 times.
10.5     According to various News reports over 4,000 hectares in Gujarat, and 190 hectares in just one district of Andhra Pradesh,
 Karimnagar, are under Bt cotton production.  There are reports that the Karimnagar plantation is intended for seed production, which
 will be used for plantation in some 80,000 hectares next year in the Kharif season.
10.6     In India today, clearance of a GMO goes through two Committees: Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) of
 the DBT, and the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) of the Ministry of Environment & Forests.  On 26.3.2002, the
 GEAC of Ministry of Environment & Forests had examined the data generated on Bt. cotton and had cleared three Bt. cotton and
 hybrids for commercial cultivation with certain conditions.

OLIVE RIDLEY TURTLE AT GAHIRMATHA BEACH IN ORISSA
12.       The issue of large scale Olive Ridley Turtles being killed by the Fishing Trawlers has attracted the  attention  for   quite  
 sometime and the Committee   too  has  noted   with   concern.
According to various news reports, experts have long established that turtle excluder devices (TED) are the only known way to reduce
 turtle casualty.  A turtle excluder device is a simple grid like instrument made of steel, aluminum or iron.  It has interspaced bars and
 a flap made of net attached to it, which allows the turtle to escape, while allowing fish to pass through between the bars into the bag
 of the trawler net. 
13.       The Committee is of the view that the non-usage of TEDS is turning the Gahirmatha beach in Orissa into the largest graveyard
 for turtles. Although, the use of turtle excluder devices (TEDS) has been made mandatory in the State, but trawler operators continue
 to flout norms with impunity.  The Ministry of Environment & Forests should take-up this issue on priority basis in coordination with
 the State Governments and take steps to strictly enforce the usage of turtle excluder devices (TED).

VEHICULAR POLLUTION CONTROL MEASURES
16.       The Committee is aware that as regards the use of CNG as a transport fuel with special reference to public transport in the
 National Capital Region, the Supreme Court in continuation of its order dated 28
th July 1998 delivered a landmark ruling on April 5,
 2002, after an exhaustive deliberation with the parties concerned.  According to the order, all public transport vehicles would now
 run on CNG in Delhi.  Another marked difference was other polluted cities such as Lucknow, Pune and Jodhpur finding mention in
 the verdict, with the Supreme Court suggesting that they, too, switch over to CNG for running their public transport. The Court has
 chalked out a clear-cut strategy wherein 800 diesel buses would be phased out every month in the city from May 2002 onwards
 against a corresponding installed production capacity of 1100 CNG buses.
16.1     The apex court’s verdict is a sharp departure from its earlier approach of setting a deadline for the government and expecting it
 to comply with the order.  Emphasis was laid this time on making “public health”, the core issue through the application of the
 ‘precautionary principle’ and by getting into the ‘polluter pays’  principle.  The Supreme Court has also imposed
a stiff penalty on diesel bus operators who, in defiance of the Court’s earlier order, have continued to run their vehicles on the
 polluting fuel.  A fine of Rs.500 per bus per day was being charged from April 6 2002.  This will be hiked to Rs.1000 from May 6
 until there is a complete shift to CNG.  The Supreme Court has also slapped a penalty of Rs.20, 000 on the Union government for
 repeatedly seeking modification of its order.
16.2     The “polluter pays principle”, is adopted as an underlying economic code for environmental policy.  According to it the
 polluters were liable to take steps to prevent in advance, or at least reduce, any inconveniences rising from their activity.  They were
 also responsible for any damage they cause to the environment.  The principle fixes the accountability of industries for the pollution
 they generate.  It emphasizes the fact that the costs of measures to prevent, control and reduce damage resulting from pollution
 should be borne by the polluter.  The principle does not mean one can pay for pollution and purchase the environment.
17.       The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Environment & Forests have adequate powers under section 5 of the Air
 Act, 1981, and the Environment (Protection) Act to enforce more stringent standards for pollution at hot spots.  Apart from the
 instance of 1997, when it notified the first ever fuel quality norms, the Ministry has never made its presence felt.  It has never
 discouraged the use of diesel by the Indian auto sector.  There has thus been no show of commitment or initiative on the part of the
 Ministry.
17.1     The Ministry of Environment & Forest’s 1997 white paper on pollution in Delhi is little more than a common position of all
 the other Union government agencies concerned, such as Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Surface Transport and Ministry of
 Petroleum and Natural gas.  It does nothing more to push for CNG than propose government tradition of making toothless but
 politically correct suggestions.

FOREST CONSERVATION, DEVELOPMENT & REGENERATION
18.       Members have raised the controls of large areas of densely forested regions in the country by Naxalites on more than one
 occasion in the Committee. In these forested areas, the state and forest administration dare not enter. Naxalites use the growing
 alienation of tribal people against forest laws to gain ground. They build check dams where governments cannot because of
 restrictive forest conservation laws. They secure tribal rights over non-timber forest produce and dispense quick justice — at
 gunpoint. There are also massive financial gains for the Naxals in looting state forests. Poachers to timber mafia and protection
 money from paper industry, all contribute to their "revolution". According to reports by ensuring people’s access to forest and
 distributing forestlands for cultivation, today Naxalites have established parallel governments and nearly 10.03million hectares (mha)
 of forests in the country are under the control of Naxalites.
18.1     According to the 1999 Forest Survey Report ,  over 0.4 mha of forests in the country were under encroachment — 60 per cent
 of which were in the Naxalite-affected areas and in  almost all the Naxalite-affected districts, forest loss has been attributed to
 encroachment due to ‘local disturbances’.
18.2     In a meeting with the Standing Committee on Developments of  Meghalaya Legislative Assembly the Committee was
 apprised of the imposition of   an interim ban on felling in forests on December 12, 1996. Having India’s one-fourth of forests, the
 seven states are worst affected as a large chunk of their population earns its livelihood from forests. The ban has come at a time when
 the region was losing 31,700 hectares every year, mostly due to the government and timber traders’ nexus. It also made the ban
 conditional: by putting in place a sustainable way of using the forests. The proposal makes sense for a region, where traditional
 village institutions control and manage 80 per cent of forests.  For a region that largely depends on forests for economic and
 livelihood survival, the ban has come short of a death sentence. The economic loss is unimaginable, particularly for poor forest
 dwellers that form a majority in the seven states — Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland, Assam, Tripura, Manipur and
 Meghalaya.
18.3     The Supreme Court has observed that till date, a clear definition of forests is not given in the existing legal instruments —
 Forest Conservation Act (FCA), 1980, Forest Conservation (Amendment) Act, 1988, and the Indian Forest Act, 1927. Under Section
 2 of the FCA forests have been defined as "reserved forest, protected forest or any area recorded as forest in the government record".
 The court also stated that forest should be understood according to its dictionary meaning — "a large area of land thickly covered
 with trees, bushes, etc". Then it ordered every state to form an expert committee, which would identify forests, irrespective of class or
 ownership; all wood-based industries and assess the sustainability of forests. The ruling also reinforced the formulation of rules
 before any felling was resorted to. Though private plantations and social forestry programmes, were excluded from the ban in the
 first ruling, the court brought these areas in the ambit of the ban in its next ruling.
18.4     State governments have been slow in formulating the working plan, mandatory for carrying out felling and as a result only 14
 per cent of the plans have been completed in the last five years and some states still do not have a single working plan in place.
 Manipur and Mizoram did not have even a single working plan in place till October 2001. Similarly in Nagaland, where timber is the
 main source of livelihood for local people, the state formulated working plans for just 0.1 per cent of forests This is despite Ministry
 of Environment & Forests setting up a regional centre in Shillong for easy access.
18.5     The Supreme Court have not been happy the way governments were trying to frustrate the implementation of the ban. 
 Therefore on February 18, 2002, the Supreme Court slapped a fine of Rs.5,000 on the Union government for not framing a
 comprehensive scheme regarding forestland approved for deforestation. Similarly, state governments too were being pulled up for
 misguiding the court.
18.6     Another area of conflict is the Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972, which also has attracted the attention of the Committee. The
 Act of 1972, amended in 1991, prohibits human intervention in national parks, and allows limited intervention in sanctuaries. There
 are about 550 of these today, covering more than 4.3 per cent of the country’s geographical area. The Wildlife (Protection) Act of
 1972 hangs like a Damocles’ sword for the thousands of people living in or around protected forests.  Some of the Communities
 living near the Protected areas and deprived of human intervention are shown here under in the Table (Table- 8).

18.7     Another area of conflict is in Gadchiroli district in the State of Maharashtra. The major cause of conflict in Gadchiroli is over
 “forest produce”. The Maharashtra government's ordinance, issued on 10 December, 1997, has made provisions for transfer of
 ownership of minor forest produce (MFP) to panchayats. But several impediments have been mentioned an accordance with the
 Indian Forest Act, 1927. These include exclusion of the ownership of land and trees in the panchayat areas, exclusion of national
 park and sanctuaries and adherence to the rules laid in the working plan. The exclusion of tendu and bamboo has become a highly
 emotive issue for the villagers.  Several villages have already stopped extraction activity even though they stand to lose wages, which
 they earn from extraction work. e.g. the case of Ballarpur Paper Mill which has already paid royalty to the government.
19.       The Committee is of the view that the Supreme Court order merely seeks to  enforce the law laid down by the government.
 Ban on felling of trees is permitted under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 but only after a working plan has been approved by the
 Union Ministry of Environment and Forests.  However, hardly any state appears to have implemented the provision. The order was
 being misinterpreted to bureaucratise forests. Since the order asks for a clear definition and identification of forest, some state
 governments have taken this as an opportunity to gain control over large areas that remain ‘unclassified’  even  today in  the 
 Northeast.  Forest officials, who  wanted  to do away  with
‘unclassified’ forests, see this as a chance to alienate local people by claiming ownership, which were otherwise under the control of
 the community.
19.1     The Committee observes that forests in the country continue to be the victims of apathy and inadequate management in the
 country.  Besides, the categorisation of forests into reserved, protected and village forests, which are essentially administrative
 categories, does not help in their growth.  The “State of the Forest Report”, does not give a detailed classification of India’s forests,
 the percentage of natural or pristine and plantation areas, which would be of interest and use to both environmentalists and wood
 based industry. The neglect of forests has resulted into loss of produce with reported smuggling by mafias, fires – which are termed
 deliberate. This has affected their growth as it discourages participation of the people.  While tribals in some parts of the country
 have a right to enter the forests and take a part of the produce, mainly wood, for meeting their bonafide requirements, it appears to
 the Committee that this has not helped in the growth of forests because the denser the forest, the more is the alienation — tribal
 people are refused entry into forests; they cannot cultivate land they believe is theirs. It is simple. People want livelihood through
 forest but government wants control over forests.  The Committee therefore feels that it is time the forests are taken out completely
 from the bureaucratic control and managed by direct participation of the people preferably through cooperatives.  There is thus a need
 to take a dynamic initiative for the management of the forests so that the objectives of the forest policy could be met with direct
 involvement of the people in the management and growth of forests.
20.       The Committee was informed that people could collect Tendu leaves and minor forest produce for their livelihood under the
 State regulations in which they could sell some produce directly and some to the Government agencies. The people have been
 granted rights to collect minor forest produce from Scheduled Areas under Panchayat (Extension to Scheduled Area) Act, 1996. The
 Ministry of Environment & Forests has already written to the various State Governments to take necessary action in this regard.
21.       The Committee further observes that the Forest (Conservation) Act is only regulatory in nature and has enough flexibility to
 meet the development needs of the State Government.  Therefore, there is no need to amend the Forest (Conservation) Act. 
 However, there is a need to re-examine issues under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 so that it takes care of the definition of forests.
SUNDERBAN MANGROVES
22.       The Committee was informed that the “Sunderban Mangroves” are the most extensive mangroves in the country and form the
 largest single mangrove of the world.  The area occupies 1434 sq. kms, which includes 578 sq. kms of dense mangroves, and 856 sq.
 kms of sparse mangroves.  It occupies 44% of the total mangrove area of the country.   The salient features of the Sunderban
 biosphere reserve include:
(i)
                  It has the  largest floral and faunal diversity and tiger population.
(ii)                It is selected as a World Heritage Site and a Biosphere Reserve in the Global Network of UNESCO.
(iii)               It is the home of several endangered, threatened and endemic floral and faunal species and acts as a fish nursery and
 supports coastal fisheries along Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean. It provides protection to the inland habitations
 against fury of cyclones and acts as a sink for the mega metropolitan pollutants.
22.1.    The Sunderbans is represented with 26 species of mangroves covering 14 genera and 11 families and 34 species of mangrove
 associates covering 28 genera and 18 families.

 mangroves, Government  has identified this area for intensive conservation and management under the Scheme on Conservation and
 Management of Mangroves and Coral Reefs since 1987.  The main objectives of the management action plan for conservation of
 Sunderban mangroves include:

JHUM/SHIFTING CULTIVATION
26.       The Secretary informed the Committee that as per estimates, about 10 million ha. of forest areas have been subjected to
 Jhum/Shifting cultivation. Shifting cultivation is practiced in tribal dominant areas mostly in the North-Eastern States where it
 accounts for most of the forest degradation. The increase in the population of Shifting Cultivators and declining productivity of forest
 soils have resulted in the Shifting Cultivation cycle shortening from about 20 years to 4 years. Such intense farming on poor quality
 soil has made the system ecologically fragile. The National Forestry Action Programme prepared for next 20 years clearly
 incorporates the objectives defined in the National Forest Policy, 1988 to control the Shifting Cultivation practice through  following
 measures:
·
        Alternative avenues of income
·        Suitably harmonised with the right land use practices
·        By propagating improved agricultural practices
·        Social forestry and energy plantations
27.       The Committee believes that the National Forest Action Programme in respect of shifting cultivation needs to be rationalised
 by Settled Cultivation with tree farming under various agro-forestry systems. Rationalisation of Shifting cultivation should be
 approached in a holistic manner, covering the socio-cultural and economic aspects and issues relating to the land tenure.

 been lying with the government since 1994.  The Ministry should examine the Report in right earnest and devise a policy for
 conservation –– both for scientific or participatory management.
 (Para 9.2)
6.         The Committee feels that a satisfactory system of assessing the risks associated with the release of genetically modified (GM)
 plants; microorganisms, animals and marine organisms into the environment must be evolved. Certain grey areas still exist in the
 field of genetically modified foods, particularly for people who have food allergies, because they are neither subjected to tests nor
 controlled.   There is thus a need to adopt a cautious approach. 
(Para 11)
7.         The Committee is of the view that the non-usage of TEDS is turning the Gahirmatha beach in Orissa into the largest graveyard
 for turtles. Although, the use of turtle excluder devices (TEDS) has been made mandatory in the State, but trawler operators continue
 to flout norms with impunity.  The Ministry of Environment & Forests should take-up this issue on priority basis in coordination with
 the State Governments and take steps to strictly enforce the usage of turtle excluder devices (TED).
(Para 13)
8.         The Committee is of the view that the levels of both the pollutants might not have come down due to the pollution load of the
 Mathura Oil Refinery.  The rise in SPM and SO2 levels has also been caused because of the heavy vehicles going via Agra.  The
 Ministry should also examine recommendations of the Vardarajan Committee, appointed by the Supreme Court to look into Taj
 pollution, which remain unimplemented while chalking out various programmes under the Taj Protection Mission.
(Para 15)
9.         The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Environment & Forests have adequate powers under section 5 of the Air
 Act, 1981, and the Environment (Protection) Act to enforce more stringent standards for pollution at hot spots.  Apart from the
 instance of 1997, when it notified the first ever fuel quality norms, the Ministry has never made its presence felt.  It has never
 discouraged the use of diesel by the Indian auto sector.  There has thus been no show of commitment or initiative on the part of the
 Ministry.
(Para 17)
10.       The Ministry of Environment & Forest’s 1997 white paper on pollution in Delhi is little more than a common position of all
 the other Union government agencies concerned, such as Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Surface Transport and Ministry of
 Petroleum and Natural gas.  It does nothing more to push for CNG than propose government tradition of making toothless but
 politically correct suggestions.
(Para 17.1)
11.       The Committee is of the view that Environmental regulation through Courts has serious drawbacks. Judicial intervention is
 most effective in correcting bureaucratic conduct when it is selective and surgical, but in significant environmental litigations such as
 the Ganga Pollution Case, the Vehicular Pollution Case and the Taj Trapezium Case the administrative agency – the Ministry of
 Environment & Forests has been reduced to preparing only knee-jerk responses to judicial orders. The Committee believes that
 despite more than a decade of judicial activism, there is no evidence to show that the Pollution Control Boards, Department of
 Forests or the Ministry have become institutionally stronger, or more capable of discharging their responsibilities today.         
(Para 17.2)
12.       The Committee is aware of the Supreme Court’s orders on April 5, 2002 regarding plying of all public transport vehicles on
 CNG in Delhi being implemented by concerned agencies but at the same time the Committee is constrained to note the sad plight of
 commuters who continue to suffer. As a result of the judicial pronouncement and the consequent steps taken by the Government, the
 commuters continue to suffer with no immediate steps in sight being taken by the government to address their problems.  On the
 other hand transporters seem to be bent upon to exploit them by over charging and making their journeys uncomfortable and costlier. 
 The Traffic Police as the Press reports suggest, are exploiting the situation by forcing the operators to grease their palm.  The
 Committee feels that the Apex Court should have foreseen these realities before pronouncing an order.

(Para 17.3)
13.       The Committee is of the view that the Supreme Court order merely seeks to  enforce the law laid down by the government.
 Ban on felling of trees is permitted under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 but only after a working plan has been approved by the
 Union Ministry of Environment and Forests.  However, hardly any state appears to have implemented the provision. The order was
 being misinterpreted to bureaucratise forests. Since the order asks for a clear definition and identification of forest, some state
 governments have taken this as an opportunity to gain control over large areas that remain ‘unclassified’ even today in the Northeast.
 Forest officials, who wanted to do away with ‘unclassified’ forests, see this as a chance to alienate local people by claiming
 ownership, which were otherwise under the control of the community.
(Para 19)
14.       The Committee observes that forests in the country continue to be the victims of apathy and inadequate management in the
 country.  Besides, the categorisation of forests into reserved, protected and village forests, which are essentially administrative
 categories, does not help in their growth.  The “State of the Forest Report”, does not give a detailed classification of India’s forests,
 the percentage of natural or pristine and plantation areas, which would be of interest and use to both environmentalists and wood
 based industry. The neglect of forests has resulted into loss of  produce with reported smuggling by mafias, fires – which are termed
 deliberate. This has affected their growth as it discourages participation of the people.  While tribals in some parts of the country
 have a right to enter the forests and take a part of the produce, mainly wood, for meeting their bonafide requirements, it appears to
 the Committee that this has not helped in the growth of forests because the denser the forest, the more is the alienation — tribal
 people are refused entry into forests; they cannot cultivate land they believe is theirs. It is simple. People want livelihood through
 forest but government wants control over forests.  The Committee therefore feels that it is time the forests are taken out completely
 from the bureaucratic control and managed by direct participation of the people preferably through cooperatives.  There is thus a need
 to take a dynamic initiative for the management of the forests so that the objectives of the forest policy could be met with direct
 involvement of the people in the management and growth of forests.
(Para 19.1)
15.       The Committee further observes that the Forest (Conservation) Act is only regulatory in nature and has enough flexibility to
 meet the development needs of the State Government.   Therefore,  there   is  no   need  to   amend   the   Forest  (Conservation)   Act.
However, there is a need to re-examine issues under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 so that it takes care of the definition of forests.
(Para 21)
16.       The Committee is of the view that the entire Sunderbans is one eco-system and for wild animals, physical boundaries have no
 relevance.  The tigers move in their entire home range, irrespective of these boundaries.  If the food availability is improved and
 habitat is better managed, the home ranges get reduced and trans-boundary migration gets minimised.  However, in the interest of the
 long term conservation of Sunderbans, the Ministry of Environment & Forests should devise Management Plans which may involve
 joint effort of  India and Bangladesh. 
(Para 23)
17.       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should co-ordinate with the State Governments / State Pollution Control Boards
 (SPCBs) to ensure that Bio-medical waste generating units are set up along with the treatment facilities and they obtain authorisation
 from the SPCBs.
(Para 25)
18.       The Committee believes that the National Forest Action Programme in respect of shifting cultivation needs to be rationalised
 by Settled Cultivation with tree farming under various agro-forestry systems. Rationalisation of Shifting cultivation should be
 approached in a holistic manner, covering the socio-cultural and economic aspects and issues relating to the land tenure.
(Para 27)
19.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment & Forests and assessing the progress of various
 important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Budgetary allocation of Rs. 1111.05
 crores, as sought by the Ministry of Environment & Forests for the year 2002-2003, under Demand No. 24, may be approved.
(Para 28)

R E P O R T
 
      The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess (Amendment) Bill, 2000**, as introduced in the
 Lok Sabha on 15 th December, 2000 and pending therein, to the Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests for examination and Report.
2.   The Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 provides for “the levy and collection of a cess on water
 consumed by persons carrying on certain industries and by local authorities, with a view to augment the resources of the
 Central Pollution Control Board and the State Pollution Control Boards for the prevention and control of water pollution
 which were constituted under the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) act, 1974”.  The existing rates of water cess
 were revised in 1991, because the responsibility and workload of the pollution control boards had increased considerably
 and the funds available with these Boards were not adequate for the overall commitments involving heavy financial
 liabilities. The Government disburses the water cess so collected to the pollution control boards/committees according to
 criteria prescribed by the Government.
3.   The Water Cess Act, 1974 lists the rates of cess applicable for various types of water consumption in Schedule II.  This
 Schedule was amended in 1991 affecting an increase in the rates.  The Schedule– II is again being amended by the current
 amendment to augment further the resources of the Boards. The proposal is to further enhance the existing cess rates
 approximately three fold.
4.   Prior to this amendment, the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess (Amendment) Bill, 1995 was introduced in
 the Parliament on 1
st June 1995 to enhance the cess rates.  The Bill was referred to the Department related Parliament
 Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Technology for review.  The Committee after
 discussing with various concerned agencies recommended the following:
(i)                  Cess on water used for domestic purposes need not be increased.
(ii)                Cess need not be levied on the use of water by hydel power generating units.
(iii)               All industries which use water and cause pollution may be covered under theWater Cess Act for levying cess. 
 For this purpose, the Ministry may examine Schedule 1 of the Water Cess Act comprehensively.
      However, the Bill lapsed due to dissolution of the 10 th Lok Sabha.  Later, a fresh exercise to introduce the Bill was
 started and subsequently the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess (Amendment) Bill, 2000 , based on the
 recommendations aforesaid, was introduced in 2000.  The Bill envisages enhancement of cess rates (approximately three
 times) specified in Schedule II and deletion of Schedule I enlisting 16 categories of industries for the purpose of levying
 cess.  After the amendment, the Act would apply to all industries, which consume water and discharge trade effluents. 
 However, the cess rate for domestic purpose category has not been enhanced and the Bill excludes the hydel power units
 from its purview.
