7.         Keeping in view the above programmes, recent trends and international developments, the Department had
 projected a requirement of Rs.450.00 crores for the year 2003-04 to the Planning Commission. However, an allocation
 (plan side) of Rs.260.00 crores has only been provided. During the year 2002-03, the plan allocation at B.E. and R.E.
 stages was Rs.225.00 crores and Rs.205.00 crores respectively. The enhanced allocation for 2003-04 will primarily be
 utilized on new programmes/initiatives. Functional genomics, vaccines and plant based products will be a priority.
8.         The Committee was informed that one of the recurring problems of the Department is the shortfall of the non-
plan budget. Recurrence of such problems on year to year basis, the Committee was apprised,  has created a compelling
 situation for the autonomous bodies whereby they had to cut down from plan funds to pay salaries to the scientists. The
 Committee is constrained to note that scientific institutions engaged in research in frontier areas of science have to
 confront such a situation. The additional requirement of the Department for non-plan expenditure is to the tune of
 Rs.5.00 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient funds may be provided to the Department to
 overcome this problem. It further underlines that the Departments dealing with science and technology should be
 accorded priority for allocation of funds  and  if  necessary,   special  provisions  may  be  made  for  them  so  that they
 do not face such problems.  Biotechnology era is waiting to dominate the World  economy in the next twenty years. 
 Investment in this field is not commensurate with the potential of this branch of Science.
9.         The new areas covered during 2002-03 are related to agriculture and plants, healthcare, bioresource conservation
 and utilization, societal development and biotech industrial growth.
10.       It has been informed that the proposed programmes are based on the Vision Document of the Department as well
 as Tenth Plan proposals. These programmes aim at enhancing the knowledge base and generating highly skilled human
 resource, nurturing leads of potential utilityby emerging bioscience enterprises areas of agriculture, health care and the
 environment and bringing bio-products to the marketplace for generation of wealth, import substitutions, export
 promotion and technological self sufficiency. The emphasis would be on excellence and relevance for socio-economic
 progress. Agricultural Biotechnology programmes such as rice genome sequencing, development of pest and disease
 resistant varieties, nutritionally rich crops, virus free tissue culture plants, improved biofertilisers and biopesticides will
 have great impact on farmers and consumers in terms of food, nutrition, health, environment and livelihood security. A
 mission mode project on food and nutritional security is under implementation.
11.       To a specific query of the Committee as to how the Department monitors and reviews the progress of its on-
going schemes before formulating/finalising proposals for budgetary support, the Department stated that elaborate
 mechanisms have been established to review its activities.  It has got specific area wise sixteen Task Forces on various
 disciplines to review the activities and progress of all the schemes and programmes at periodic intervals, 2-3 times in a
 year.  Besides, the Department stated that a multidisciplinary high level Biotechnology Research and Promotion
 Committee consisting of experts from research institutions, universities, industry and NGOs does the same exercise. 
 Further, the Department maintained that the Scientific Advisory Committee of the Department and Standing Advisory
 Committee (Overseas) with eminent NRIs Scientists assess the overall policy issues, identify priority areas and review
 major projects. In addition to these, the Planning Commission also undertakes review of plan schemes at quarterly
 intervals. 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
12.       The focus of the programme has been to train a large number of scientists/students. An integrated manpower
 development programme comprising M.Sc./M.Tech./Post doctoral courses in biotechnology at various universities/
 institutes of many states and union territories is in operation. Programmes such as Biotechnology national and overseas
 associates, short-term training courses, seminars and symposia, popular lectures, biology scholarships, publications etc.
 have been implemented.  Five bioscience career development awards and three women bio-scientists awards were
 given to eminent scientists. The main focus of the programme has been to generate a large number of highly trained
 scientists/students. 
13.       The method of selecting a University for starting a teaching programme in biotechnology was based on the
 scientific merit of the proposal.  A DBT-UGC joint Task Force considers the proposals based on the evaluation by
 experts.  Generally, the DBT insists that a strong faculty and diverse expertise in biotechnology should be available
 with the University before starting a teaching programme.  The Department also provides for guest faculty from
 neighbouring institutions to enable better type of teaching programmes in the absence of many well-trained faculty
 members.
14.       The Committee was informed that as a result of continued support to this programme, a large number of highly
 skilled manpower in the field at Postgraduate as well as Post Doctoral levels have been generated which is catering to
 the requirements of academics, R&D and Biotech industries including pharmaceutical sector.  The proposed
 activities/programmes will further strengthen human resource development to meet the growing needs of this sector and

PLANT TISSUE CULTURE
17.       Tissue culture is an important tool of biotechnology which can be used to improve the productivity of planting
 material through enhanced availability of identified plant stock with desired traits.  The main object of the programme
 is to develop protocols for regeneration of economically important plant species covering Forest Trees, Horticulture and
 Plantation Crops.  Plant Tissue Culture technology is being used for mass multiplication of elite forest species and also
 for producing large quantities of planting material with desired characteristics.   The shortage of biomass and the
 increasing gap between supply and demand due to the mounting population pressure necessitated the mass propagation
 of trees through Tissue Culture.  The tree species identified cover a wide spectrum including trees of desert and arid
 zones, tropical and temperate zones.  DBT has supported programmes on priority crops to increase productivity per unit
 area by developing a strong R&D component concentrating on the production of high yielding and improved varieties
 and fresh methods of multiplication of elite plus trees.
18.       The Committee was informed that during 2003-04 the ongoing efforts in R&D programmes on tissue culture
 protocol standardization would continue for the identified priority crops.  Protocols for in vitro production of Saffron
 and Kalazira will be refined and scaled up.  Studies will continue for complete technology development for coffee, tea,
 spices, apple and citrus.  The Network programmes on Apple and Citrus will be launched and the germplasm will be
 characterized.  The certified virus free plants would be field planted and evaluated.  The novel orchid hybrids produced
 will be evaluated based on commercial parameters and an effort will be made to take these hybrids for commercial
 production.  Field demonstration of tissue culture raised Black pepper will be taken up in all identified sites.
19.       The Committee was apprised that under Plant Tissue Culture, 20 regeneration protocols have been developed
 and a molecular diagnostic kit for detection of Bunchy top Virus in Banana is in use at present.  The Micropropagation
 Technology Parks are serving as a platform for transfer of proven technologies and training in tissue culture.  So far,
 6.5 million plants have been produced and planted in 7500 hectares in 17 States.  Technologies for 10 species have
 been transferred to the industry.  A satellite park has been setup in North-East for popularization of technology and
 production of planting material for the region.  In addition, five Regional Hardening Units in different States are
 functioning well.
20.       The Committee is of the view that efforts should be made to make use of the tissue culture and floriculture
 technology in rural areas. Additional incentives should be given to persons willing to work in these areas.
BIO-INFORMATICS
21.       The plan scheme of bio-informatics envisages to provide a National Bio-informatics Network in the country
 designed to bridge the gaps in Biotechnology information and to establish links among scientists in Biotechnology. 
 The network aims to provide a single reference to various information resources of importance to biotechnology and
 modern biology including data banks of genetic importance published literature, patents and other information of
 scientific and commercial value.  It also aims to provide necessary infrastructural support for modern research in
 biology involving computationally intensive analysis.  The network consists of 11 Distributed Information Centers
 (DICs) and 46 sub-DICs computational facilities at the national level.  It has also established linkages with international
 institutions like International Centre for Co-operation in Bio-informatics (ICCB), a UNESCO based funded bio-
informatics programme and is also linked with EMB net, as well as international legume-data base and information
 services (ILDIS).  Educational and training activities in bio-informatics will also form part of the scheme.  National Jai
 Vigyan Mission on Mirror Sites for Genomic Research to establish four major databases have progressed well. These
 projects are being pursued at Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore; University of Pune; Jawaharlal Nehru University
 and Institute of Microbial Technology, Chandigarh.  New projects for establishing Centres of excellence in bio-
informatics will be taken up.
22.       The Committee was informed that there are 57 Bioinformatics centres at various research
 institutions/universities.  Each centre of the network has built up Bioinformatics resources in their specialized areas in
 the form of databases, software packages for application to Biotechnology and Molecular Biology, which are shared by
 the researchers in the country.  Towards the development of molecular modelling and simulation studies in

23.       The Bio-informatics programme offers a single window information resource in the country covering inter-
disciplinary areas of biotechnology and molecular  biology.    Human resource development has been recognized as an
 important area for effective sustenance of the bioinformatics programme.  Towards meeting the needs for trained
 bioinformatics professionals, long-term courses are being run as part of this network in five reputed Universities.

 activities.  The Biotechnology Information  System (BTS) centers have developed more than 100 databases on various
 aspects of biotechnology.  Several major International databases for application to genomics and proteomics have been
 established in the form of mirrors as part of the network.  A Virtual Private Network (VPN) has been established to link
 these databases through high speed and large bandwidth network to promote faster sharing of information. 
24.       The Biotechnology Information System Network (BTISnet) under the bioinformatics programme presently
 consists of sixty-one centres spread all over the country. Over the years, the network has created a resource base
 including computational infrastructure, databases and software. Six National Facilities on Interactive Graphics are
 dedicated to the promotion of molecular modelling and other related activities. The five one year advanced diploma
 courses and a M.Tech course on bioinformatics are being conducted through the reputed institutions for development of
 leadership quality in human resources on bioinformatics. About 100 subject specific databases have been developed
 through the BTISnet. Several major International databases for application to genomics and proteomics have been
 established in the form of Mirror sites as part of the network. These databases are being linked through high speed and
 large bandwidth network in the form of VPN, now termed as BIOGRID INDIA, to promote faster sharing of
 information as well as to encourage tandem research by various R&D labs and industrial units. At the micro level, the
 programme deals with the various issues related to the biological data. It covers the development of data analysis tools,
 modelling of biological macromolecules and their complexes, metabolic pathways, designing of new molecules such as
 drugs, peptide vaccines, proteins etc.
25.       During 2003-04, the Department proposes to upgrade five of the Distributed Information Centres (DICs) into
 Centres of Excellence (CoEs) on bioinformatics to generate high quality human resource and to carry out competitive
 R&D activities in the area of bioinformatics and computation biology for producing world class bioinformatics tools. 
 This will in turn help in revealing several applications in the area of molecular biology in general and genomics and
 proteomics in particular. It has also been recommended to upgrade five Sub-DICs in to the level of DICs to enhance the
 activities. More and more institutions have been proposed to be part of the Biogrid India in its second phase execution.
 At least three new Bioinformatics centres might be established to cover un-represented and remote institutions as part
 of the BTISnet.  More than 50 short-term courses have been proposed to be organized for training the researchers and
 scholars on the latest developments, which are taking place on bioinformatics.
26.       The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in the field of bioinformatics  which are expected
 to yield multidimensional results in variety of areas. The Committee, however, recommends that the Department should
 make all out efforts to ensure that biological data created in agricultural and other sectors is disseminated in a way that
 it also reaches the people working at grassroot levels.
JAI VIGYAN NATIONAL S&T MISSION
27.       Of the 21 National Jai Vigyan Missions initiated by Ministry of Science & Technology, four were launched by
 DBT in the areas of new generation vaccines, herbal product development, improvement of coffee and establishment of
 mirror sites of genomic databases in India. 
28.       The objectives of the programme include generating candidate vaccine(s) for diseases like cholera, rabies,
 Japanese encephalitis, tuberculosis, malaria and HIV.  The programme has been grouped under three categories. 
 Category (A) includes those ‘candidate vaccines’ where potential research leads are available and which now require
 clinical trials for generating pre-clinical data.  Under this category, vaccines for cholera and rabies are being attempted. 
 The programmes under category (B) are related to available leads on candidate vaccines where efficacy and
 immunogenicity need to be worked out.  The target vaccines are tissue culture-based Japanese encephalitis, DNA
 vaccines.  Under category (C), programmes require sustained R&D efforts with the possibility for development of

29.       The Committee was informed that under the programme about 25 technologies have been transferred to different
 industries. These include, diagnostic kits for detection of HIV, Hepatitis, Dengue, assessment of reproductive

30.       The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in vaccine research and development. The
 Committee hopes that the research done by the Department on microbial genomes, especially pathogens, in view of the
 burden of   infectious diseases on our people, will result in the elimination of diseases like Malaria and Tuberculosis in
 a time bound manner.  The Committee understands that India is on the threshold of producing the first ever DNA
 vaccine in the world, for rabies.  It is appropriately said that “In the area of infectious diseases, drugs, vaccines and
 diagnostics are the ultimate products expected out of genomic information”.  While the Committee commends the
 efforts of the Department and notes such achievements with satisfaction, it hopes that vaccines/medicines would be
 priced reasonably so that these are within the reach of common people.
BIO-TECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT
31.       Under this project, the Department is pursuing three programmes. Under Bio-technology programme for SC/ST,
 the aim is to provide the benefits for biotechnological processes and techniques to SC/ST people.  The projects funded
 under the programme are generally focused on technology transfer covering training, field demonstration and extension
 oriented activities on proven biotechnologies with the involvement of targeted groups.  The programme helps in
 increasing  skills  and income  of  the SC/ST people.  The  Bio-technology  based programme for Women aims to
 promote and use biotechnological processes and tools for entrepreneurship development and provide employment
 opportunities especially for women.  One of the objectives of the programme is to set up Women Biotechnology Park
 for economic empowerment of urban as well as rural women.  The Biotechnology Park aims to establish linkages
 between research institutions and industrial units.  The Park would also scale up the basic technologies for commercial
 utilization, and impart training in relevant areas to develop a pool of skilled and well trained women.  It would also
 evolve cooperation among women entrepreneurs and the corporate sector for joint marketing strategies.  The objectives
 of the third programme i.e. Programme for Rural Areas is to create awareness on biotechnology packages for income
 generation and better health care in rural areas; to use biotechnological process and tools for creating new avenues of
 employment for people living in rural areas; and to promote bio-village concept for socio-economic upliftment of rural
 areas. 
32.       The Committee was informed that several biotechnological programmes for the benefit of SC/ST population,
 women and rural areas have been implemented in the areas of biopesticides, biofertilisers, vermicompost &
 vermiculture, sericulture, floriculture, mushroom cultivation and medicinal plant production, poultry & fish farming
 and improvement of human health.  Universities, national laboratories, state government institutions, krishi vigyan
 kendras, NGOs and voluntary organisations implemented the projects under the programme. Fifty-five thousand
 families have benefitted through more than 125 projects. Further, special projects for earthquake victims of Kutch
 region of Gujarat benefitted 4000 families.
33.       When the Committee wanted to know as to why funds at the R.E. stage have been reduced for the year 2002-03,
 the Department explained that such reduction took place because many of the proposals received under the programme
 lacked scientific merit or relevance to the objectives of the programme.   However, The department has written to a
 large number of institutions covering ICAR institutions, CSIR laboratories, agriculture & other universities, Krishi
 Vigyan Kendras, State S&T Councils etc. to make them aware of the programme and encourage them to submit their
 proposals.  The Department also invited fresh proposals for Bio-village projects, organic farming, redressal of the
 problems of food and nutritional, health and hygiene particularly among women, SC/ST population and other weaker
 sections.  It is expected that during the year 2003-2004, many new projects in the above areas would be implemented in
 addition to the ongoing activities and keeping the same in view the enhanced allocation has been earmarked for 2003-
2004.
34.       The Committee is of the view that the farmers and other needy people from the target groups should be provided
 with latest biotechnologies for mushroom cultivation and vermi-composting. The Committee notes with satisfaction
 that the Department has started approaching the State Governments for getting their support for production of bio-
fertilizer. While it is important for the Department to augment their efforts in this regard, the Committee recommends

HUMAN GENETICS
36.       The programme aims at identifying, mapping and characterizing genes associated with genetic disorders
 prevalent in India and exploiting the knowledge created by available human, microbial and parasitic genomic sequences
 so as to usher in the tools of molecular medicine for better management of diseases and disorders.
37.       Under Human Genetics, sixteen genetic clinics were established for providing molecular diagnosis and
 counselling for the common genetic disorders such as beta-thalassemia, Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) and

 genetic diagnosis including prenatal diagnosis and counselling for major genetic disorders. In the programme on
 functional genomics, powerful computational capability for handling large scale human genome sequence data, robotic
 methodologies for genotyping and PCR based diagnostics for common genetic disorders have been developed.

 ongoing research on major initiatives that have been taken up during the current financial year. The initiatives taken
 include: transgenic animals, virology–HIV/AIDS and Japanese encephalitis, small animal facilities, technology
 incubator etc.

Production of important biological and bioactive molecules using suitable expression systems and modern fermentation

Programme support for creation of infrastructures in newer areas of biotechnological research.

EXPEDITIOUS CLEARENCE OF PROJECTS SUBMITTED BY THE DEPARTMENT
76.       The Committee was apprised that the proposals submitted by the Department are subjected to periodic review
 and assessment by different agencies including the Planning Commission. The Department further stated that it
 remained ever ready to subject itself and its activities to scrutiny. However, it informed the Committee that time taken
 for review of its projects is too long and therefore comes in the way of its expeditious implementation. While pursuing
 research in the field of science, the Department has to constantly innovate to remain abreast of the ever-evolving
 activities of the scientific community across the globe. Delay in clearing a project, therefore, will throw a spanner in the
 wheel of scientific progress which the Department is carrying forward within a limited budget, to fulfil the objectives
 set before them in a goal oriented and time bound manner. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that all the
 proposals of the Department must be cleared expeditiously and within a set time frame.
BUDGET PROPOSALS AT R.E.STAGE
77.       The Department informed the Committee that the reduction of its budget at the R.E. stage causes a lot of
 problem in resetting its priorities. It prepares its plan as per the budget proposals and accordingly prepares its schedule
 of activities. Time taken to re-do the priorities due to cut in R.E. stage is not less than three or four months. Such re-
planning for scientific projects deviates the Department from the set objectives. The Committee is constrained to note
 that such problems are confronted by the Department.
Professor G. Padmanabhan, the UNESCO Professor in Biotechnology Department of Biochemistry, Indian Institute of
 Science, Bangalore in an important article “Contrary to reports, India has not missed the biotech bus” has written about
 the budget requirements of biotechnology which is revealing:
“A single funding agency in the USA has a Rs.4,000 crores budget for genomics. In India, all the funding agencies
 together can mobilise about Rs.100 crores a year for research in this area. It is interesting to note that the country can
 still come up with new drugs, vaccines and diagnostics within this limited budget. If India plays its cards right, it can
 hope to become a world leader in modern vaccine manufacturing, since MNCs are not interested in this field due to
 poor economic returns. All that is needed is a commitment on the part of the Government to ensure availability of the
 committed amount for the next five years, release of grants in time, a mechanism for quick clearance of clinical trials to
 convert the results of the laboratory into commercial products”.
78.       Determination and will of the scientists to achieve the goal which is comparable to international standards and
 within a limited but committed fund is indeed heartening. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgets for
 all the Departments dealing with science and technology including that of the Department of Biotechnology may not be
 reduced at the R.E. stage.

 programmes in a comprehensive and an integrated manner for the benefit of women in remote areas such as islands,

 women established in Chennai in 1998 has become a huge success. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Department may take initiatives to establish more such parks in different parts of the country for the benefit of women

 and society at large.

8.         The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department to provide molecular diagnosis and counseling
 for the common genetic disorders prevalent in the country.   The Committee recommends that the Department may
 provide wide publicity to the programme through print as well as electronic media so that the benefits of these activities
 of the Department could percolate to the underprivileged and weaker sections of society.
(Para 38)
9.         The Committee feels that the country has the advantage of production of all four commercial silk varieties viz;
 mulberry, tusser, eri and muga.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department is according priority on
 Seri biotechnology with special focus on non-mulberry silk. It is heartening for the Committee to know that the Indian
 Institute of Science, Bangalore has, for the first time, done the important job of adopting control measures for pests of
 silk worm. As sericulture is suitable for marginal, small and landless farmers, it has tremendous scope for expansion in
 view of its employment generation potential.  Efforts should therefore be made to strengthen the linkages between
 extension and R&D units.  The technology delivery systems should be streamlined by providing need based training
 and effective field demonstration. Various communication channels should also be used to disseminate information
 about the new measures to improve Sericulture.
(Para 40)
10.       The Committee recommends that the technology developed at the laboratory stage under the programme should
 be brought to the level of pilot plant scale and should be transferred to the industry.  Moreover, the technology
 developed should be patented so as to safeguard the rights of those who develop it.
(Para 43)
11.       The Committee also recommends that some new projects in the area of microbial and industrial bio-technology
 should be started with emphasis on development of novel molecules for application in the pharmaceutical and industrial
 sectors.
(Para 44)
12.       The Committee recommends that the Department may explore the possibilities of applying for a patent at the
 midway stage of producing a product so as to safeguard the rights of scientists engaged in doing valuable research in
 biotechnology.
(Para 45)
13.       The Committee notes that biotechnology holds the key to food security as well as farmers’ security. Therefore,
 the            Committee recommends that the on-going and new initiatives concerning food biotechnology may be further
 augmented. It notes with satisfaction that the Department has developed a food which is so nutritious that One kg. of
 food is equivalent to five 5kg. of normal food. While producing more such foods, care must be taken to make the price
 affordable. The Committee understands that the technology for such foods is transferred to industry and therefore it is
 all the more important to remain vigilant about keeping the price of such products affordable.
(Para 47)
14.       The Committee observes that the National Institute of Immunology (NII) should also take steps to focus its
 research activities on certain unexplored areas in the field of Immunodiagnostics.
(Para 52)
15.       The Committee also recommends that the Department may explore the possibility of raising funds by
 collaborating with the industry for providing additional support to research activities. It will open opportunities for
 making the Institute self-sufficient.
 (Para 53)
16.       While the Committee notes with satisfaction the contributions of the Centre to forensic medicine and wildlife
 preservation, it recommends that in order to disseminate the DNA fingerprinting technology, a number of lectures and
 workshops should be conducted for the benefit of various police officers, judicial officers, forensic scientists and
 environmentalists.  This technology also needs to be included in the syllabus of National as well as State Police
 Training Academies & Institutions.
(Para 60)
17.       The Committee notes with satisfaction the research activities undertaken at the National Brain Research Centre
 (NBRC). 
(Para 64)
18.       Moreover, in order to inform Medical Colleges and concerned Departments of Neurology about the research
 findings of the NBRC, the Department should undertake activities in a networking manner with the existing

 neuroscience groups/institutions in the country and promote multidisciplinary research in neuroscience.

19.       The Committee endorses the vision of the Department to make agriculture sustainable by using biotechnology.
 To get better yields, we need plants and methods of cultivation which will be in harmony with biodiversity and eco-
system and therefore will not bring down the fertility of land and kill useful animals, pests and weeds. This objective
 can be achieved by, among others, changing plant characteristics through genetic modification. The Committee
 impresses upon the Department to work with full vigour to realise this objective. Prof. M.S.Swaminathan, one of the
 leading figures who spearheaded green revolution in our country, has said that green revolution can become ever green
 revolution by making it pro-nature, pro-poor and pro-women. Therefore, the Committee emphasizes that the
 Department while focusing on biotechnology should also harness social forces for making our agriculture sustainable.
(Para 68)
20.       The Committee was apprised that the proposals submitted by the Department are subjected to periodic review
 and assessment by different agencies including the Planning Commission. The Department further stated that it
 remained ever ready to subject itself and its activities to scrutiny. However, it informed the Committee that time taken
 for review of its projects is too long and therefore comes in the way of its expeditious implementation. While pursuing
 research in the field of science, the Department has to constantly innovate to remain abreast of the ever-evolving
 activities of the scientific community across the globe. Delay in clearing a project, therefore, will throw a spanner in the
 wheel of scientific progress which the Department is carrying forward within a limited budget, to fulfil the objectives
 set before them in a goal oriented and time bound manner. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that all the
 proposals of the Department must be cleared expeditiously and within a set time frame.
(Para 76)
21.       The Department informed the Committee that the reduction of its budget at the R.E. stage causes a lot of
 problem in resetting its priorities. It prepares its plan as per the budget proposals and accordingly prepares its schedule
 of activities. Time taken to re-do the priorities due to cut in R.E. stage is not less than three or four months. Such re-
planning for scientific projects deviates the Department from the set objectives. The Committee is constrained to note
 that such problems are confronted by the Department.
Professor G. Padmanabhan, the UNESCO Professor in Biotechnology Department of Biochemistry, Indian Institute of
 Science, Bangalore in an important article “Contrary to reports, India has not missed the biotech bus” has written about
 the budget requirements of biotechnology which is revealing:
“A single funding agency in the USA has a Rs.4,000 crores budget for genomics. In India, all the funding agencies
 together can mobilise about Rs.100 crores a year for research in this area. It is interesting to note that the country can
 still come up with new drugs, vaccines and diagnostics within this limited budget. If India plays its cards right, it can
 hope to become a world leader in modern vaccine manufacturing, since MNCs are not interested in this field due to
 poor economic returns. All that is needed is a commitment on the part of the Government to ensure availability of the
 committed amount for the next five years, release of grants in time, a mechanism for quick clearance of clinical trials to
 convert the results of the laboratory into commercial products”.
(Para 77)
22.       Determination and will of the scientists to achieve the goal which is comparable to international standards and
 within a limited but committed fund is indeed heartening. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgets for
 all the Departments dealing with science and technology including that of the Department of Biotechnology may not be
 reduced at the R.E. stage.
(Para78)
23.       India is rich with traditional knowledge. Our people with centuries of experiences have emerged as practitioners
 of such knowledge.  This rich reservoir of such resources must be understood scientifically and safeguarded.  The
 Committee was informed  by a Member that Ganga Jal, Gou Mutra and Gober have anti-bacterial properties. It was also
 told that Gober is radiation resistant. It was told that when hospital wastes were treated with layers of Gober for five
 months, it was found that all bacteria, toxin and poison had been neutralised.  Therefore, the Committee recommends
 that steps must be taken by the Department to explore the anti-bacterial properties of Ganga  Jal, Gou Mutra and Gober,
 specially the effectiveness for treating hospital waste.
(Para 79)

 various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary
 allocation of Rs.273.35 crores, as sought by the Department for the year 2003-2004, under Demand No. 82, may be
 approved.

C. RAMACHANDRAIAH

REPORT
Indian tradition of pursuing science and science related activities dates back to thousands and thousands of years. 
 After we attained independence the Government accorded top priority to science and scientific research.  Prime Minister
 Jawaharlal Nehru described our planning process as nothing but science in action.  He declared that “It is science alone
 that could solve the problems of hunger and poverty”.   In spite of resource constraints India’s success in the fields of
 science and technology is spectacular.
To give a direction to the promotion of Science and Technology the Department of Science and Technology was
 established with the primary objective of promoting new areas of Science and Technology and to play the role of a nodal
 department for organising, co-ordinating and promoting S&T activities in the country.  The mandate given to DST
 include, among others:
Ø      Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on S&T
Ø      Promotion of new areas of scientific research
Ø      Co-ordination of inter-departmental S&T efforts
Ø      Support basic and applied research in universities and other institutions
International S&T Co-operation

Ø      Catalyzing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development

Besides, the Department provide services in the areas of:

v               Technology Development and Application (TDB)

 namely; Foundation to promote grass root level invention, Women Scientists Scholarship Scheme, Swarnajayanti
 Fellowships for outstanding young scientists, Fund for Improvement of S&T Infrastructure (FIST) in universities and
 related institutions, Kishore Vigyanik Protsahan, Technopreneur Promotion Program (TePP), Indian Climate Research,
 Establishing high performance computing network facilities for  research purposes, Executing Joint Technology
 Development projects with industry and socio-economic Ministries, Strengthening Seismicity programme, Modernizing
 autonomous research institutions, Setting up of a National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration (NABL) and
 Setting up a Patent Facilitating Cell to provide support to scientists and technologists on all aspects of patenting.
 
3.         The   Department has set the following targets to be achieved during the year 2003-2004:
Research and Development Support
v
                 Strengthen support to basic research in frontier areas of science and technology
v                 Encouragement to young scientists
v                 Creation of Centres of Excellence in R&D in Universities and Institutions
v                 Modernize autonomous S&T institutions

v                 Support to students at school level onwards to take interest in scientific pursuit.

 areas identified in “Vision 2020”.
2.                  Promote R&D in Drugs and Pharmaceuticals through joint projects with the industry.
3.                  Promote S&T Mission Mode Projects
4.                  Technology for Bamboo Products
5.                  Provide support to technopreneurs for developing innovative ideas.
6.                  To provide and integrate S&T output with the programmes of socio-economic Ministries.
7.                  TIFAC Technology Vision 2020 Mission Mode Projects.
8.                Seismology

SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY FOR WOMEN
11.       Women form a very important part of the national scientific workforce.  Indian science requires induction of more
 women scientists and technologists to improve the quality of science and its application towards national development.
 Women face special problems due to their
duties towards motherhood and family and, most of them, suffer “break in their careers” due to these responsibilities.  
 There has been a long-felt need to have special schemes to revive their professional careers.
12.       The Committee was informed that through the scheme ‘Science and Technology for Women’ support is provided
 to time bound action-research projects designed to reduce drudgery, provide newer opportunities for income generation
 based on local resources, address problems pertaining to women’s health and nutrition including occupational health. 
 Successful technology packages are then replicated to field test the model through coordinated programmes.  The
 Department also provides support for the setting up of rural Women’s Technology Parks to showcase technology
 packages relevant to the area, provide technical and entrepreneurial training to women and interface with S&T institutions
 to address specific problems faced by women.
13.       The Government of India, in keeping with its commitment towards welfare and empowerment of women, has come
 up with a special and innovative new scheme which  envisages support to woman scientists, with or without a break in
 career, to pursue science in all its aspects and encourage them to continue in the scientific profession and also to
 contribute towards application of science and technology to societal development.  Approximately 100 scholarships a year
 will be awarded in the specialized subject areas. It is also interesting to report that the women scientists have showed an
 overwhelming response for the scheme. Approximately 5000 women scientists have already approached the department
 for support under this scheme.
14.       Women Scientists Scheme will provide opportunities to women scientists and technologists between the age group
 of 30-50 years.  Under this scheme, women scientists will be provided attractive financial support to pursue research in
 frontier areas of science and engineering, on societal problems requiring S&T intervention and for receiving training for
 possible self-employment in S&T related services sector.

TECHNOLOGY FOR BAMBOO PRODUCTS
33.
       The Committee was informed that while some of the national centres of excellence in India possess rich expertise
 in bamboo technology, the knowledge flow to the industry has not come up to the desired level.   As such it is high time to
 bring the technology sourcing avenues and industries for technology development transfer and commercialization.   Thus
 the aim is to undertake a programme at the national level which could impart a significant boost to the usage of bamboo,
 promote specialized products for commercialization and would generate good employment opportunities.
34.       The Planning Commission has taken a new initiative to additionally develop and support in the Tenth Plan, a range
 of bamboo related activities, and responsibilities.  A National Mission on Bamboo Applications(NMBA) has already been
 invested with increased activities.
35.       The basis for the increased allocation are the additional tasks and activity areas that have devolved on the NMBA,
 as a result of discussions with the Planning Commission.  The additional funds are, therefore, earmarked for:
a)            Demonstration of newly developed technologies, in the composites/ wood substitutes segment, and for structural
 application, agro-processing, grid reinforcement and soil stabilization.
b)            Development of product and application standards, testing and certification, market surveys and market
 promotion of new products, and preparation of manuals, codes of practice and technology dossiers.
The programme on technology for bamboo products is being designed more in the development-financing pattern
 while keeping the market acceptance, commercialization, and product branding as the ultimate objectives: The
 programme would be so designed that some seed capital could be provided on returnable basis to various identified sub-
projects aimed at specific product development activities.
While all the projects would necessarily be taken up in partnership with the industries, some may require a
 tripartite arrangement on knowledge share/transfer from academic/research institutions in India & abroad. The programme
 would also support technology transfer & absorption from advanced overseas sources towards domestic consumption and
 export opportunities. With certain technological maturity in the Indian system, the programme could encourage
 technology tie-ups & transfers from Indian industry to their counterparts in the developing world.
A provision of Rs. 43.25 crores has been proposed for the scheme during 2003– 04.

THE PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT SUPPORT FUND (PRDSF)
40.       The emerging economic, trade and intellectual property scenario, nationally and internationally, necessitates a
 qualitative change in the industry, to drive Indian pharmaceutical industry away from manufacturing only known drugs to
 discovering and commercializing new molecules. The availability of trained scientific manpower of high quality, S&T
 infrastructure, accumulated knowledge of traditional medicinal system and large bio-diversity of our country offer a great
 opportunity to our industry. However, at present, most Indian drug firms, due to their small size compared to international
 operators and limited resources, are not in a position to invest in a viable new drug development programme. At the same
 time, several Indian academic institutions and national laboratories have established impressive infrastructure and
 developed excellent expertise in selected areas of drug development.
41.       The Committee was informed that the scheme aims at enhancing capabilities of the Indian drugs and
 pharmaceutical industry towards development of new drugs by synergising the strengths of publicly funded R&D
 institutions and the Indian Pharmaceutical drug industry for discovery and introduction of new drugs and practices in all
 systems of medicine.
42.       During the tenth plan the Department has a provision of Rs.150 Crores for the Pharmaceuticals Research and
 Development Support Fund (PRDSF).   This is the corpus fund.  The interest earned from this fund will be used for the
 purposes of supporting Research & Development (R&D) Programmes and setting up of the National facilities for
 furthering R&D activities in the country.  Since the interest on this corpus will be accrued only after a year, an initial
 budgetary support of Rs.10 crores has been provided for sustaining various activities during the financial year 2003-2004. 
 It is proposed to constitute a Drug Development Promotion Board to administer the fund.
43.       It was stated that under this scheme financial support would be provided to national labs and academic institutions
 for joint research programmes conceived by the industry and public funded R&D institutions. The broad objectives of this
 programme include: Development of new molecules and practices for diseases prevalent in the Indian climatic zone by
 bringing together the scientific expertise existing in the country in research institutions and industry; Promote R&D at any
 stage of development in all systems of medicine including alternative system of medicines and Creating state-of-the-art
 infrastructure facilities at par with international standards for the benefit of the Indian Industry and other users.
44.       The existing ongoing Plan Programme on Drug and Pharmaceuticals Research will be merged with this new
 activity.  The broad objectives of this fund are: -
1.         Funding research in all the systems of medicine in particular development of new molecules, natural products
 including plant, mineral and animal based preparations, development of new drug delivery systems,       application of
 genomics/proteomics and development of key chemicals/reagents used in drug research.
2.         To create an enabling infrastructure for promotion of R&D at all stages including clinical research.

 effects on par with the studies on side effect from synthetic drugs.
c)         A well knit coordination and collaboration among the cultivators of the different raw materials for the Siddha
 drugs, micro-propagators of some industries, Department of Science and Technology, national laboratories and university
 departments involved in the development of Siddha Medicine has to be thought of.
d)         A well established universal nomenclature and methodology of naming the plants and development of well trained
 manpower to identify the different raw materials is considered to be the basic necessity.   Above all, it is also pointed out
 that a guide manual for identification of medicinal plants particularly to the industrialist has to be brought out at the
 earliest.
e)         There is a need to develop Siddha Drugs for killer diseases like HIV, cancer etc. through collaborative research
 project mode.
Based on the seminar interactions, certain collaborative projects on arthritis, HIV leucoderma, psoriasis and fibroid
 uterus are being contemplated.
48.       The Committee commends the Department for reorienting its strategy to produce molecules for production of drugs
 so that it can meet the challenges of product patent arising out of the enforcement of intellectual property rights          
 from December 2004.  While the Committee notes that the Department has earmarked Rs.150 crores as corpus fund for
 pharmaceutical research and development it recommends that the benefits derived from the funds provided by the
 Government of India should be utilised correctly.   The Committee was told that many multinational corporations could
 help in pharmaceutical research and development.   The Committee noted with anguish and pain that most of the
 pharmaceutical formulation developed under the exemptions given by the Government of India is taken by the

 multinational corporations to their head offices abroad and patented there and marketed as international brands and at
 international rates.  The Committee was agonized to know that such formulations are produced by Indian scientists and
 with the help of Indian tax payers’ money and yet the benefits are reaped by the multinational drug companies who sell
 the products at a price which most of the Indians cannot afford.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that
 such technology or formulation produced by Indian scientists must be patented in India before these are transferred or
 taken abroad.  The Committee further recommends that patenting of such formulations in India should be made
 compulsory.   The Committee notes the alarming trend of multinational companies manufacturing even Ayurvedic
 products, branding them and selling them with a high commercial pitch.   The Committee recommends that all out efforts
 must be made to reverse this trend and safeguard our traditional knowledge from appropriation by foreign agencies.
SYNERGY PROJECTS
49.       The Committee was informed that the objective of the synergy projects is to synergise and synchronise various
 critical technology related issues by providing seed funds in the
frontiers areas of science & technology. When the Committee asked the Department the details of the projects to be
 initiated with the provision of Rs.10 crores, it was informed that they have proposed, the following programmes for this
 scheme during 2003-2004
1)         Rural Development –related technologies
2)         Energy, health and water security
3)            Environmental Security – related technologies
4)         Safety and disaster preparedness
5)            Incubation Centres for supporting small and medium industries.
6)            National Security.
7)         Science in India
8)            Advanced Manufacturing & Process Technologies
9)         Up-gradation of indigenous technologies for research infrastructure development.
CENTRE FOR LIQUID CRYSTAL RESEARCH
50.       The Committee was informed that the original objective of the Department was to build a center of excellence,
 which will have a focus on basic sciences, and would also develop a bias towards technology, keeping in line with
 international trends on liquid crystal materials and devices.   The infrastructure for research and development was
 strengthened to enlarge the scope of the research investigations.  This expansion is required to keep up with the
 international trends in this sector.  Modifications in the proposed plan will also be based on the needs of the industry as
 and when desired. The Centre was set up in 1985 as a society under the Department of Electronics but now this Centre has
 been transferred to the Department of Science & Technology.
51.            Highlighting the achievements made by the centre, the Committee was informed that a highly sophisticated
 magnetic suscepto-meter with super conducting pick up coils and SQUID to measure very low currents has been procured
 and installed.  This is the only such facility in the country, which is an important tool in characterizing many materials.
52.       It was further stated that the synthetic organic chemists of the Center form one of the leading groups, which has
 prepared a variety of new materials (both calamitic and discotic ) and some of the contributions by the group rank
 amongst the most accessed papers, as judged by the Journal of Materials Chemistry brought out by the Royal Institute of
 Chemistry.  This is an indication of the front line work being carried out at the Center.   The compounds have enormous
 potential applications as wide viewing angle, high contrast ratio and faster devices.
53.            Besides, the Centre carries out other major research studies, which include:
            a)   In another scientific work very high conductivity along the columnar axis of disc shaped molecule has already
 been achieved.   These can be thought of as analogous to molecular wires, using which one can envisage numerous
 applications like photoconductor, light emitting diodes, photovoltaic cells, etc.
            b)   Re-entrance of twist grain boundary mesophases that is analogous to the Abrikosov flux lattice phase in
 superconductors has been unambiguously proved.
c)      A novel example photoinduced disorder to order transition, which is contrary to the normal order to disordered

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/117threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:27:52]
 transition, has been observed for the first time in liquid crystals.
d)         Studies have been done on azobenzene doped materials having smectic A-chiral smectic C a transition, which
 showed enhancement in the tilt fluctuation mode.
e)         The first achiral bent core banana-shaped measogen consisting of a thermally and hydrolytically stable aromatic
 core has been systhesized that exhibits electrically switchable mesophsed over a wide temperature range.
f)          New reagents have been developed for the synthesis of triphenylene based discotic LC’s.
g)         First rational synthesis of dibenzopyrene based discotic LC’s was achieved.
h)         A variety of novel discotic LC’s and matellomesogens were prepared and characterized.
54.       Informing the Committee about the collaboration with industry, it was stated that Centre For Liquid Crystal
 Research (CLCR) has been working in close collaboration with the Bharat Electronic Ltd. (BEL) for the production of the
 Twisted Nematic LCDs for electronic instruments, petrol bunk displays, airport and railway station displays, etc.  Efforts
 are underway to start developmental activities in the area of Super Twisted Nematic dotmatrix displays which will be
 required for small hand held low cost SIMPUTERs.
55.       During the year the Centre aims to conduct the programmes namely:
a)
                  Quasi-one dimensional electrical conductivity of columnar phases of discotic liquid crystals, the anisotropy
 in electrical conductivity (the ratio of parallel to perpendicular conductivity along and perpendicular to the
 columns) attaining value as high as 10 10  . The possible uses include molecular wires for transport of
 charge or excitons, and applications as fast, high resolution scanning and xerography, hybrid computer
 chips, etc.
b)                 Discotic nematics for use as wide viewing angle LCDs.  A problem with this device is that, firstly, it is a
 slow device, and secondly the temperature of the discotic Nematic phase is rather high.  Solutions to these
 difficulties have been found quite promising and may lead to practical devices with improved
 characteristics.
c)
                  Effect of pressure on phase transitions and properties of liquid crystals.  Pressure being a fundamental
 thermodynamic parameter, the importance of these studies can hardly be overemphasized.   It would be fair
 to say that the centre’s laboratory is probably one of the most well equipped center in this special field.  A
 variety of new phenomena e.g. pressure induced liquid crystallinity, critical, multicritical points etc. have
 been discovered here which have important theoretical consequences.  It is also proposed to set up high
 pressure x-ray diffraction apparatus, which will throw light on structural
changes taking place with the application of pressure.  In addition, one can envisage some results of
 practical importance, e.g. in oceanography and the effect of pressure (or depth) on the structural stability,
 especially of biologically important liquid crystalline systems.
d)                 Photo induced effects in liquid crystals.  This topic is of great interest from the fundamental point of view
 and also has important potential applications for optical storage devices, optical communication, light
 dependent capacitance and resistivity etc.    
56.       The Committee commends the research being conducted by the centre and notes with admiration the excellence of
 its results.  It hopes that the centre will further build on its manifold achievements and emerge as a leading scientific
 institution in the country. 
POPULARISATION OF SCIENCE
57.       The Committee was informed that the Department is making the children the real starting point for popularizing
 science and technology.   However, the Committee notes with concern that there are no laboratories and other
 infrastructure for promoting science among children.  The Department itself has informed the Committee that there is
 marked decline of interests among students to pursue science courses in our educational institutions.   To generate interest
 among students for science and scientific research, the Committee recommends that science cafes and children’s scientific
 parks may be established in rural and urban areas with local as well as corporate assistance.   Apart from this the
 Committee recommends that wide spread publicity must be given for the works done by our scientists and scientific
 institutions for making people aware about their achievements.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 allocations at R.E. stage for all Departments dealing with science & technology may not be reduced.

(Para 20)

 such activities for the benefit of scientists, researchers and the general public.   After all to save our traditional knowledge

(Para 25)

 seems to be a necessity.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Department must concentrate its attention
 towards producing such technologies which will be consistent with ecology and industrial development.

R E P O R T
 
            Dal is a Himalayan urban lake comprising of five basins and a myriad of inter- connecting channels. It is one of the
 most beautiful lakes of India and the second largest lake in the capital city of Srinagar of the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
 Mountains on its three sides surround the lake and at the foothills of the Zabawan mountain-an offshoot of the Himalayan
 chain the Dal Lake is located. The famous Moghul gardens around the lake have been laid along the shores during 16-17th
 century and their number was about five hundred but now only a few of these have survived. Dal Lake is unique in having
 hundreds of houseboats that afford an opportunity to tourists to reside on the lake in an atmosphere of peace and tranquility.
 The boats are served by Shikaras, which more or less resemble the gondolas of Venice but are smaller in size and are
 tastefully decorated. Besides the Moghul monuments, the campus of the University of Kashmir is also located along the
 shores of the lake. Overlooking the lake are two hillocks that house the famous temples of Shankaracharya and Hari Parbat.
 A perennial inflow channel enters the lake from the north and supplies about 80% of the water. Towards the southwest side
 an outflow channel drains the lake water into a tributary of the River Jhelum. Parallel to this exit is a stone-lined canal,
 which connects the lake with the tributary. This channel is used for movement of boats in and out of the lake and prevents
 inundation of floating gardens during high floods.
2.         This Lake has historically been the centre of Kashmiri civilization and has played a major role in the economy of the
 state through its attraction of tourists as well as its utilization as a source of food and water.  Traditionally the markets of
 Srinagar have thrived from the famous floating gardens and irrigated land within the lake area.
3.         Of late there has been great concern about the fast deterioration of this lake’s ecosystem.   The gradual reclamation of
 the lake to provide building and vegetable growing land and the increase in the area of floating gardens have combined with
 natural processes to reduce the area of open water within the lake area.  The present open lake area of only 12 km
2 (approx.)
 is but a vestige of what was there even in the 18 th century, and is little over half of the area existing at the turn of this
 century. The shrinking of the lake is due to "siltification" - where the feed rivers dump huge silt deposits into the water
 catchment, a process dramatically accelerated by local deforestation. Primarily, however, it is sewage of the one million
 residents of the nearby city of Srinagar, compounded by the human waste created by the 48,000 Lake Dwellers, which is
 'suffocating' the lake and contaminating its water mass. Raw sewage is feeding an already rapid growth of algae and raising
 weed growth to critical and unmanageable levels.
4.         Increases in agricultural activity and the reduction of plant cover on the hillsides surrounding the lake with the
 consequential increase in surface erosion and leaching of soil nutrients have added increasing quantities of nutrient-rich

 runoff.  Human settlements within and around the edges of the lake have also added nutrient-rich seepage and effluent.  The
 direct discharge from houseboats had added human waste to a point where health hazards are assuming serious proportions.
 Diseases, notably gastro-enteritis and cholera, are believed to be linked directly to this ecological deterioration. Further,
 interruptions to the internal flow of lake water caused by weirs, islands, bunds, land between houseboats, etc, has reduced
 the capacity of the lake to respond to the stresses placed on it.  Almost opaque and stagnant water and its poor quality are all
 too apparent.  Lake weed growth is prolific.   As a consequence of such factors, today the health and very life of the Dal
 Lake are threatened and in short, the once watery jewel set within the crown of Himalayan Mountains is inflicted with slow
 death.
5.         Today, critiques often describe “Dal Lake”, as “Dull Lake” and even accuse concerned authorities of preparing for its
 funeral.   They sadly compare it with ‘Anchar Lake’ which is already finished and to ‘Wular Lake’ which was recently
 shown as only knee deep due to extensive silting and area of the lake has drastically reduced by over 60% from original 200
 sq. kms. The vistas have become a sewage canal. Srinagar city’s drains are clogged with human waste. The city has created
 satellite slums around it. Population is increasing at an alarming rate putting pressure for housing them in the land locked
 valley. As a result, mountains are losing their forests, rivers and lakes their limpidity, valley its chinars that stood as
 sentinels of time and living witnesses of the rise and fall of many a kingdom, roads their poplar and willow avenues, Mughal
 gardens the great variety of their flowers.
PHYSICAL FEATURES OF THE LAKE
6.         The Dal Lake is a postglacial lake of shallow depth and is believed by some geologists that it is the remnant of a
 Pleistocene oligotrophic Lake that once covered the entire valley of Kashmir. There are other geologists who opine that it
 was a flood plain lake. The Dal Lake is at an altitude of  1600 m above sea level and lies between 34
o 5’ and  34o 10’ North
 Latitude and 74o 8’ and 79o 7’ East Longitude. With a catchment area of about 300 sq., km the lake is fed by several small
 streams around the shoreline, by springs under the lakebed and by one large stream, Telbal Nalla on the northern end of the
 lake.  Outflow from the lake is though a weir and lock system, Dal Gate at the south-western corner into Chinar Bagh which
 is a loop channel of Jhelum River and through Amir Khan Nalla into the Anchar Lake.
7.         The Dal Lake is multibasined with Hazratbal, the Bod-Dal, and the Gagribal and the Nagin as its four basins. The
 Hazratbal basin is situated between the Telbal and the Nishat.  On the eastern side of the basin is situated Nagin Bagh, while
 on its western side two famous Mughal gardens are located. The area of the Bod-Dal extends from Kotarkhana to Nishat
 Bund.  A small island, Ropa Lank, in its centre is the conspicuous feature of this part of the lake.   The Gagribal basin
 extends from Kotarkhana to Nehru Park.  This part of the lake touched the outer fringes of Shankaracharya hill before 1930
 when the present Boulevard Road was constructed.   The Nagin basin, which is separated from the main lake by a narrow
 strip of marshy land, is connected with the Hazratbal basin on the northwest.
8.         Morphometrically, these basins differ markedly in regard to their area, volume, maximum depth and indices of
 shoreline development, etc. Among different lake basins of Dal Lake the largest in area is the Hazratbal (3.54km
2) and the
 smallest the Nagin (0.89km2), but the Nagin is the deepest (6.0 m) and the Gagribal the shallowest (2.5 m).  The lake basin
 walls are essentially convex towards the water as the volume index figures are less than unity. The ratio between and mean
 and the maximum depth ranges between 0.20 and 0.25, indicating the gentle slope of the lakebed. The total water surface of
 the Dal Lake is 11.45 sq. km and total volume estimated at 9.83 X 10 6  m 3.  Floating gardens covers a sizeable portion
 (approx.0.3 km.) of the lake extending from the Hazratblal basin to the Gagribal, on the western side.  The lake has been
 extensively manipulated in this part to form man-made islands separated by canals and areas of water covered by floating
 gardens. Natural deposition of silt from the Telbal Nalla has also created extensive marshes around the northern end of the
 lake.   Many dwellings have been built on these islands and reclamations, apart from the areas used for agriculture, are
 extensively covered by willow and poplar trees.
9.         The catchment area of Dal Lake can be broadly divided into five subcatchments: (i) Dachigam, (ii) Telbal, (iii) Lake
 Hillside, (iv) Srinagar North, and (v) Srinagar City.   Among these subcatchments, Dachigam is the largest in area (145 x
 106 m2) and comprises mainly the Dachigam Game Reserve and south-facing slopes.  The Dachigam Game Reserve is a
 restricted area and has good forest and ground cover but the south-facing slopes have been denuded of forest cover due to
 overgrazing of cattle and in the past by burning off.  It is evident that denudation of this area is resulting in significant
 contribution of silt to the Dachigam Nalla which drains this catchment area.  At the outlet of the catchment, the flow of the
 Dachigam Nalla is diverted to the irrigation canals in Telbal catchment, the Harwan.  The balance continues to flow through
 Telbal Nalla into Dal Lake. The Telbal catchment, which begins at the foothills of the south-facing hills, has been denuded
 by overgrazing.  The gentle slopes in lower reaches of this area are, however, extensively used for paddy cultivation. The
 Lake Hill side catchment drains into Dal Lake via a number of small streams around the east and south sides of the lake.  
 Around the lake shore, the lower land slopes of this catchment have been utilized for rice cultivation, orchards and gardens. 
 Beyond this, the land rises very steeply to 1000 m above the lake.   The steep expose slopes do not support any vegetation,

 and in some areas overgrazing has contributed to denudation.  The Srinagar North catchment comprises mainly outer
 suburbs of Srinagar City and is extensively used for paddy cultivation.   The topography is very flat and drainage is via slow
 flowing canals and open drains which in parts are badly contaminated with sewage and rubbish.  The Srinagar City
 catchment is fully urbanized and in most parts it drains via the Brari Nambal (a large swampy area which is grossly polluted
 with sewage and rubbish) that in turn drains into Dal Lake via a canal.
SOURCES OF POLLUTANTS
10.       One of the main factors contributing to the environmental deterioration of the lake comes from the pressure of human
 settlements along its shores and within the lake itself. With the growth in population, the pressure on the lake and it’s
 surrounding as potential settlement areas has increased.   Agricultural activities within floating gardens and reclaimed land
 have also contributed to the pollution of the lake. A serious issue of contention is that islands have been formed and
 residences built on them, when the title to the water surface in fact restricts the use to water only.  Similarly some areas
 have been converted into solid horticulture land.  Despite increased vigilance on the part of the authorities and restrictive
 legislation and ordinances, a small number of people are continuing to develop and extend their illegal encroachments.
11.       Apart from 250 houseboats a number of villages have come up in the floating gardens i.e Tang Bagh and Chowdri
 Bagh. Treated water is available only in some areas at present.  Most of the houseboats use the lake water, which is elevated
 into a bolding tank in the roof with a hand pump.  Sewage and sullage waste is discharged directly into the lake.   Solid
 wastes such as vegetable scraps and paper are dumped into the lake.  Toilets used by the local residents have been
 constructed over water.  The Dal Lake receives pollutants from these point sources as well as non-point or diffuse sources. 
 The point sources include (i) sewage and other human wastes from the houseboats and residential huts within the lake area
 (ii) sewage outfalls from the adjoining settlements including some tourist spots. The non-point source, which cannot be
 exactly pinpointed, includes the run-off from agriculture fields and erosion from the catchment area.
POINT- SOURCES
12.       Continuing pressure of human settlements along the shores and within the lake itself could be singularly identified as
 one of the major causes of pollution in respect of organic load.  Over the years, a number of settlements have come up in the
 floating gardens from Tang Bagh to Chowdri Bagh.  It has been estimated that about 10,500 people live within the house
 boat area and almost the same number of people live outside this area on islands, boats etc.   The total population living
 within the other catchments of the Dal Lake is about Rs.2.5 lakhs.  As per the records of the State Town and Country
 Planning Department, there has been an increase of 25,040 people within the catchment area during 1971-77 (the population
 increased from 1,66,040 to 1,91,000) and since then about 50,000 persons have been added to this area over the passage of
 time.
13.       There are several hundreds of houseboats in the area adjacent to Boulevard Road from Dal Gate to Kotal Khana. It is
 said that houseboats represent a long tradition and basic infrastructure of tourism. The number of houseboats has
 considerably increased in recent years without significant improvement in commensurate facilities of sanitary waste
 disposal.  As a result, sewage, human wastes and sullage waste including solid wastes are directly discharged into the lake. 
NON-POINT SOURCES
14.       Run-off from the agricultural fields and erosion of hillsides in the catchment area are the major non-point sources of
 pollution causing silting and loading of nutrients. It has been mentioned in the proceeding pages that the catchment area of
 the lake can be broadly sub-divided into five sections viz. (i) Dachigam-Telbal area (ii) Lake Hill side (iii) Srinagar North,
 (iv) Srinagar City and (v) littoral area of the Dal Lake.  Among  these, Dachigam is the largest in area (145 X  10
6 m2) and it
 comprises mainly   Dachigam Game Reserve and south facing slopes with Telbal area at its foothills. Dachigam Game
 Reserve has a reasonably good forest and ground cover but its south facing slopes have been denuded due to overgrazing
 and fire.  It has resulted in increasing movement of silt to Dachigam Nalla, which drains this catchment area.  A major
 portion of the flow from this catchment area is diverted to the Harwan Reservoir and the water treatment plant at Harwan. 
 However, considerable quantities of flow laden with silt and nutrients are also led through the Telbal Nalla into the Dal
 Lake.  The gentle sloping lower reaches of the Telbal area are extensively used for paddy cultivation and as such the run-
off-from these fields significantly contribute to the concentration of soluble phosphorus.
15.       The ‘Lake Hillside’ catchment drains into the Dal Lake through a number of small streams in the east and south sides
 of the lake.  Around the lake shore, the land slopes of this catchment have been utilized for paddy cultivation, orchards and
 gardens.  Beyond this, there is steep gradient in land slope about 1000 m above the lake level, which is heavily grazed and
 denuded.
16.       The  ‘Srinagar North’ comprises mainly outer suburbs of Srinagar city that is extensively used for paddy cultivation.  
 The topography is very flat and it drains through slow flowing canals and open drains which, in parts, are grossly polluted
 with sewage and rubbish.

17.       The ‘Srinagar City’ sub-catchment is highly urbanized and in most areas it drains through Brari-Nambal, a large
 swampy area that is also polluted with sewage and rubbish.
18.       The Lake itself forms the ‘Dal Lake’ sub-catchment and it includes floating gardens, marshes and land areas within
 the lake.  This sub-catchment is being extensively utilised for cultivation of vegetables etc.   In fact, the vegetables in the
 Srinagar City are mostly provided from the area.
LOADING OF POLLUTANTS
19.       Dr. C.L. Trisal who obtained his doctorate from Kashmir University on “Dal Lake”, has stated that the problem of
 pollution is mainly due to the addition of nutrients particularly phosphorus and nitrogen at an accelerated rate.   These
 nutrients have been chiefly responsible for recurrence of dense macrophytic growth and deterioration of water quality.  
 "Eutrophication", is a scientific process in which the lake changes colour due to the blossoming of an algae called
 Euglenineae, which only happens when the lake is sufficiently rich in organophosphates i.e nitrates, phosphates, and
 potassium found in raw sewage and agricultural effluents. As the water becomes overloaded with nutrients, the algae
 spreads and oxygen levels falls consequently resulting in the death of plant and animal life. Man-made eutrophication as
 opposed to natural eutrophication is linked to the addition of major plant nutrients viz. phosphorus and nitrogen derived
 from human wastes, detergents, fertilizers, agricultural activities, etc. which thrives as a result of the floating population on
 the lake.
20.       According to a research study, carried out by ENEX- a group of consultants from New Zealand who prepared a report
 for the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Cooperation in 1978, among the non-point sources, the Dachigam Telbal
 subcatchment contributes significant amount of nutrient input to the lake  (5.3 tonnes P/year and 228 tonnes N/year) and a
 comparison of the nutrient input from both point and non-point sources reveals that Srinagar city and Dachingam-Telbal
 sub-catchments are mainly responsible for heavy load of nutrients going into to the lake system.
21.       Prof. (Dr.) Helmut Kroiss of the Vienna University of Technology submitted a report entitled Dal Lake Conservation
 Project in 1998’, in which he has also observed that “Dal Lake: The beauty of Kashmir is in a critical state since waste
 water, solid waste and fertilizer discharge to the lake have caused increased eutrophication with excessive growth of weed
 and algae in most of the areas”.
22.       However, the picture is slightly different when nutrient outflow pattern of the Lake is taken into consideration.   The
 two principal outflows that carry water out of the Dal Lake are Amir Khan Nalla    and the Dal Gate.  The Amir Khan Nalla
 carries water from the southern end of the lake into the River Jhelum.  Together, these represent an average outflow of
 47.3x  106  m3/year. It has been calculated that these outflows carry 1.7 tonnes of phosphorus and 42.4 tonnes of nitrogen
 out of the lake each year.  Besides, the nutrient inputs from Srinagar North are directly discharged through the Dal Gate and
 Nalla Amir Khan and as such do not enter the Dal Lake.  Thus, Dachigam-Telbal area, and the houseboat area of Dal Lake,
 are chiefly responsible from nutrient loading into the Lake.
23.       Based on the data collected for preparation of a report for the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Cooperation by
 ENEX of New Zealand Inc., the nutrient balance of the lake indicates that there is a net positive inflow of 15.5 tonnes of
 phosphate and 322 tonnes of nitrogen per year. The total outflow of nutrients from the lake ecosystem has been estimated to
 be 10 tonnes of phosphorus and 275.6 tonnes of nitrogen per year.  Thus, there is a net build up of 5.5 tonnes of phosphorus
 and 88.9 tonnes of nitrogen annually into the lake. 
24.       The Committee is of firm belief that Conservation of Dal Lake is a national issue.  It forms the axis of life for the
 Kashmir valley and therefore it is not only important from the point of view of ecology, but also from the point of
 augmenting economy of the people and ensuring peace in the region.  The Committee is therefore deeply worried about the
 deterioration of water quality and other associated problems arising out of development of eutrophic conditions, which have
 reduced the environmental, recreational and aesthetic value of this lake. The Committee therefore is strongly of the view
 that in order to formulate a plan of action to control pollution, the principal sources of these nutrients have to be identified
 and the rate of accumulation of these nutrients in the lake basin should be precisely known.
25.       The Committee was informed by the Vice Chairperson of the Jammu and Kashmir Lakes and Waterways
 Development Authority that the threat to the Dal Lake is not only posed by the encroachment problem but also by the silt
 within the nutrients which becomes a land mass over a period of years. 
26.       Hence, the Committee strongly recommends the following of these procedures and suggests acquiring a precise
 knowledge about the rate of accumulation of these nutrients at the lake basin:
·
                                            Removal of excessive bio-mass and diversion of pollutants both from point and non-point sources is
 needed on war footing basis; and
·                                            Outright prevention of dumping of garbage in the lake should be accomplished without any further

 This amount was not routed through the Ministry of Environment & Forests and was released to the State Government

 (2003-2004). In the Committee’s meeting on 24
th July 2003 the Secretary, Ministry of Environment & Forests, Advisor,

29.       The Committee expressed surprise that the Planning Commission did not have any control over the money released
 by it to the State Government to start the basic work and therefore recommends that central assistance must be backed by
