The Report deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Environment & Forests on the Recommendations
 contained in the One Hundred-Eighteenth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Conservation & Environment Management Plan for Dal-Nagin
 Lake, Srinagar which was presented/laid on the Table of both Houses of Parliament on 19 th December, 2003.  The One
 Hundred-Eighteenth Report of the Committee on Dal Lake contains twenty-two recommendations and Action Taken
 notes on each of the Recommendations of the Committee have been received from the Ministry of Environment & Forests
 on 11th November, 2004.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by
 the Ministry of Environment & Forests are set out in the succeeding paras:-
 
LOADING OF POLLUTANTS
 
Recommendations
The Committee is of firm belief that Conservation of Dal Lake is a national issue. It forms the axis of life for the
 Kashmir valley, and therefore, it is not only important from the point of view of ecology, but also from the point of
 augmenting economy of the people and ensuring peace in the region. The Committee is therefore deeply worried about
 the deterioration of water quality and other associated problems arising out of development of eutrophic conditions, which
 have reduced the environmental, recreational and aesthetic value of this lake. The Committee therefore is strongly of the
 view that in order to formulate a plan of action to control pollution, the principal sources of these nutrients have to be
 identified and the rate of accumulation of these nutrients in the lake basin should be precisely
 known.                                                    (Para 24)
 
Action taken by the Ministry
The principal sources of nutrient inflow to the lake have been identified and the nutrient budget for the lake has
 been worked out in the Detailed Project Report (DPR) for Dal Lake Conservation Project (DLCP) prepared through M/s
 Alternate Hydro Energy Centre (AHEC), IIT, Roorkee. Dal Lake has been found to be receiving large quantity of nitrogen
 and phosphorous from point sources i.e. incoming nallah - (Telbal Bota Khul) and sewage drains as well as from non
 point sources like seepage and diffused run off. Fifteen drains along lake shore carrying significant quantity of sewage
 form major point source of nutrient ingress. The effect of nutrient contribution from a large population living on hamlets
 within the lake, houseboats and doonga boats has also been evaluated. According to information provided by the J&K
 Lakes and Waterways Development Authority, the total phosphorous inflow to the lake is of the order of 111 tonnes from
 all sources where as 220.80 tonnes of NO
3-N and 158.55tonnes of                 NH 4-N(corresponding to a flow of 237.13
 million m3/year-2003) flow to the lake. Similarly 4.50 tonnes of total phosphates and 18.14 tonnes of nitrogen are added
 to the lake from non-point sources.
Comments
            The Committee is distressed to know from the information provided by the J&K Lakes and Waterways
 Development Authority (J&KLWDA) that total phosphates inflow into the lake is of the order of 111 tonnes from all
 sources and 4.50 tonnes of total phosporous and 18.14 tonnes of nitrogen are added to the lake from non-point sources. 
 This apparently reflects the fact that the conservation effort by the Government is not at an advance stage and the quantum
 of discharge of effluents of such a scale is quite deplorable.  The Committee, therefore, feels   unless a meaningful
 comprehensive programme is undertaken to stop the inflow of unwanted effluents into the lake by involving all NGOs and
 other agencies for civil maintenance of the lake, no lake equilibrium can be sustained.  The Committee, therefore, urges
 that immediate action with a suitable action plan must be initiated to preserve the lake.
 
            The Committee would like to suggest the following comprehensive methods, which could be implemented for
 holistic preservation of the lake:
i)
                    It is necessary that water quality of Dal Lake in terms of physico-chemical parametes (pH temperature
 profile, secchis transparency, dissolved oxygen BOD, COD and nutrients), biological profile (density of
 population, biomass and species diversity of phyto, zoo plankton and macrobenthos)  needs to be assessed
 and subsequently monitored on a regular basis.
ii)                   It is necessary that long-term limnological changes also need to be assessed and anticipated with
 meaningful planning.

132nd Report of Committee on Science & Technology
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/132ndreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:32:04]
iii)                 It is extremely necessary to reduce Eutrophic level of the lake.
 
The Committee feels that in addition to the above, the withdrawal of Hypolimnetic water of the Lake by siphoning,
 controlled aeration of hypolimnetic water, bioremediation, biomanipulation and shore line development are also
 necessary.
            The Committee feels if a comprehensive measure including all the above is implemented in a holistic manner, the
 basic objective of achieving the lake equilibrium in future will be possible.
 
Recommendations
The Committee was informed by the Vice Chairperson of the Jammu and Kashmir Lakes and Waterways
 Development Authority that the threat to the Dal Lake is not only posed by the encroachment problem but also by the silt
 within the nutrients which becomes a land mass over a period of years.
 Hence, the Committee strongly recommends the following of these procedures and suggests acquiring a precise
 knowledge about the rate of accumulation of these nutrients at the lake basin:
•  Removal of excessive bio-mass and diversion of pollutants both from point and non-point sources is needed on
 war footing basis; and
            •  Outright prevention of dumping of garbage in the lake should be accomplished without any further delay by
 effectively managing the solid waste.                        (Para 25 & 26)
Action Taken by the Ministry
From 1997-98 onwards, the Planning Commission has provided Rs. 102.42 crore to J&K Government as
 Additional Central Assistance (ACA) for conservation of Dal Lake, against which an expenditure of Rs. 88.97 crore has
 been reported by the J&K Lakes & Waterways Development Authority on various activities as per the break-up given in
 Annexure-I. As can be seen, the activities on which expenditure has been incurred by the J&K Lakes and Waterways
 Development Authority includes the measures recommended by the Committee above.
In continuation to the activities being implemented by the J&K Government from the ACA provided by the
 Planning Commission, the DPR for the Dal Lake Conservation Project has been prepared. The project was earlier being
 processed by the Government on 70:30 cost sharing basis between the Central and the State Government, the current
 funding pattem for National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) and National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP). However,
 on receipt of the recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee for 100% central funding for the project as a
 special case, the matter was taken up again with the Planning Commission. The matter was constantly pursued with them,
 as a result of which their 'in principle' approval for taking up the Dal Lake Conservation Project on 100% funding by
 Government of India was subsequently received. The draft EFC Memo for the project has since been circulated on
 29.9.2004 to all concerned ministries and the Planning Commission for their comments. On receipt of the comments, the
 project shall be put up to EFC for consideration. Since the cost of the project is more than Rs.100 crore, the case will be
 put up to the CCEA for final approval after is it cleared by the EFC.
The rate of accumulation of nutrients to the Dal Lake has been evaluated and reported in the DPR for the Dal Lake
 Conservation Project, which also provides for removal of excessive biomass and diversion of pollutants both from point
 and non point sources as well as prevention of dumping of garbage in the lake through solid waste management.
For removal of excessive biomass, yearly activity in two operationsi.e. spring and autumn is being conducted for
 selective manual de-weeding, mechanical harvesting and skimming of floating weed since the inception of J&K Lakes &
 Waterways Development Authority in 1997. The J&K Lakes and Waterways Development Authority has informed that
 selective manual and mechanical de-weeding of the lake has removed about 1,40,000 m
3 of wet weed consequently
 reducing the nutrient i.e. nitrogen by 109.30 tonnes and phosphorous by 11.40 tonnes on cumulative basis since 1997. The
 activity shall also be continued on approval of the DPR for the Dal Lake Conservation Project during the project
 implementation period of five years.
The solid waste management activity is presently being carried out through NGOs namely 'Green Kashmir' and
 ‘HOPE’, which are servicing 9600 structures, including houseboats, within the lake and its peripherals. The solid waste so
 collected on daily basis is brought to pre-identified dumping spots, wherefrom it is carried by Srinagar Municipal
 Corporation to its landfill site at Achan, Eidgah. The solid waste management programme is also envisaged in theDPR
 prepared for the project.
 
Comments
The Committee notes the action taken by J&K Lake and Waterways Development Authority.  However, the
 implementation measures as per its opinion for the removal of biomass and measures to prevent dumping of garbage in

132nd Report of Committee on Science & Technology
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/132ndreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:32:04]
 the lake fails to explain logically the presence of the high level of organic pollutants in the lake.  The Committee,
 therefore, feels that besides in-situ conservation, the J&KLWDA should take comprehensive measures so that the
 quantum of discharge of organic pollutants into the lake could be minimized if an ideal place for dumping of wastes is
 earmarked combined with prevention of accidental spillage by identifying environment friendly appropriate disposal
 methods for wastes and effective monitoring mechanism which may be assessed and monitored strictly on quarterly basis.
 
Recommendations
The Committee expressed surprise that the Planning Commission did not have any control over the money released
 by it to the State Government to start the basic work and, therefore, recommends that central assistance must be backed by
 regular monitoring.     (Para 29)
 
Action Taken by the Ministry
The Ministry is regularly monitoring the projects for which funds are provided under the NRCP and NLCP.
 Similarly, regular monitoring will be carried out for the Dal Lake Conservation Project also after it is approved by the
 Government. As recommended by the Parliamentary Standing Committee, a Monitoring Committee, which also includes
 two experts, would also  be set up after the project is approved.
 
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and recommends that an effective monitoring committee must be ensured to be set
 up at  state level by introducing a two-tier mechanism for strict monitoring of Dal Lake Management Plan in
 collaboration  with the Central Government so that the Committee can function with the single objective of preserving Dal
 Lake from the clutches of pollution.
 
Recommendations
The Committee while examining the National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) of the Ministry of Environment &
 Forests observed that the NLCP was initiated in 1994 for cleaning important urban lakes infested with high levels of
 silting and pollution. Initially, ten lakes were identified for cleaning etc.- Ooty Kodaikkanal, Powai, Dal, Sukhana, Sagar,
 Nainital, Udaipur, Rabindra Sagar and Hussain Sagar. However, work has started only in one Lake and project reports for
 three lakes namely Ooty, Powai and Kodaikanal have been prepared and approved till date. The progress regarding other
 lakes is extremely slow because of persistent delays in the finalization of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), tendering
 procedures and award of contracts.
(Para 30)
Action Taken by the Ministry
The National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) was conceptualized in 1994 and posed for approval of Government
 of India (CCEA) in December, 1997. However, only an 'in-principle' approval was accorded for Dal Lake Conservation
 Project while for other lakes, the Ministry was asked to seek external assistance. Since no, external agency evinced any
 interest in NLCP, the NLCP was finally initiated from June, 2001 after seeking waiver from CCEA. Since then the
 programme has gathered pace. Conservation Plans for 28 lakes have since been approved at a total estimated cost of about
 Rs. 145.60 crore. Out of these, works in respect of 3 lakes have been completed and others are in various stages of
 implementation. A Statement giving the details of the various projects approved under NLCP till date is enclosed as
 Annexure-II.
The Ministry had also instituted a study to National Institute of Ecology for identification of lakes for conservation
 under NLCP. The report of this study has been sent to all State Governments for prioritization of lakes in their State for
 inclusion of these under NLCP. This shall also enable the resource allocation for future projects under NLCP.
 
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.  However the better management of the lakes in the country could be achieved by
 involving strategic integrated management action plans.  The guidelines issued by the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests in this regard are a good beginning.  However, the Committee feels that the  same need to be pursued vigorously
 to ensure their effective implementation.
            As per the opinion of the Committee, the first step is to survey all water bodies with a view to categories them on
 the basis of their problems being faced by each of them, region-wise for enabling a critical analysis/assessment of the
 environmental impact on these water bodies and restoration works should be designed on the basis of the findings of such
 environmental impact audit.  The survey should cover Post Project Evaluation and Hydrological studies of the lakes.  The
 next step is to initiate action on Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) with specific emphasis on lakes
 reservoirs at the basin or sub-basin levels.  The Lake Management should be a subset of IWRM at the basin level. 

132nd Report of Committee on Science & Technology
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/132ndreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:32:04]
 Permanent solution depends on institutional restructuring for effective governance.  The components, which the
 Committee feels needs to be addressed, are :
a)                  Enabling effective environmental management; and
b)                  Institutional reframing
The Enabling Environmental Management:  To deal with the problems of lakes and reservoirs and their
 restorations, the existing Acts, legislations and legal framework need to be integrated suitably to give it the  form
 of holistic single legislation appended with new amended legislation, if any.  There is need for a continued
 assessment of water quality and land use in catchments areas of lakes and reservoirs etc.  The national and state
 level policy in respect of water and environmental management too requires integration into one unit. Standards
 for the lake and reservoir management have to be framed in a functional manner so that by implementing the same
 with a meaningful objective for outright preservation of the water bodies which could be achieved.
The Institutional Reframing: The institutional reframing is the most important step towards the sustainable
 management of the lakes.  Their functions and responsibilities have been widely discussed.  They can be made to
 have specific emphasis on functional management of lakes and wetlands if an effective assessment of functions
 and responsibilities, which have been widely discussed, are given a meaningful shape for implementation.
            The Committee is of the view that as Dal Lake has a unique position in terms of high influx of tourist, thereby
 disturbing the biodiversity of flora and fauna, which thrive on Dal Lake; it is necessary to frame an environmental friendly
 tourist policy with a view to reducing the quantum of pollution level on this water body.  Therefore, the Committee is of
 the view that Dal Lake cleaning and management should be taken up on priority basis by the State Government jointly
 with the Central assistance.
 
MEASURES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF THE LAKE
 
Recommendations
     The Committee understands that the lake has reached a critical stage as the nutrients are deposited in the
 sediments, rather than in the lake water. Since macrophytes have an adaptive advantage to derive nutrients from lake
 sediments, the recurring growth of these weeds is obvious in the lake ecosystem. The macrophytes provide a biological
 sink to the nutrients, and thus, play a very important role in suppressing the plankton population. Continual expansion of
 macrophytes, have accelerated the process of eutrophication, as they have the capacity to translocate nutrients from the
 sediments into water thereby increasing nutrients available to the plankton and floating plants such as "Sylvinia-Lemna"
 complex. With the subsequent release of nutrients from sediments, growth of plankton will be accelerated. In conjunction
 with floating plants, such growth might cause anaerobic conditions which would make the lake unsuitable as a source of
 drinking water.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that any management programme  to be adopted for the conservation of
 the lake ecosystem should primarily aim at minimizing the inflow of nutrients into the lake. Some of the measures which
 the Committee strongly feels would be helpful in diversion of pollution and would reduce the inflow of pollutants to a
 great extent are:
(a)
                An extensive reafforestation programme is a must in the Dachigam-Telbal catchment area so as to
 minimize soil erosion from the area. Suitable steps are also needed for control of grazing on the steep
 slopes;
(b)
               To monitor the operation of the Telbal Nalla basin to find out the deposit of sediments;
(c)                To construct a settling basin prior to the entry of Telbal Nalla into the Dal lake, which will help to settle
 out the bulk of the sediment load and insoluble nutrients;
(d)               Construction of sewer system to carry the wastewater to the ring sewerage system and finally to the
 treatment plant has to be accorded priority;
(e)                 Forthwith stoppage of encroachment by hamlets and floating gardens through carefully woven ‘action
 plan’; and
(f)                 Immediate arrests of deforestation, quarrying, increased land use for unabated urbanization.                  
                                                              (Para 37& 38)
 
Action Taken  by the Ministry
Minimization of inflow of nutrients into the lake is one of the most important components of the  DPR prepared for
 the Dal Lake Conservation Project.
(i)                  The extensive re-afforestation programme in Dachigam-Telbal catchment so as to minimize soil erosion
 from the area and steps for controlling of grazing on steep slopes has been envisaged in the DPR under its

 treatment is being separately prepared by the State Government for submission to Government of India.
(ii)                The operation of the settling basin at Telbal Nalla is being constantly monitored by J&K Lakes and

Comments
The Committee appreciates the measures adopted by the J&K LAWDA in initiating steps towards construction of
 sewerage treatment plants on priority basis. It would also like to impress upon that appropriate ‘precautionary measures’
 should also be adopted to reduce soil erosion at the catchment area of the lake and the lake benthos which could be
 minimised by applying appropriate disposal methods of earth resources for preserving the natural landscape of this water
 body.  Application of ‘Fluidized Aerobic Bed technology’ for sewerage treatment is an ideal method and possibilities
 could be explored for using the treated effluent for use in small Hydropower Station with electricity generating capacity of
 150 KW.
 
Recommendations
The Committee is strongly of the view that provision of proper sewage disposal facilities will reduce the organic
 loading in the lake to a great extent. The Committee, therefore, recommends, that it is necessary to look into the
 possibilities such as a common sewerage system for a cluster of house boats, sanitary systems in individual units and
 devices for removal of the wastes in containers. The Committee notes with satisfaction that some NGOs are engaged in
 collecting the solid waste on a day-to-day basis from inside the lake. It will also be desirable to rearrange the mooring
 areas of the house boats so as to have them in an orderly manner instead of being located in an unplanned and random
 manner, as these are now. It will help in ensuring common service facilities including sewage disposal
 systems.                                      (Para 39)                                              
Action Taken by the Ministry
The DPR for the Dal Lake Conservation Project, besides the peripheral scheme of J&K UEED envisages six STPs
 all around the Iake with its appurtenant sewerage system. Work on three of the STPs has already been initiated as reported
 in the para above. The J&K Government has made it mandatory for the houseboats and doonga boats to have floating
 septic tanks. The supernatant liquidfrom these tanks is envisaged to be carried to low suction under-water sewer on the

132nd Report of Committee on Science & Technology

 lakebed for transmission to a terminal sump, wherefrom the same shall be pumped to STP. This will ensure proper
 management for houseboat sanitation. The houseboats are also required, to be re-aligned to facilitate implementation of
 the scheme with respect to their present mooring sites.
Comments
The Committee is strongly of the view that merely making the installation of floating septic tanks mandatory in all
 house boats in Dal Lake by the J&K Government will not totally ensure a proper management of the lake.  The lack of
 involvement of stakeholders in planning and implementation processes often makes the legislation ineffective.  During
 one of the interactions with the Houseboats Owner’s Association, it has come to light that most of the bio-toilets are non-
functional and agencies were not persistently checking the functioning of these toilets after they are installed.  The
 Committee would, therefore, recommend that the implementing agencies should ensure functional installation of these
 bio-toilets.
 
            The Committee would further like to recommend that efforts should also be made by both Central and State
 Governments to import lightweight portable toilet aided by hundred per cent  biodegradable toilet bag which is 
 compostable.  It is the opinion of the Committee that such toilet is not only environmental friendly but also user friendly.  
 With no need for a septic system, no chemicals, no odour and no hassles, a composting toilet is a great way to encourage
 disposal of human wastes in an environmental friendly manner.  Every living organism consumes nutrients and creates
 waste.  To transform this water back into nutrients, nature uses a process of decomposition and evaporation.  The bio-
toilets are mainly designed with a view to optimize and accelerate these natural processes.  The aerobic breakdown of
 human wastes in a bio-drum is the most advisable technique for preventing the inflow of human wastes into the lake eco-
system.  These bio-toilets, as what the Committee feels, is also suited for winter operation, particularly in a cold region
 like Jammu & Kashmir since it is often easier to keep the bathroom warm.   The Committee, therefore, feels that Rota
 Loo   toilets which is widely used in Australia could also be used on the houseboats in Dal Lake that would be
 environmental friendly.
 
Recommendations
The Committee recommends that following specific measures be adopted for restoring the health of the lake:
(i)
            Selective harvesting of macrophytes, particularly, emergent and submerged at the time of peak growth can
 substantially help removal of nutrients from the lake sediments;
(ii)     Increasing water circulation is also an effective method of diverting nutrients along with out flowing water;
(iii)    Sediment removal, in-situ manipulation of the bottom sediment and manipulation of the biological components in
 the lake ecosystem are among the various other measures which need to be considered for reducing the detrimental
 symptoms of the  eutrophication;
·
        Afforestation of degraded forest land through plantations, contour, hedgerows and in-situ moisture conservation.
·        Fuel, wood and fodder plantation of indigenous exotic species;
·        Drainage line treatment through properly designed structures such as check dams, RCC dropstructures, stone walls,
 trenching, fencing, water tanks and troughs and wetting;
·        Forage production through silvi-pasture development and on farm fodder development;
(iv)       Although the Ministry has apprised the Committee that infestation of the 'Euglena rubra' in the lake water has been
 declining persistently since 1997 thereby extensively thinning the emerging school of red algal bloom, it, however,
 apprehends that any element of complacency in the matter may help the problem to manifest in near future. Hence, as per
 the opinion of the Committee, on going monitoring of algal bloom should be carried on by preventing continuous outfall
 of wastewater, seepage of nutrients from the adjoining areas  along  the  lake shore   resulting in negative redox potential  
 of sediments in the area. The Committee, hence, advises the Ministry atleast to adopt the following temporary measures
 from time to time to check the menace:
(a)        Skimming, agitation of water, removal of scum; and
(b)        Aeration of stagnant pockets with anoxic sediments and oxygen depleted underwater and the construction of ring
 bounds to check ingress of solid waste/organic matter.
(v)        The Committee is happy to note that in pursuance of its recommendation made in its 112
th Report at para 64 of
 page 29, desilting and deepening of the bed of Dal Lake had been done by the State Government along its northern shore.
 Although, the project is still in progress, the Committee, however, feels that general tempo of activities is essentially
 sluggish and hence again suggests for enlisting the assistance of Army Engineering Corps in the matter as was earlier
 recommended by it in its aforesaid report so that the work would be speeded up.          (Para 40)

The Committee would like the Ministry to keep it informed of the progress in the measures taken for restoring the

Recommendations
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Environment & Forests may examine such
 mechanisms/processes developed by 'Clean-Flo Laboratories, Inc.', USA which was started in 1970 and operates with a

The Clean-Flo Laboratories, Inc., USA uses the bio-remediation technology for in-situ cleaning of lakes involving

 agencies of State Government with the help of the Centre should select an appropriate company for implementation of

Comments
The Committee notes the reply.  The Committee is of the view that mere implementation of “polluters pay”

 ‘Precautionary Principle’ which has been accepted as part of the law of the land. The “Precautionary Principle” makes it

Recommendations
The Report of Prof. (Dr.) Helmut. Kroiss, which has been mentioned earlier, observed that "all actions within the
 lake such as deweeding, local aeration and skimming of algae help to fight the symptoms of the degradation process but
 will not be able to restore the desired water quality and sustainable, ecological development for the future". The same
 Kroiss report had also observed, "the actual population of about 50,000 people living in the lake area without proper

 lake to an area outside the lake".                                                                                          (Para 47)
Describing the relocation of the population as "the only economically feasible method to reduce pollution of the
 lake" the report however acknowledged that, "transfer of this population to new housing areas is a complex and sensitive

 recommended "to immediately start this process as each inhabitant leaving this area will reduce the pollution potential".

 Authority is in the process of acquiring land for the balance Rehabilitation Plan.
Comments
The Committee, therefore, urges that measures for irreversible rehabilitation plan should be taken up by the State
 Government without further delay.

NATIONAL MISSION ON BAMBOO APPLICATIONS  
Recommendation 
        Bamboo is an important resource in the Soci o-economic functional cont ext. Apart from its 
traditional uses, it has various new applications as an alternative to rapidly depleting wood resources. To
extend the utilization of bamboo, consideration shoul d be given to promote or upgrade the existing
research and development institutions assisting the small-scale bam boo industries. The Committee feels 
that this mission mode programme should introduce new techniques for utiliz ation of bamboo, which
would promote the use of  bamboo and also generate good em ployment opportunities. The Department
through its institutes should take the new techniques to cooperatives/industries where it can be put to use
for commercialization.(Para 28) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        The National Mission on Bamboo Appl ications (NMBA), forma lly launched on 25 Novembe r
2004, is one of the key initiatives of the Department of Science a nd Technology (DST) for the Tenth
Plan. It is structur ed as a Technology Mission, and impleme nted by the Technology Information,
Forecasting and Assessment Council (TIFAC). 
        Bamboo is a fast growing and woody grass.  Hardy and adaptable, it grows throughout the country.
It is a strong and highly renewable material, and its usage an integral  part of the country’s cultural, 
social and economic traditions. In many parts of the country th e use of bamboo is ubiquitous.
Communities have put the material  to functional yet aesthetic use,  their skills having evolved ove r
centuries. Even today, by far the most important us es of bamboo are in the every day lives of people.
There is dependence, and a corresponding respect fo r the material; people are repositories of knowledge
about bamboo and its usage. 
        In recent years, a range has emerged of products and applications that  use bamboo in newer and
value-added ways. These have been developed thro ugh the application of scie ntific and engineering
skills; many of them bu ild on traditional usage, in the proce ss enlarging and enriching traditional
livelihood patterns. 
        The provision of employment and opportunity has been accorded the highest priority in the agenda
of the Government, and in the National Comm on Minimum Programme (NCMP). One of DST’s 
commitments to the NCMP, the Mission has been ta sked with creating the basis for enlarging the
bamboo sector, and with supporting the efforts of the Government  of India towards augmenting
economic opportunity, income and employment. 
        The core application and thrust areas of the Mission include wood s ubstitutes and composites,
structural and constructi onal applications, bamboo shoots, propa gation and cultivation, machinery and
process technologies, industrial products and energy. 
        The Mission has carried out property testing and assessment of growing stock, and a matching with
end use. Based on this testing and assessment the Mission has provi ded to the Planning Commission a
recommendation for a focus on 15 co mmercially significant species , an objective starting point fo r
action. A series of assessment, doc umentation and knowledge gatheri ng exercises have been taken up.
These include technology and process testing and docum entation preparation of data bases. A range o f
training manuals, designed in user  friendly formats have been co mmissioned. A comprehensive and
annotated bibliography of bamboo li terature will shortly be  issued, to meet the needs as well of the
research community. 
        In the area of wood substitutes and composites, a 60,000m2 per annum capacity plant is being
established with Mission support at Guwahati to manufacture co mposites/flooring boards. Mat based
and glass fibre composites have  been developed, and are ready for commercialisation. Technology
packages are available for bamboo based plywood substitutes, roofing material and panels. 
        The Mission is workin g to develop ran ges of efficient, sturd y and inexpensive toolin g and
Page 5 of 12133rd REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/133rdreport.htm

processing machinery, suited for Indian conditi ons and species, to reduce drudgery, improve
productivity and reduce wastage. At the same time process tec hnologies are being validated, and
converted to techno-economic packages for use by entrepreneurs. Primar y processing equipment,
indigenously developed, and suited to Indian bam boo has been prototyped, test ed and validated. It is
now available from a growing range of manufacturers. 
        The Mission supports a pplication oriented research and deve lopmental activity, utilising bamboo
for constructional applications. It also seeks to also demonstrate the virtues of combining bamboo with a
range of material - locally available and appr opriate, newly developed and non-conventional. The 
Mission supports innovation with  different construction techniques, and sets benchmar ks of quality o f
construction, functionality, strengt h and safety and aesthetics. Mode ls of low cost housing for rural
areas, utilising bamboo and bamboo composite material, have been developed, and demonstrated. 
        Bamboo shoots carry the potential of va lue added economic activity at the entrepreneurial and
community level through cultivation, processing and packaging. Th e Mission has developed technology
packages for bamboo shoot processing at the indus trial scale, and for co mmunity/ village level
enterprise. Two processing units, at Dimapur and Jorhat respecti vely, are being established. The
community level technology package has been demo nstrated at 24 locations , and has received an
overwhelming response. 
        In most application areas there is a re quirement of adequate quantities of quality bamboo the
quality being defined by species, maturity, bamboo characteristics,  harvesting technique and post-
harvest treatment. The Mission has de veloped guidelines for intensive cultivation, intended to achieve
productivity levels of over 20 tonnes per hectare, and for a range of commercially significant species. 
        Good quality plant material and in suffic ient quantity is a necessary condition if a large-scale 
programme of high yielding  plantation is to be taken up. Bamboo seeds are available infrequently, and
at long intervals, and traditional vegetative propagation practices will not suffice to meet the quality and
quantity aspects of such a programme. 
        There have been breakthroughs in the commer cial availability of high quality tissu e cultured plant
material, and, for the first time, an  export order of 50,000 tissue cultured  plants of Bambusa balcooa has
been received, by a NMBA supported unit in Hosur. 
        Gasification of bamboo can produce en ergy and a range of valuable by-products, including 
charcoal and activated carbon. It can reinforce a commitme nt to clean, renewabl e and cheap electricity
and thermal energy. It ca n utilise waste generated by processing ope rations, substitute the use of fossil
fuels, and lower operating costs. This  is particularly suitable for of f-grid and remote locations, and to 
meet captive industry and utility needs. Several gasification units are in the proc ess of being inducted in
the field, with capacities ranging from 5 Kwe to 1 MWe. 
        Working with tiny and small scale entrepre neurs, the Mission is also supporting the establishment
of mechanised units for sliver and stick making, and for a range of  products using whole and woven
bamboo. 
        Multi-disciplinary in its approach, and mult i-dimensional in its range of activities, the National 
Mission on Bamboo Applications is poised to provide a new impetus to the bamboo sector. 
Comments 
        The Committee is satisf ied with the objectives of the missi on and hopes that by the end of Tenth
Five-Year Plan there would be a marked increase in  the use and application of bamboo in the range o f 
products produced in the country.

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM RANGE WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF) 
Recommendation 
        The Committee feels that the de ficit rainfall throw up a new challenge to the scientists fo r

        In order to improve the forecasting system on weather in general and monsoon rainfall in particular,

        The Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the Department of Space on the
recommendations contained in th e One Hundred Twenty-ninth Re port of the Depa rtment-related

        The Committee's recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the
Action Taken by the Department of Space are set out in the succeeding paragraphs:— 
INDIAN LUNAR MISSION - CHANDRAYAAN-1  
Recommendation 
        Although, the Committee is happy with ove r all scientific objectives of the mission programme, it
would also like to add from resear ch perspective, the following few more objectives that should also be
considered and fulfilled by DoS for future lunar explorations:—

           (1)  Distribution and utilisation of the lunar energy resources; 
           (2)  Distribution and utilisation of the lunar mineral resources; 
           (3)  Utilisat ion of the lunar unique environment i.e. high vacuum, no atmospheric activity, no 
global magnetic field, stable geological structure, week gravity, no pollution;
                                                                   (Para 18) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        DoS/ISRO has noted these suggest ions. The overall lunar/planet ary exploration programme is 
being discussed at various levels to chalk out a road map including lunar soft landers, rovers and robotic
sample return missions. These technologies would n eed to be developed to explore possibilities o f
utilising lunar mineral resources and conduct experiments utilising the unique lunar environment. 
Comments 
        The Committee notes the reply and is satisfied wi th the programme chalked out by the Department 
for the Indian lunar mission -CHANDRAYAAN-1. 
Recommendation 
        The Committee further feels that for be tter understanding of the moon’ s resources, environmental 
characteristics and surface topography, the Department may consider the following for further study: - 
           (1)  Detection of three dimensional imaging of lunar surface; 
           (2)  Measurement of three dimensional imaging of lunar surface; 
           (3)  Analysis of lunar structure and topography of shapes, sizes distribution and density of impact
craters on lunar surface; 
           (4)  Study of the ages of the lunar su rface with a special evaluation of  the evolutionary history of
moon and its structure; 
           (5)  Determination of the contents a nd distribution of some basic and key elements on the luna r
surface including Chromium, Manganese, Oxyge n, Potassium, Sodium, Thorium, Uranium
and Rare Earth Elements etc.  in addition to Magnesium, Al uminum, Silicon, Calcium, Iron
and Titanium which the Chandrayaan-1 missi on has already kept fo r chemical mapping on
lunar surface as a part of its objectives by the Department; 
           (6)  A study regarding chemical evolution of moons crust along with its geophysics; 
           (7)  Measurement of thickness of lunar regolith to determine abundance of noble gas on the
satellite including Helium; and 
           (8)  Exploration of the environments of  the moon with a deep study of  irradiation history of the
satellite by obtaining useful data about the high energy part icle flux and low energy ion
around the moon.               (Para 19) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        It is to bring to the ki nd attention of the Committee that several of the sc ience objectives suggested 
above will be fully or partially achieved during the Chandray aan-1 mission. The following are brought 
to the kind attention of the Committ ee with specific reference to the various suggestions made above by
the Committee: 
        Sl. No. 1, 2 and3: The Chandrayaan-1 mission will carry a terrain mapping camera and a lase r 
ranging instrument to achieve these particular obj ectives and will produce a three dimensional map o f
the lunar surface with a spatial resolution (~5 metr e) that is better than  those achieved earlier.
Determination of size distribution of small craters that will be f easible with the improved spatial
resolution is also one of the science objectives of the Chandrayaan-1 mission. 
        Sl. No. 4: The ages of surface matter can be determined by using dati ng technique once these 
samples can be returned to earth. This would re quire lunar landin g and sam ple return missions, which

are to be planned for future. 
        Sl. No. 5: The surface concentration of the elements mentioned incl uding the rare earth elements
are extremely low to allow detection from orbit. Th e high energy X-ray detector (HEX) to be flown in 
Chandrayaan-1 will attempt to ma p Uranium (U) and Thorium (Th) c oncentrations in the lunar pola r
region. 
        Sl. No. 6: There are pos sibilities of modeling the chemical evolution of the l unar crust along with
its geophysics, based on the data to  be obtained by Chandrayaan-1 missi on. This mission is expected to 
provide for the first time data for both Iron (F e) and Magnesium (Mg) from the low-energy X-ray 
spectrometer payload experiment a nd the Mg/Fe ratio is a crucial parameter in modelling the early
evolution of the moon and formation of lunar crust. The determinati on of both these elements requires
the mission to be flown during higher solar activity period and the Chandrayaan-1 mission is planned for 
such a period (2007-2009). 
        Sl. No. 7: The abundance of Heli um is planned to be measured  by one of the international
experiments selected for Chandr ayaan-1 through announcement of o pportunity. However it would be
difficult to measure the thickness of the lunar regolith from this measurement as it require a lander/rover
mission. 
        Sl. No. 8: Several instruments select ed from among the large numbe r of proposals submitted by
other nations in response to IS RO’s ‘Announcement of Opportunity ’ have been included in the 
Chandrayaan-1 mission. One of the European instruments chosen will specifically measure the energetic
particle flux in the lunar environm ent and fulfil the above objective.  However more detailed particle
energy spectrum may be possible in future missions. 
Comments 
        The Committee hopes that this progr amme would provide a unique  opportunity for frontie r
scientific research and in unders tanding the origin of the moon a nd also lay the foundations for a
manned mission in the future. Besides, this would he lp in expanding its scien tific knowledge about the
moon and upgrade the technological capability.

REMOTE SENSING APPLICATIONS MISSION (RSAM) 
Recommendation 
        Although the Committee is satisfied with  the progress achieved by De partment in IRS technology,
it however feels data generated by IRS technology needs proper interpreta tion in view of recent failure
in accurate prediction of the ad vancement of monsoon in Northern
India.                                                                                                      (Para 47) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        In regard to prediction of monsoon, the Depar tment has been providing  valuable inputs from 
INSAT series of satellites to I ndia Meteorology Department (IMD) towards improving its capability fo r
providing accurate short-term weat her forecasting. The data from Kalp ana and INSAT-3A satellites are 
operationally received by IMD, and along with the numerical models available at the National Centre for
Medium Range Weather Forecasti ng, the data is operationally us ed for weather forecasting. Fo r
example, the 3-level wind information available a nd assimilated effectively in the numerical models
improves the accuracies of  short-term weather forecasting. With the proposed INSAT-3D system with 
imagers and sounders, providing temperature and humidity prof iles, further improvements in
understanding the complex tropical weat her systems should be possible. In addition, the data from IRS
satellites such as Oceansat-1 and the planned Oceansat-2 and Megha-Tropiques provide add-on inputs to 
improve the forecasting capability of IMD. 
Comments 
        The Committee believes that a gr eat deal can be done for the perf ection in use of remote sensing 
data as the recent Tsunami disaster ha s revealed that the remote sensing data is not being utilised to the
optimum level. 
Recommendation 
        The Committee, therefore, is of the str ong opinion that in order to in crease accuracy of IRS data
and also for more realistic interpretation of retrieved data, the DoS needs to the following:— 
           (a)  Integration of GIS, GPS and IRS technology to enhance accuracy of derived data; 
           (b)  Production and distribution of satellite data; 
           (c)  Design of different data base by taking the help of the latest technology; 
           (d)  Processing of remote sensing data  using functional approach towards difficulties being faced
by Department for accurate interpretation of the data retrieved; 
           (e)  Carrying out constant latest re search on remote sensing tec hnology facilities and equipment
including sensors and ground stations; 
           (f)   Updating of technology at par with world standards; 
           (g)  Promotion of remote sensing appl ications in co-ordination wi th universities and research 
centres; 
           (h) Holding adequate training c ourses for advanced handli ng of data generation and
interpretation; 
           (i)   On the job training of DoS personnel to considerably enhance their scientific capabilities; 
           (j)   Co-operation and co-ordinati on with international society relating to space science and 
remote sensing technologies;

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR CELL SCIENCE (NCCS), PUNE 
Recommendation 
         The Committee is of the view that the Centre should give more emphasis on stem cell research 
through development of specific lines from human a nd animal tissues such as tumours, lymphoblast
cells for patients with genetic disorders. Besi des, the Committee hopes that  the Centre should make
efforts to identify factors influe ncing the lineage specification of stem cells into neurons, cardiac &
pancreatic islets and study their tran s differential potential which can bring further improvement in this
area of research. 
(Para 19)
   Action Taken by the Department 
NCCS has been engaged in stem cell research for the last couple of years. They are utilizing stem
cells derived from all possible sources; eg., embryonic stem (E S) cells, cord blood and adult stem cells.
Methods have been standardized for successful cr yo-preservation of adult st em cells. Some of the 
highlights of the work are as follows:   
The Centre has successfully differentiated the murine ES cells into both neural and non-neural lineages. 
The ES cell generated dopaminergic neurons do s ecrete dopamine and henc e physiologically active.
Efforts are underway to enrich this population and explore their therapeutic potential by transplanting
into parkinsonian animal models.  
The centre has developed one of the human embr yonic stem cell lines su ccessfully. The detailed
characterization of the same is underway.   
Studies are being carried out for differentiati on into Beta-cell lineage for insulin production an
d 
increasing the Beta cell mass for transplantation.   
The Centre has developed two cell-lines in different stages of transformation from brain tumors with
neural stem cell features refered to as HNGC-1 and HNGC-2.    
The Centre has developed 19 cancer cell-lines from  various tumors of neuroectodermal origin an d
characterized them extensively. 
Comments 
             The Committee notes with satisf action the steps taken by the Nati onal Centre for Cell Science
(NCCS) in the area of stem cell research.  
  
Recommendation 
The Committee is aware of the f act that researches in Embr yonic Stem cell involve a lot o f
hindrances due to infant stage of de velopment of knowledge in  this field.  However,  this infant stage o f
research in fact urges the Comm ittee to strongly recommend that  Department of Biotechnology should
initiate Comprehensive Research Programme to bri ng up coming development in this sphere at par with
the international standard and ex plore for a more wider a pplication of embr yonic stem cell research so

that some concrete achievement could be made in critical areas.  The Committee feels that in
order to move ahead in the field, the DBT needs to  work on both embryonic stem cell and adult derived
stem cell for more functional applications in the field of Biotechnology.  
            The Committee has been given to unders tand that Researches in the field of Tissue Engineering
will deliver new medica l techniques and devices,  including small blood vess el replacement, bone,
tendon, ligament and cartilage repair, healing of skin wounds and advan ces in nerve re-generation.  It 
will also lead to cellular based therapies for de-g enerative problems in muscles for cardiac regeneration 
in the heart and in treating de-generative conditions in the brain.  In view of this, the Committee strongly
recommends for the in-depth research in the field.                                                                           
          (Para 20)                                               
 
Action Taken by the Department 
Department of Biotechnology has laid  major thrust in the area of stem cell research.  A separate
Task Force has been set by the Department to expand this area and to deal with the programmes on stem
cells.  The Department has also identified priority areas of resear ch both for embryonic and adult stem
cells based on the inputs / suggestions received from the experts and detailed discussion held during the
Task Force. These areas have been mainly categorized into Basic research, Applied research, Human 
Resource Development  and Facility.  In order to explore wider applications of stem cell research, efforts 
are being made to form city based clusters in the country for stem cell research by involving basic
researchers and clinicians.  In addition, the Depa rtment has also supported a number of programmes on
hematopoitic, limbal, liver and neural stem cells and to establish stem cell lines. 
The Department has organise d a brainstorming session on bi oengineering to  discuss the 
identified key areas i.e. tissue engineering and stem cells; biomat erials for drug delivery; biomedical
instrumentation and biosensors by i nviting scientists, clinicians and industry representatives. It has been
felt that the involvement of clinic ians and industry at appropriate stag e is equally important as they are
the end users of the developed products. The issues  like developing linkage s among the institutes fo r
research in these areas; mechanisms for nati onal / international netw orking; Human Resource
Development (HRD); R&D programme s; infrastructure st rengthening etc. were discussed during the
brainstorming. The action will be initiated as per the recomme ndation of the brainstorming on
bioengineering.   
  
Comments 
            The Committee commends the effort s of the Department on the se tting up of a separate tas k
force to focus on the area of stem cell research. The Committee is also awar e that Tissue Engineering
has a lot of potential in transp lantation and reconstruction of Hu man tissues and organs; which are
considered to be among the most expensive therap ies, costing huge amounts of  money. The availability
of off-the-shelf tissues and organs  would mean a substantial saving s, being less expensive than donor 
organs and would allow physicians to  begin treatment before patients are critically ill.  The Committee
therefore recommends that the Department should focus on such critical areas.

Recommendation

Action Taken by the Department 
As recommended by the Parliamentary Standing Committee, the National Brain Research Centre
(NBRC) Gurgaon has already initiate d major projects in the areas of computational neuroscience,
system and cognitive neuroscience, stem cell res earch, developmental neur obiology and basic research
towards understanding of neurologica l and psychiatric disorders. Besi des, it is planned to focus on
modern imaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission
tomography, optical imaging for noninvasive methods for understanding brain functions in human etc.   
  
Comments 
            The Committee is aware that mo st Functional Magnetic Resona nce Imaging (FMRI) techniques
are noninvasive and do not involve the injection of radioactive materials so that a person can be imaged
repeatedly. This may allow imaging of a patient repeatedly through different disease states o r
developmental changes (ie. learning, cognitive stages of deve lopment, stages of grief recovery). It also
allows for investigations in healthy children due to the low risk. Thus, the technique may be of immense
use in understanding how a given individual’s brain functions and perhaps, in the future, making 
psychiatric diagnoses and treatment  recommendations. Perhaps the most  important clinical utility o f
FMRI for the future is that it involves only some  upgrading of conventional MRI machines and, thus,
may become widely availa ble. Similar advantages are also seen  with noninvasive techniques, such as
positron emission tomography and optical imaging. 
The Committee therefore strongl y recommends that the plan regarding focus on the modern
imaging techniques such as functional magnetic re sonance imaging, positron emission tomography and
optical imaging should be finalized and started at the earliest.

IISc., Bangalore, (v) MKU, Madurai and (v) Bose Institute, Kolkata. The Department is also considering
establishment of a world class Institute on Bioinformatics with state-of-art facility for promoting human 
resource development and R&D. In addition to th is, the Department is providing necessary support
towards augmentation of infrastruct ure facilities of the BTIS net cen tres to cope up with the enhanced
activities in bioinformatics. 
  
Comments 
The Committee notes wi th concern that onl y five centres of excel lence have been set u p in the
Page 8 of 17135th Report of Committee on S & T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/135threport.htm

country to focus on Research and Development in bioinformatics and high end human Resource
Development. The Committee is awar e that bioinformatics, which is a new branch, tries to make sense
of the colossal amount of data on ge netics and extract useful data from  it for the benefit of researchers.
The Committee therefore recommends that more such world-class centres of excellence should be set up 
in the country to focus on Research  and Development in bioinformati cs and the establishment of the
planned institute on bioinformatics should be expedited. 
BIOTECH FACILITIES, CENTRE OF EXCELLENCE AND PROGRAMME SUPPORT 
Recommendation 
The Committee hopes that the acti vities of International Depos itory Authority (IDA) should be
broadened. Besides, efforts should be made to augm ent the network programme in microbial diversity;
an international training programme should also be conducted in order to expose our scientists to the
advances on microbial research world over.     (Para 40)                                                                               
Action Taken by the Department 
The infrastructure at IDA has been upgraded by creating facility for supply of liquid nitrogen and
preservation in a separate building and a security system has also been installe d. A separate cold room
with facility for proper storage of  freeze dried culture has also been  established. Ever y year 5-6 M.Sc. 
students from different parts of India undergo training for eight w eeks in microbial taxonomy including
molecular approach at Intern ational Depository Au thority, Institute of  Microbial Technology
(IMTECH), Chandigarh. They have organized two workshops on “Fungal Taxonomy: Classical and 
Molecular Approaches” and “B asic Microbial Taxonomy” duri ng March 3-19, 2004 and June 9-18, 
2004, respectively. One workshop on “M olecular Ecology of Biodegradat ion” has been scheduled fo r 
December 6-17, 2004 in association with ASM, USA.  
The Department, augmented a pr ogramme in ‘Microbial Divers ity’ in 1998, by constituting an 
“Expert Committee”. The endeavour was to isolate,  characterize, index, cla ssify and preserve the
microbial germ plasm from  various ecological niches includi ng extremophilic. N ovel bacterial and
fungal species have been explored  from marine area;  Himalayan belt; arid z ones; psychrophilic zones;
hot springs and oil spills, by various investigators executing this programme. These have been deposited
in “Microbial Type Culture Collection” at IMTECH, Chandigarh. 
  
Comments 
            The Committee expresses satisfaction at the fact that the infrastructure at the International
Depository Authority has been upgrad ed and post-graduate students from  various parts of the country 
are undergoing training at the centre. The Committ ee hopes that more and more students would be
encouraged to receive training and pursue research in high technology areas. 
CROP BIOTECHNOLOGY 
Recommendation 
            The Committee notes with satisf action the advances made in the area of genomics and gene 
sequencing. Further it hopes that efforts should be taken on programme on functional genomics o f
various crops. A multi-institutional programme on development of crops resistant to viral disease should 
be considered.                                                    (Para 42)      
  
Action Taken by the Department 
Different ongoing research  projects under Functi onal Genomics in the area of nutritional and
stress genomics, cell signalling, light  signalling, developmental genetics and fruit ripening in crops e.g.,
potato, tomato, rice, chick pea, lathyrus, Arabidopsis, pea and catharanthus are continuin g. Apart from
Page 9 of 17135th Report of Committee on S & T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/135threport.htm

sequencing of several genes, large number of EST sequences  in Chickpea (about 3000) and
catharanthus (about 500) has been  done. Under the Plan t Biotechnology area, programmes have been
supported on development of horticu lture and plantation crops resistan t to viral diseases. A special
initiative on Solanaceae Genome Sequencing is to be launched shortl y under which a major emphasis is
on development of Tomatoes resist ant to viral diseases. The other crops being studi ed are banana,
capsicum and floricultural species. 
Comments 
            The Committee feels that a large portion of the ag ricultural produce is lost  due to viral diseases 
in the crops throughout the countr y. Though the Department has initia ted programmes to produce some
crops resistant to viral diseases, the Committee feel s that the area of research  needs to be expanded to
include a variety of other crops as well. Further the result of such resear ch should reach the farmers
across the country, so that they can avoid their crop losses. 
  
Recommendation 
            Our country has been facing a serious drought condition, which has dr astically reduced the 
production of food as well as comm ercial crops. The Committee is of  the view that the Department
should take initiatives to tackle the problem s of drought by introducing dr ought resistant crops through
the application of functional genomics. 
                                                                                                                                             (Para
43)                                   
  
Action Taken by the Department 
After the successful completion of the Ri ce Genome sequencing of chromosome 11, the
Department has been supporting projects in the area of functional genomics of rice. The main objective
is identification and functional anal ysis of genes related to yield a nd biotic stress tolerance. The
Department has also suppor ted multi-institutional projects on dehydration stress to lerance in rice:
cloning of responsive genes, their promoters and development of transg enics.  The ultimate objective is
to develop plant transformation vect ors for making abiotic stress tolera nt rice. R&D projects in the area
of crop biotechnology are being supported on molecula r analysis of dehydrati on response in certain
crops.  A joint project on developm ent and evaluation of salt and dr ought tolerant transgenic rice is
being considered under the Indo-US collaborative programme in the area of agricultural biotechnology. 
As regards drought resistance, under the biopr ospecting programme a study has been supported
for identifying genes resistant to  drought from plants of the dese rt regions. Express Sequence Tags
(EST) database is being developed under this project. 
  
Comments 
The Committee commends the role of the Department in producing drought resistant rice variety.
However, the Committee feels that the Department should promote research towards developing drought
resistant wheat varieties and other crops. In this regard the advances made  by other countries facing
droughts can also be taken note of .  
The Committee is also aware of the fact that to mi nimize the impact of drought, soil needs to
retain the rainwater and store as much of that water as possible for future plant use. These conditions can
be achieved through management of organic matter, which can increase water storage by 16,000 gallons
per acre-foot for each 1% organic matt er. Organic matter also increases th e soil's ability to take in wate r 
during rainfall, assuring that more water will be stored. When all th ese factors are ta ken together the
severity of drought and the need for irrigation are gr eatly reduced. Keeping this in view, the Committee
hopes that the De partment would examine the feasibilit y of the aforesaid procedure to minimize the
Page 10 of 17135th Report of Committee on S & T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/135threport.htm

impact of drought. 
BIOTECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT 
Recommendation 
            The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department for upliftment of SC/ST 
population and women.  The Committe e feels that Department should publicize their entrepreneurship
programmes so that concerned companies could co me forward for marketi ng their products through
these communities. Further, Biot echnology based projects  should also be strengthened, which may be
helpful in amelioration of ec onomic mission of women, SC/ST and rural population engaged in
agriculture, presently suffering on account of recent decline in  the competitiv eness of Indian
agriculture.                 (Para 47)                                                              
 
Action Taken by the Department 
The Department is making every effort to ensure that there is a market link for the products
generated under the programme for upliftment of SC/ST population, women and rural folk. This is being
done through emphasis on skill devel opment, quality assurance and li nkages to assured markets. In
larger projects, representatives of industry are cons ulted, and the investigators are requested to take up
only such activities for which there is an assured market. 
  
Comments 
            Biotechnology can bear out the knowledge gained by the women and SC/ST population an d
skills arising from their role in food production, trad itional healing practices and management of natural
resources. The new technol ogies can enhance their skills and marketing oppor tunities. Keeping this in
view the Committee feels that sp ecific programmes should be introdu ced for upliftmen t of the women
and SC/ST population.

INCUBATORS, PILOT PROJECTS, BI OTECHNOLOGY PARKS AND BIOTECH
DEVELOPMENT FUND

industrial entrepreneurs. The Committee hopes that the Department should pr ovide need based inputs

facilities such as Biotechnology Incubators, Downst ream Processing Facilities, Pilot Plants; Tissue
Culture Hardening facilities etc. by various States at Biotech Parks, by providing scientific and technical
inputs apart from identifying resource persons. The Department has a pproached the Planning
Commission, as recommended by th e Parliamentary Standing Commit tee for additional grants to
support more project proposals in addition to the two a pproved earlier for Lucknow and H yderabad and

(ICGEB) 
  
Recommendation 
            The Committee hopes that the Cent re continues its research work  in the areas of Hepatitis,

which will help for the devel opment of Biotechnology in ou r
country.                                                                                                              (Para 55) 
 
Action Taken by the Department 
The International Centre for Genetic Engine ering and Biotechnology (ICGEB) is committed to
continue its research work in the areas of Hepatitis, Malaria,  Recombinant Gene Products, Plant

well as development of biopesticides suitable fo r Indian agricultural c onditions. Some of these

“Bioprahar” was commercially launched on 5 th October, 2004 by Shri Kapil Sibal, the Hon’ ble

Government of India.  
  
Comments 
         The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Centre to pursue research in various diseases and  
agricultural sciences and in developing new technologies.

Recommendation 
            The Committee recommends that the Department continues to augment its  efforts to undertake

(TIFAC), Indian Institute of Petroleum (IIP), IPMD   and other like minded in stitutions; and liaison with
the PSUs,  National Research Development Corporation (NRDC), patent attorneys and the patent offices

GREEN COWS 
Recommendation 
            The Committee would like to suggest that a section of research in Biotechnology should 
concentrate on the br eeding of special cows that naturally produce low-fat milk that boost immune 
system which may be termed as ‘g reen cow’ and which are specifi cally engineered to produce less 
methane to help stem global warming.  Green cows generally deliver low fat milk that boosts immune
system, improve lactose utilization and relive diarrhoea.  Recent a dvances in Biotechnology as what the
Committee has been given to understa nd have identified gene for milk  fat synthesis th at may one day
allow scientists to selectively breed cows that naturally produce low fat milk. This will also considerably
improve the efficiency of the m ilk production of the cows. Since th e green cows are environmentally
cleaner cows they produce less signi ficant amount of methane, which is a major contributor to green
house effect, in the atmosphere, second, only to CO 2 which generally contribut es to global warming.  
Green cow can alter cattle diges tion either by removing microorgani sms from their stomachs that
produce methane or by creating mi croorganisms that can produce metabolic products other than
methane.  The Committee also feels that if DBT makes a concentration on such type of  research, the
emphasis on food safety will increas e and by increasing the body’s defen ce mechanism, a great section 
of population could be saved from constant attacks of common incurable diseases.     (Para 59) 
  
Action Taken by the Department 
The concept of the designer cows and green co ws is one among the many promises of genetic 
engineering  and  recombinant  DNA technology. Producing animal products that selectively suits 
human beings with the specific de mand is one of the goal. Depart ment of Biotechnology has already
supported a programme  on developm ent / standardization of  transg enic  technology in  mice model 
and  more than  20 lines of transgen ic  mice  have  been developed.  Efforts are on to  develop  similar 
programme  in cattle keeping in view of the need  of the country . Embryo tr ansfer  technology  is now
well established in catt le, buffalo, goat, camel et c. through the  support of the Department and the
technology  can be  used to  multiply designer/ elit e animal  at a  faster ra te. A major cattle breeding
programme using DNA mark ers and embryo technology is on the anvil. Selective use of creating
knockdown livestock for undesirable traits without affecting the ba se genetic make  up of livestoc k
population is one of the most important thrust area for which programmes are being initiated. 
  
This De partment has also initiated a programme on ex ploration of unconventional rumen
Page 13 of 17135th Report of Committee on S & T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/135threport.htm

microflora from wild ungulates. Its recolonisation in the rumen of domestic livestock has already
been done. A 1200 lit. capacity reactor  has been desi gned for solid state ferm entation and associated
processes for large scale bioconversion of lignocellulose residues to animal feed. Programmes have also
been supported for selection an d improvement of lignin degrad ing microorganism and Genetic
manipulation of microbes for enhanced ligninase expression. Efforts  would be made to develop specific
programme on identifying microorganism or to de velop recombinant microor ganism that can produce
useful  metabolic  products other than methane. 
  
Comments 
            The Committee notes the steps take n by the Depart ment in initiating research in the area o f
producing animal products that selectively suit human needs. The Committee is of the opinion that since
India is basically an agri cultural country with lo t of cattle population and hence milk production, the
concept of ‘green cows’ holds a lot of promise, especially for the ru ral population.  Further, since ‘low 
fat milk’ has a lot of market poten tial, it can prove to be a boon for the agricult ural and cattle rearing
community. The Committee therefore recommends that the de partment should initia te research in the
aforesaid areas at the earliest and spread the know ledge thus gained among th e cattle rearing population
of the country. 
  
BIO-TERRORISM 
Recommendation 
            The Committee recommends that th e Department of Bio- technology should take steps to ensure 
bio-security without hampering le gitimate research or  free flow of inform ation in the field o f 
biotechnology. First, there must be an increased awareness of risk of Bio-Terrorism among scientists 
and scientific leaders.  In order to augment aw areness about security, th e Committee would like to
suggest arrangement of training and accreditation programmes th at would increase considerable
awareness and stimulate better  
communications between scientific  and national security communities .  The Committee feels that any
Bio-security policies must take  a ‘bottom up’ approach  by including direct i nvolvement of working
scientists.  The security provisions should work hand in hand with the progress in biological research.  It
is the categorized opinion of the Committee that the strategies th at block the publication of certain
research materials would deter the fr ee flow of information, impede car eers of scientists in the field o f
bio-technology and discourage new incumbents in entering the field of research in Bio-Technology. 
            The guidelines should, therefore, be developed to allow researchers to publish their work without
providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities
and design full proof action plan to prevent any strategic inform ation leakage relating to Bio-
Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare.  
            Biological weapons pose a strategic threat mirrored by no other form of attack other than nuclear
weapons.  The Committee feels that as there is no simple solution to  bio security, the Department o f
Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.   
                                                                                                               (Para 60) 
                                                                                            
Action Taken by the Department 
The Recommendations of the Co mmittee that the Department  of Biotechnology should take
steps to ensure bio-securit y without ham pering legitimate research and free fl ow of information in the

field of biotechnology have been taken note of and efforts woul d be made to increase the
awareness of risk of bio- terrorism amongst scientists and scientif ic leaders.  The whole issue of bio-
security would be looked into from the viewpoint of bio-safet y, bio-security and information
dissemination and if necessary St andard Operating Procedures w ould be developed. The Department
would set up a small group, which would look into the details of  the recommendations of the
Parliamentary Standing Committee and suggest ways for implementations. 
  
Comments 
            The Committee is of the opinion th at an expert group consisting of eminent scientists and
security experts would be set up at the earliest by the Department to study th e whole gamut of bio-
security keeping in view the security threat posed to the country on account of biological weapons.

Recommendation 
  
         The Committee appreciates the Departme nt for carrying out research  in many frontier areas o f
science and technology.  It is true that science is one of the areas, which can bring leadership and meet
the kind of objectives that India ha s set for itself.  However, the Co mmittee is of the opinion that the
Department should make efforts fo r transfer of technologies to in dustry and also strive for wide r
dissemination of technologies to raise funds from  Industry by having a greater interface between
Industry & R&D laboratories.                                                                                                                
(Para 27) 
  
Action Taken by the Department 
  
The suggestions made by the Committee are well taken. CSIR has been proactive in reaching to
the industry. CSIR is the only orga nization which involves industry fr om early stage of development
with a view to build an organic linkage with the industry. Recognizi ng the diversity of activities and
complexity of marketing R & D outputs, CSIR has adopted and put in place a decentralized approach
for marketing the entire knowledgebase generated at  different locations. The laboratories maintain
database of industry relevant to th eir sphere of activities. The laborat ories also make special efforts to
constantly maintain interactio ns with the industries to di sseminate the knowledgebase through
conventional as well as non-conventional approaches, including the print and electronic media. In each
of the laboratory a dedicated group inter- alia acts as a window for the marketing of the entire
knowledgebase of the laboratory. 
  
Comments 
         To realize the full potential of  the efforts involved in  the research and development in the CSI R 
laboratories, the Committee hopes th at a close contact with the i ndustry may be maintained. The
Committee recommends that a special cell may be set up to coordinate and pool the knowledge gained
in the CSIR laboratories and thereaf ter disseminate it through  direct interactions  with the industry o r
through the print and electronic media.

RESEARCH SCHEMES, SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS 
  
Recommendation 
           The Committee notes with satisf action the efforts made by Depart ment for stimulating interest 
and awareness among students for sc ience. The Committee recommends that the fellowships be given
for basic sciences as fewer student s are showing interest in them. It  is hoped that individual record o f
progress of scholarship  holders is being
maintained.                                                                                                (Para 32) 
Action Taken by the Department 
             CSIR provides fellowships to br ight young men and women in th e form of Junior Research
Fellowship (JRF), Senior Research Fellowship (S RF), SRF (Extended) and Research Associateship to
do research under the expert guida nce of faculty members / scient ists working in universities,
laboratories/institutes in various fields of scie nce and technology.  CSIR conducts CS IR-UGC NET 
Exam for Junior Research Fellowsh ip to do PhD and eligibility for l ectureship in five basic sciences
subject areas viz life, chemi cal, earth, physical and mathemat ical sciences. About 2000 Junio r
Research Fellowships are given each  year. Furthermore, about 450 Se nior Research Fellowships and
100 Research Associateships are provided to me ritorious science student s to do Ph.D and Post
Doctoral Research, respectivel y. Recently, CSIR has introdu ced Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
Fellowship Scheme to identify and nurture budding young scientific talent in  basic sciences from
amongst top 20% of the CSIR-UGC  NET qualified students. Indi vidual record of progress o f
scholarship holders are being maintained & based on progress report, their fellowships are extended /
upgraded. 
Comments 
             The Committee notes that most of the schlorsh ips/fellowships are provided to students at the 
higher level i.e. PhD/ Research levels. The Committee recommends that schlorships/fellowships may
be provided at the entry level i. e. graduation level and may be incr eased for students in Post-graduate 
level to stimulate interest am ong the new generation towards basi c sciences. The Committee also
recommends that the number of fellowships/scholarships should be increased over a period of time.
